When the night of Brahmā had passed and the lotus-born one had awakened,
Viṣṇu, desiring to create living beings, perceived that the earth was submerged by water.
Just as in former ages at the beginnings of the kalpas, Viṣṇu, desiring the auspicious sport in the waters,
assumed the form of a boar and lifted up the earth.
Viṣṇu has the Vedas for his feet, the sacrificial post for his tusks, the sacrifices for his teeth, and the fire-altars for his mouth;
he has fire for his tongue, the *darbha* grass for his hair, the Brahman for his head, and possesses great ascetic power.
The divine one has day and night for his eyes, the Vedas and their auxiliary limbs for his ornaments,
clarified butter for his nose, the sacrificial ladle for his snout, and the sound of the Sāman chants for his great voice.
Viṣṇu 1.05: He consists of righteousness and truth, is glorious, honored by his measured strides and valorous steps;
he has expiation for his great snout, knees of animals, and a vast form.

Viṣṇu 1.06a: He has the Udgātṛ priest for his entrails, the act of oblation for his characteristic mark, and seeds, herbs, and great fruits for his [limbs]. Viṣṇu 1.06c: He has the sacrificial altar for his inner self, the sacred mantras for his buttocks, and Soma for his blood.
Viṣṇu 1.07a: He has the sacrificial mound for his shoulders, the fragrance of the oblation for his scent, and he possesses the momentum of the offerings to gods and ancestors.
Viṣṇu 1.07c: His body was the sacrificial hall, he was radiant, and he was endowed with various initiations.
Viṣṇu 1.08a: Great, with his heart set on sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), consisting of the great mantras of yoga;
Viṣṇu 1.08c: Beautiful with the *upākarma* rite as his lip, adorned with the *pravargya* ceremony as his earrings.
Viṣṇu, whose path is the movement of various meters, who has the secret Upaniṣads as his seat,
and who is accompanied by Chāyā as his wife, has indeed arisen like a mountain of jewels.
The Lord, having entered the single ocean, [beheld] the earth— bounded by the oceans and containing its mountains, forests, and groves—
fallen into the waters of that single ocean.
Having lifted [the earth] with the tip of his tusk out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
the primordial god, the great yogi Viṣṇu, restored the world once again.
Thus, in ancient times, having become the Sacrificial Boar and desiring the welfare of all beings, Viṣṇu raised up the goddess Earth when she had sunk into the netherworld of Rasātala.
Having lifted [the earth] and established it in its own place,
Madhusūdana, having distributed the waters situated therein according to their proper places, remained there.
Viṣṇu 1.14: And those born of the ocean are in the oceans; those born of rivers are in the rivers;
those born of ponds are in the ponds; and those born of lakes are in the lakes.
Viṣṇu created the seven netherworlds (pātālas), as well as the seven worlds (lokas),
and the various locations for the continents (dvīpas) and the oceans.
Viṣṇu 1.16: The guardians of the regions, the guardians of the worlds, the rivers, the mountains, and the trees;
the seven sages who know the Dharma, the Vedas with their auxiliary sciences, and the gods and demons.
Viṣṇu 1.17: Piśācas, uragas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and humans;
cattle, birds, wild animals, and so forth—the fourfold collection of beings;
as well as clouds, rainbows, lightning, and the like, and various kinds of sacrifices.
Thus the Lord Varāha, having created this world with its moving and non-moving beings,
departed for that destination of the worlds which is unknown.
When Janārdana, the god of gods, had departed on an unknown course, the Earth reflected: "What support will there be for me?"
"I shall go to Kaśyapa and ask him; he will tell me without a doubt. For that great sage is constantly occupied with my very same anxiety."
Having thus made her resolve, the goddess, assuming the form of a woman, went to see Kaśyapa; and Kaśyapa beheld her.
Viṣṇu 1.22a: Her eyes were like the petals of a blue lotus; her face resembled the autumnal moon.
Viṣṇu 1.22c: She was radiant, with hair dark as a swarm of bees, and her beautiful lips were the color of the bandhujīva flower.
Viṣṇu 1.23a: She possessed beautiful eyebrows, very fine teeth, a lovely nose, and arched brows;
Viṣṇu 1.23c: she had a neck like a conch shell, closely joined thighs, and full thighs and hips.
Viṣṇu 1.24a: Her two breasts shone forth, being symmetrical, full, and close together.
Resembling the frontal globes of Indra’s elephant and possessing a radiance equal to refined gold.
His two arms were as tender as lotus stalks, and his hands resembled young sprouts;
his thighs were like pillars of gold, and his knees were well-concealed and closely set.
His shanks were hairless and perfectly symmetrical, and his feet were exceedingly beautiful;
his hips were firm, and his waist was like that of a lion cub.
Her copper-colored nails were endowed with radiance, her form was captivating to all minds,
and she constantly made the quarters of the sky appear as if filled with blue lotuses by her glances.
The goddess, making the quarters free from darkness with her radiance as she acted thus,
was clothed in very fine white garments and adorned with the finest jewels.
With the placement of her feet, she made the earth appear as if adorned with lotuses;
endowed with beauty and youth, she stood before him with humble demeanor.
Seeing her approach his presence, Kaśyapa honored her and then said,
"O lady of beautiful hips, that which was in your heart has been understood by me."
"O Earth, O large-eyed goddess, go to Janārdana;
he will explain to you in its entirety how your fortitude shall be, O blessed one."
"O fair-faced one, I have learned through the yoga of meditation— by his grace and for your sake, O lovely-limbed one— that his dwelling is in the Ocean of Milk."
Having been addressed in this manner, the Earth then honored Kaśyapa and departed for the Milky Ocean,
the sea of Kṣīroda, in order to see Keśava.
She beheld that treasure-house of nectar, enchanting with its moonbeams,
and agitated by hundreds of waves produced by the agitation of the wind.
Viṣṇu 1.35a: Resembling a hundred Himalayas, it was like another orb of the earth.
With its moving hands of waves, it seemed as if calling out to the earth.
By those very rays, he was made to appear as if constantly bestowing whiteness upon the moon;
with all impurities removed by Hari residing within him.
Therefore, he who maintains a very white and powerful body—
pale, moving through the sky, inaccessible [to others], yet dwelling in the lower realms— [is Viṣṇu].
Rich with sapphire-blue and tawny [clouds], it was like the sky turned upside down;
it was as if covered by a multitude of forests from which rows of fruit had emerged.
Indeed, seeing that [ocean] which was exceedingly vast in its extent, like the slough of the serpent Śeṣa,
he beheld there the abode of Keśava situated in its midst.
In that [lotus], he beheld the slayer of Madhu, whose dimensions are indescribable, who is endowed with inconceivable supernatural power, and who was reclining upon the couch of Śeṣa.
Viṣṇu 1.41a: His lotus-face is difficult to discern due to the rays from the jewels on the hoods of the serpent Śeṣa;
Viṣṇu 1.41c: it resembles a hundred moons and possesses a splendor equal to ten thousand suns.
Clad in yellow garments, as unshakeable as a mountain, adorned with all kinds of jewels,
and resplendent with a crown the color of the sun and two earrings.
His pair of feet were being massaged by Lakṣmī with her auspicious palms,
while he was being attended on all sides by the personified weapons.
Having seen that lotus-eyed slayer of Madhu, he prostrated before him;
then, falling upon the ground on his knees, he addressed him with this request.
"O Lord Viṣṇu, I was raised up by you from the depths of the netherworld;
O Viṣṇu, I have been established in my own place out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds."
"O Lord of Gods, what indeed will be my sustenance there now?
Having been addressed thus by the Goddess, the God spoke these words.
O Earth, the virtuous who delight in the conduct of their castes and stages of life, being solely devoted to the scriptures, will support you; upon them your burden has been placed.
Thus addressed, Vasumatī spoke to the God of gods:
"O Eternal One, declare the duties of the social classes and the stages of life."
O Viṣṇu, I wish to hear from you, for you are my supreme refuge.
Salutations to you, O Lord of the gods of gods, O destroyer of the hosts of the enemies of the gods.
O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the World, wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace;
O lotus-navelled Hṛṣīkeśa, possessed of great strength and prowess!
O Viṣṇu, beyond the senses, exceedingly difficult to cross over, O God who wields the Śārṅga bow;
O Varāha, O Bhīma, O Govinda, O Ancient One, O Supreme Person!
O golden-haired one, O universal-eyed one, O embodiment of sacrifice, O stainless one;
O Lord of the field, the knower of the field, and the Lord of gods, O you who recline upon the ocean of waters!
O Mantra, bearer of mantras, inconceivable one, whose body is the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences;
O you who are the cause of the creation and destruction of this entire world!
O Knower of Dharma and Adharma, O Limb of Dharma, O Source of Dharma, O Bestower of Boons;
O Viṣvaksena, O Immortal One, O Sky, O Slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha!
O Viṣṇu, nourisher of the great, unknowable one, bestower of fearlessness upon all;
O most excellent, sinless one, cloud-like one, creator of the world's manifestation!
O nourisher of the waters, O abode, O support of consciousness, O inactive one;
O teacher of the seven-headed sacrifice, O ancient and supreme Person!
O Viṣṇu, eternal, imperishable, most subtle Lord, compassionate toward your devotees, purifier! You are the refuge of all the gods; you are the refuge of those who discourse upon Brahman.
Likewise, O Supreme Person, you are the goal of those who have known all that is to be known;
O Lord of the World, I have taken refuge in you, the eternal Master of Speech.

Viṣṇu 1.59: [He who is] the one most worthy of Vedic invocation, the unassailable, the army of wealth, the bestower of wealth, endowed with the power of great yoga, the offspring of Pṛśni, and the bearer of radiance.
Vāsudeva, the Great Soul, the lotus-eyed, the Infallible;
the God who is the teacher of gods and asuras, the All-pervading Lord, the Supreme Sovereign of all beings.
"O Blessed One, tell me of Viṣṇu— who is the single manifestation, who has four arms, and who is the cause of the cause of the world— and also the eternal duties of the four castes."
"Those [dharmas] associated with the conduct of the stages of life (āśramas), together with their secret doctrines and their compendiums"—
having been thus addressed by the Earth, the Lord of Gods spoke to the Earth.
"Listen, O Goddess Earth, to the eternal duties of the four castes,
together with the conduct of the stages of life, along with their secret doctrines and their essential summaries."
O fair-thighed one, sit down upon this excellent golden seat, which shall be the ultimate refuge for those virtuous ones who uphold you.
"Sit comfortably and learn the duties as I proclaim them," [said] Viṣṇu 1.65a;
"Then, sitting comfortably, Dharā heard the Vaiṣṇava duties," [it is said in] Viṣṇu 1.65c.
Viṣṇu 2.01: Om! The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra—these are the four castes.
Among them, the first three are the twice-born.
Viṣṇu 2.03: For them, the entire collection of rites, beginning with the impregnation and ending with the funeral pyre, is to be performed with mantras.
And their duties [shall be as follows]. (Viṣṇu 2.04)
Viṣṇu 2.05: Teaching is the duty of a Brāhmaṇa.
Viṣṇu 2.06: For a Kṣatriya, there is a constant obligation to bear arms.
For a Vaiśya, [the duty is] the tending of cattle. (Viṣṇu 2.07)
Viṣṇu 2.08: For a Śūdra, service to the twice-born is [the duty].
Viṣṇu 2.09: For the twice-born, [the duties are] sacrificing and studying.
Now, the modes of conduct for these [castes] are as follows.
For a Brāhmaṇa, officiating at sacrifices and accepting gifts [are the means of livelihood]. (Viṣṇu 2.11)
For a Kṣatriya, the protection of the earth is his duty.
Viṣṇu 2.13: Agriculture, cattle-rearing, trade, money-lending, and the cultivation of the soil are the duties of the Vaiśya.
For a Śūdra, all crafts are [lawful occupations]. (Viṣṇu 2.14)
Viṣṇu Smṛti 2.15: In times of distress, the next lower mode of livelihood may be adopted.
Forgiveness, truthfulness, self-restraint, purity, charity, control of the senses, non-violence, service to the teacher, visiting sacred fords, and compassion— Viṣṇu 2.16.
Uprightness, freedom from greed, worship of the gods and Brahmins,
and likewise the absence of malice— this is declared to be the common dharma.
Viṣṇu 3.01 Now, the duties of kings.
Viṣṇu 3.02: The protection of subjects.
Viṣṇu 3.03: The establishment of the social classes and stages of life in their respective duties.
And the king should take refuge in a region that is arid, suitable for cattle, and endowed with crops. (Viṣṇu 3.04)
And [the world] will consist mostly of Vaiśyas and Śūdras. (Viṣṇu 3.05)
In that regard, one should take refuge in any one of the following types of fortresses: a desert, a human stronghold, an earthwork, a body of water, a forest, or a mountain fortress (Viṣṇu 3.06).
And remaining there, he shall appoint the respective village headmen.
Viṣṇu 3.08: [He shall appoint] ten superintendents.
Viṣṇu 3.09: [He shall appoint] hundreds of superintendents.
And [he should appoint] provincial governors, Viṣṇu 3.10.
The village headman shall provide a remedy for the faults of the village. (Viṣṇu 3.11)
One who is unable [to do so] should report it to the superintendent of ten villages.
If he too is unable, he shall report it to the superintendent of a hundred.
If he too is unable, he shall report it to the district governor (deśādhyakṣa).
The provincial governor, moreover, should eradicate wrongdoing with his whole being.
Viṣṇu 3.16: He should appoint trustworthy persons as superintendents over mines, tolls, ferries, elephants, and forests.
Viṣṇu 3.17: [He should appoint] those most devoted to dharma to matters of dharma.
Viṣṇu 3.18: Those who are skillful in matters of wealth and duty.
Viṣṇu 3.19: [He should appoint] heroes for the duties of battle.
Viṣṇu 3.20: [He should place] fierce [beings] among the fierce.
Viṣṇu 3.21: [One should not give] eunuchs to women.
Viṣṇu 3.22: For the sake of tribute from the subjects, he should take a sixth part of the grain every year.
And from all kinds of grain, [one should give] according to Viṣṇu 3.23.
Viṣṇu 3.24: Two hundred [paṇas] for animals, gold, and clothes.
Viṣṇu 3.25: From meat, honey, ghee, medicinal herbs, perfumes, flowers, roots, fruits, juices, wood, leaves, skins, earthenware, stone vessels, and wickerwork, the king shall take a sixth part.
Viṣṇu 3.26: One shall not collect taxes from Brāhmaṇas.
For they are indeed the ones who perform the duty for the king. (Viṣṇu 3.27)
And the king receives a sixth part of the merits and demerits of his subjects. (Viṣṇu 3.28)
From the merchandise of his own country, he shall take a tenth part as the customs duty (*śulka*).
And from goods brought from foreign lands, [the king shall take] a twentieth part. (Viṣṇu 3.30)
One who flees from the place where the toll is collected shall incur the forfeiture of his entire property.
Viṣṇu 3.32: Artisans and those who live by their manual labor shall perform one day's work for the king every month.
Viṣṇu 3.33: The sovereign, the minister, the fort, the treasury, the army, the realm, and the ally are the constituent elements [of sovereignty].
And he should execute those who revile him. (Viṣṇu 3.34)
Viṣṇu 3.35: He should have spies as his eyes in both his own kingdom and the kingdoms of others.
One should perform the worship of the virtuous. (Viṣṇu 3.36)
And he should slay the wicked ones. (Viṣṇu 3.37)
Viṣṇu 3.38: One should employ conciliation, sowing dissension, bribery, and force against enemies, friends, neutrals, and those in between, as appropriate and at the proper time.
One should resort to peace, war, marching, halting, seeking shelter, and duplicity at the appropriate times.
In the month of Caitra or Mārgaśīrṣa, one should undertake the pilgrimage.
Or during the misfortune of an enemy—Viṣṇu 3.41.
Upon arriving in a foreign land, one should not abandon the customs of that country. (Viṣṇu 3.42)
And even when attacked by an enemy with all his might, he should protect his own kingdom with his whole soul.
Viṣṇu Purāṇa 3.44: For kings, there is no duty equal to the sacrifice of one's body in battle.
Those who are killed while protecting cows, Brahmins, kings, friends, wealth, wives, or their own lives, partake of the heavenly world.
And for the purpose of protecting against the intermixture of castes, Viṣṇu 3.46.
Viṣṇu 3.47: Upon the conquest of an enemy's city, the king should install there a member of that [enemy's] family.
Viṣṇu 3.48: One should not exterminate the royal family.
Viṣṇu 3.49: Except from the families of kings who are not of noble birth.
One should avoid addiction to hunting, gambling, women, and drinking.
And [the same applies] to verbal harshness and physical assault, Viṣṇu 3.51.
One should not cause the loss of wealth. (Viṣṇu 3.52)
One should not cut off the primary gateways. (Viṣṇu 3.53)
Viṣṇu 3.54: One should not shower [gifts] upon an unworthy recipient.
Viṣṇu 3.55: He may take everything from mines.
Having found a treasure, one should give half of it to Brāhmaṇas.
Viṣṇu 3.57: One should cause the second half to enter the vessel.
A Brāhmaṇa, having found a treasure-trove, may take it all for himself.
A Kṣatriya should give a fourth part to the king, a fourth part to the Brāhmaṇas, and take half for himself.
A Vaiśya, however, should give a fourth part of his income to the king, half to the Brāhmaṇas, and take a fourth part for himself.
And a Śūdra, having divided what he has acquired into twelve parts, shall give five shares to the king, five shares to the Brāhmaṇas, and take two shares for himself.
Viṣṇu 3.62: One should confiscate everything belonging to a person who is known to have eaten food that was not offered [to the gods].
Viṣṇu 3.63: From what has been hidden by themselves, those other than Brāhmaṇas shall give a twelfth part to the king.
Viṣṇu 3.64: One who claims that what was deposited by another was deposited by himself shall incur a fine equal to the value of that deposit.
The king shall protect the property of children, the helpless, and women.
And Viṣṇu 3.66 states: "Having recovered wealth stolen by a thief, one should give it all back to those of all social classes."
And even if he cannot obtain it from his own treasury, he should give [the gift] from [elsewhere]. (Viṣṇu 3.67)
One should pacify the afflictions caused by fate through means of propitiation, auspicious rites, and protective prayers.
And he should ward off the attacks of enemy armies by means of constant readiness with weapons. (Viṣṇu 3.69)

Viṣṇu 3.70: One should choose as a domestic priest (purohita) one who is well-versed in the Vedas, the Itihāsas, and the Dharmaśāstras, who is of noble birth, free from physical defects, and devoted to austerity.
Viṣṇu 3.71: [He should appoint] those who are pure, free from greed, attentive, endowed with capability, and capable of assisting in all matters.
Viṣṇu 3.72: He himself should examine legal cases together with learned Brāhmaṇas.
Viṣṇu 3.73: Or, when presiding over legal proceedings, he may appoint a Brāhmaṇa.

Viṣṇu 3.74: The king should appoint as members of his assembly those who are endowed with [noble] birth, conduct, and religious observances; who are impartial toward both enemy and friend; and who cannot be subverted by desire, anger, fear, greed, or other motives related to their duties.
And the king shall be dependent upon the astrologer in all his affairs. (Viṣṇu 3.75)
One should constantly worship the gods and the Brahmins.
One should serve the elderly. (Viṣṇu 3.77)
And one who performs sacrifices is also [a Brahmin], according to Viṣṇu 3.78.
And in his realm, no Brāhmaṇa shall perish, afflicted by hunger.
And no one else either, even if devoted to virtuous deeds.
Viṣṇu 3.81: He should bestow land upon Brāhmaṇas.

Viṣṇu 3.82: And he should cause to be written on a cloth or a copper plate the names of those to whom he bestows it, along with the members of their own lineage, the measurement of the land, and a description of the boundaries of the gift; this, marked with his own seal, he should give for the purpose of informing future kings.
And one should not seize land given by another, as stated in Viṣṇu 3.83.
Viṣṇu 3.84: He should bestow all gifts upon the Brāhmaṇas.
But one should protect oneself from all sides. (Viṣṇu 3.85)
And he shall be named Sudarśana.
And he should be one who maintains the mantras for antidotes that destroy poison.
Viṣṇu 3.88: One should not consume anything that has not been examined.
One should speak with a smile as a prelude. (Viṣṇu 3.89)
Even toward those deserving of death, one should not knit one's brows in a frown. (Viṣṇu 3.90)
And he should cause punishment to be inflicted upon those deserving of it, in accordance with their offense. (Viṣṇu 3.91)
Viṣṇu 3.92: He should administer punishment correctly.
Viṣṇu 3.93: He would not forgive a second offense from anyone.
Viṣṇu 3.94: There is no one who, failing to protect his own dharma, is exempt from punishment by kings.
Where the dark-complexioned, red-eyed Punishment stalks fearlessly,
there the subjects flourish, provided that the leader perceives rightly.
Within his own kingdom, he should administer justice through punishment; toward enemies, he should be severe in punishment;
toward friends and affectionate Brahmins, he should be straightforward and endowed with patience.
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even if he lives by gleaning ears of grain,
his fame spreads throughout the world like a drop of oil upon water.
The king who finds happiness in the happiness of his subjects and who is sorrowful in their sorrow is endowed with fame in this world and is glorified in heaven after death.
The particle of dust situated in a sunbeam passing through a lattice is known as a *trasareṇu*.
Eight of those [atoms] make one nit (likṣā). Viṣṇu 4.02.
Three of those [rājika-s] are a rāja-sarṣapa.
Those three [mustard seeds] make one white mustard seed (*gaura-sarṣapa*).
Six of those [viṣṇutailas] make one yava.
Those three [māṣas] constitute one *kṛṣṇala*.
Five of those [rathikas] make one māṣa.
Twelve of those [muhūrtas] constitute half an akṣa. (Viṣṇu 4.08)
A *suvarṇa* consists of exactly half an *akṣa* plus four *māṣakas*.
Viṣṇu 4.10: Four suvarṇas constitute one niṣka.
Two *kṛṣṇalas* weighed together constitute one silver *māṣaka*.
Viṣṇu 4.12: Sixteen of those [māṣas] constitute one dharaṇa.
A *kārṣāpaṇa* consists of one *karṣa* of copper.
Two hundred and fifty paṇas is declared to be the first amercement;
five hundred is to be known as the middle, and one thousand is the highest.
Viṣṇu 5.01: Now, with the exception of Brāhmaṇas, all those who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātakin) are liable to capital punishment.
Viṣṇu 5.02: There shall be no corporal punishment for a Brāhmaṇa.
Viṣṇu 5.03: He shall banish from his own country a Brāhmaṇa who has been branded with a mark.
And in the case of killing a Brahmin, one should fashion a headless man on his forehead.
Viṣṇu 5.05: For drinking liquor, the mark of a tavern flag.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 5.06: For theft, the punishment is the mark of a dog's foot.
Viṣṇu 5.07: [The penance for] violating the teacher's bed is the Bhaga [penance].
Viṣṇu 5.08: Even in other cases involving capital punishment, one should banish the person while leaving his entire property intact and unharmed.
And the king shall execute those who forge false edicts. (Viṣṇu 5.09)
And those who forge documents, [shall be punished], according to Viṣṇu 5.10.
Viṣṇu 5.11: Those who administer poison, those who set fire [to dwellings], violent robbers, and those who kill women, children, or men.
And those who would steal more than ten jars of grain; Viṣṇu 5.12.
Viṣṇu 5.13: [The fine for] things measured by weight shall be more than one hundred [paṇas].
And those who are of low birth who might desire sovereignty. (Viṣṇu 5.14)
And those who cause the destruction of a bridge (Viṣṇu 5.15).
And those who forcibly provide shelter, food, or provisions to thieves, [Viṣṇu 5.16].
Viṣṇu 5.17: Except in cases of inability on the part of the king.
A woman whose husband is incapable [of providing for her] and one who has transgressed him (Viṣṇu 5.18).
Viṣṇu 5.19: If a person of lower caste commits an offense against one of higher caste with a particular limb, that very limb of his shall be mutilated.
One who sits on the same seat [as the king] or makes a mark on his hip shall be banished.
Having spat, one should be made devoid of both lips (Viṣṇu 5.21).
And one who habitually passes gas becomes devoid of a rectum.
And one who reviles others is "fork-tongued" (vijihva). Viṣṇu 5.23.
Viṣṇu 5.24: The king shall pour boiling oil into the mouth of those who, out of pride, give instructions on dharma.
And for the malicious utterance of another's name or caste, a ten-finger-long wooden stake shall be driven into his body.
One who speaks falsely regarding what has been heard, or regarding place, caste, or occupation, shall be fined two hundred kārśāpaṇas. (Viṣṇu 5.26)
According to Viṣṇu 5.27, even one who speaks the truth regarding those who are one-eyed, lame, or otherwise disabled, shall be fined two kārśāpaṇas.
One who insults his teachers shall pay a fine of two hundred kārśāpaṇas. (Viṣṇu 5.28)
Viṣṇu 5.29: But when an accusation of a sin causing loss of caste is made against another, the highest amercement shall be imposed.
In the case of one who has committed a secondary offense (upapātaka), the middle [amercement] is prescribed. (Viṣṇu 5.30)
Viṣṇu 5.31: [The fine for] reviling those advanced in the three Vedas and for [reviling] groups of people according to their caste.
And for [theft from] a village or a district, the first amercement shall be imposed.
For an insulting speech accompanied by physical deformity, the fine shall be one hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
But when it is joined with the mother [syllable], it is the most excellent. (Viṣṇu 5.34)
For insulting someone of equal caste, one shall be fined twelve paṇas. (Viṣṇu 5.35)
Viṣṇu Smṛti 5.36: For reviling a person of inferior caste, the fine is six [paṇas].
Viṣṇu 5.37: For insulting a member of a superior caste at the appropriate time, the punishment shall be proportional to that [insult].
Or three kārṣāpaṇas, according to Viṣṇu 5.38.
In the case of speaking words that are sour or harsh, the same applies. (Viṣṇu 5.39)
Viṣṇu 5.40: One who has sexual intercourse with the wife of another shall be punished with the highest amercement if she is of the same caste.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 5.41: For approaching a woman of a lower caste, the middle amercement shall be imposed.
And [the same penance applies] for sexual intercourse with a cow. (Viṣṇu 5.42)
Viṣṇu 5.43: He who has sexual intercourse with a woman of the lowest caste is to be put to death.
Viṣṇu 5.44: For having sexual intercourse with a female animal, one shall be fined one hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
And he who gives away a maiden without declaring her defects [is also guilty]. (Viṣṇu 5.45)
And he should support her. (Viṣṇu 5.46)
One who says of a woman who is not wicked that she is wicked shall be punished with the highest amercement.
One who kills an elephant, a horse, a camel, a cow, or a bull should be made one-handed and one-footed.
And one who sells meat is also [excluded]. Viṣṇu 5.49.
One who kills a domestic animal shall be fined one hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
Viṣṇu 5.51: He shall pay its value to the owner of the animal.
One who kills a wild animal shall pay fifty kārṣāpaṇas. (Viṣṇu 5.52)
A killer of birds and a killer of fish shall pay ten *kārṣāpaṇas*.
And one who kills insects shall pay a kārṣāpaṇa fine.
But one who cuts down a tree that bears fruit at the proper season commits the highest amercement.
One who cuts down trees that have flowered incurs the Madhyama penance.
One who cuts down creepers, shrubs, or climbing plants shall pay one hundred kārṣāpaṇas.
One [day and night] for cutting grass. (Viṣṇu 5.58)
And all [the sons] shall receive that [property] from their respective fathers at the time of its distribution.
One who threatens with the hand shall pay ten kārṣāpaṇas.
With one foot, twenty [times]. Viṣṇu 5.61.
Striking with a wooden stick constitutes the first *sāhasa* (lowest fine).
According to Viṣṇu 5.63, [a wound] caused by a stone is of middling severity.
By means of a weapon, [the gift] is most excellent. (Viṣṇu 5.64)
For the plucking of a foot, hair, garment, or hand, the fine shall be ten paṇas. (Viṣṇu 5.65)
One who causes pain without shedding blood shall be fined thirty-two paṇas.
Along with blood, [one commits] sixty-four [transgressions]. (Viṣṇu 5.67)
In the case of breaking a hand, foot, or tooth, or cutting off an ear or nose, the middle amercement shall be imposed.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 5.69: [The same penance applies] for the suppression of movement, eating, or speech, as well as for the inflicting of a blow.
And in the case of a fracture of the eyes, neck, arms, thighs, or shoulders, it is the highest [grade].
Viṣṇu 5.71: A king shall not release from bondage for as long as he lives one who pierces both eyes.
Or one may construct it in exactly that same manner. (Viṣṇu 5.72)
Viṣṇu 5.73: When many people strike a single person, the punishment for each shall be double that which has been prescribed for a single offender.
Viṣṇu 5.74: [The same applies] to those standing near him who do not run toward one crying out, and to those passing by.
And all those who cause injury to a person shall pay the expenses incurred for his recovery.
And those who cause suffering to domestic animals [are also liable]. (Viṣṇu 5.76)
One who steals a cow, a horse, a camel, or an elephant shall have one hand and one foot cut off.
Viṣṇu 5.78: He is unborn, unchanging, incapable of being carried away, and single-handed.
One who steals grain shall be fined eleven times its value. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 5.79)
And one who steals grain [is also liable]. Viṣṇu 5.80.
According to Viṣṇu 5.81, one who steals more than fifty measures of gold, silver, or clothing is a Vikara.
Viṣṇu 5.82: He who [causes] a deficiency in that [measure] shall be fined eleven times that amount.

According to Viṣṇu 5.83, one who steals articles made of thread, cotton, cow-dung, molasses, curds, milk, buttermilk, grass, salt, clay, ashes, birds, fish, ghee, oil, meat, honey, split pulses, bamboo, earthenware, or metal vessels shall be fined three times their value.
And [the same applies] to cooked foods, according to Viṣṇu 5.84.
For the theft of flowers, green shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, or leaves, the fine is five kṛṣṇalas.
And [the same applies] to leafy vegetables, roots, and fruits, according to Viṣṇu 5.86.
One who steals gems shall be punished with the highest amercement.
One who steals articles not specifically mentioned [in the preceding rules] shall pay a fine equal to their value.
Viṣṇu 5.89: Thieves shall be made to pay the owner the full value of whatever has been stolen.
Then follows the application of the prescribed punishment for them, according to Viṣṇu 5.90.
Viṣṇu 5.91: He who gives the wrong path to those for whom a path must be given shall be fined twenty-five kārṣāpaṇas.
And one who does not offer a seat to one worthy of a seat [incurs a fault]. (Viṣṇu 5.92)
And not worshipping one who is worthy of worship—Viṣṇu 5.93.
And [the same penalty applies] for neglecting an invitation to a neighboring Brāhmaṇa, Viṣṇu 5.94.
And those who, having invited [others], do not provide them with food—Viṣṇu 5.95.
Having been invited and having replied "So be it," one who does not eat [at that time] [should give] a gold māṣaka.
And for one who provides a dwelling, double the amount of food [is required].
One who defiles a Brāhmaṇa with forbidden food shall pay a fine of sixteen suvarṇas. (Viṣṇu 5.98)
For one who causes another to lose their caste, the penance lasts for one hundred years.
According to Viṣṇu 5.100, he is to be executed by means of liquor.
For one who defames a Kṣatriya, the fine is half of that. (Viṣṇu 5.101)
For defiling a Vaiśya, the fine is half of that as well—Viṣṇu 5.102.
For one who defames a Śūdra, the first amercement is prescribed. (Viṣṇu 5.103)
One who, out of lustful intent, touches a member of the three twice-born castes who is not to be touched, shall be put to death.
Viṣṇu 5.105: One should strike a woman in her menses with a whip.
One who commits an act of impurity even near a path, a garden, or water shall be fined one hundred paṇas. (Viṣṇu 5.106)
And that [impurity] one should cast off. (Viṣṇu 5.107)
One who breaks the ground, walls, or other parts of a house shall be fined the middle amercement.
And one should apply that [mantra] as well. (Viṣṇu 5.109)
One who throws an object that causes pain into another's house shall pay a fine of one hundred paṇas. (Viṣṇu 5.110)
And one who denies what is common property, Viṣṇu 5.111.
And one who does not give what has been sent by Viṣṇu (5.112).
And one who abandons any of the following—father, son, teacher, sacrificial patron, or officiating priest—provided they have not fallen from their status, is also [an outcaste].
And one should not abandon them.
Viṣṇu 5.115: And those who feed Śūdras and renunciants at rites for the gods or the ancestors [are also excluded].
And one who performs unsuitable actions [is also excluded]. Viṣṇu 5.116.
And one who breaks into a house by the sea. Viṣṇu 5.117.
One who swears an oath when not authorized [to do so]—Viṣṇu 5.118a.
Viṣṇu 5.119: One who causes the destruction of the virility of animals.
Viṣṇu 5.120: In a dispute between a father and a son, the fine for witnesses is ten paṇas.
And whoever should be between those two, for him there shall be the highest amercement.
And for one who practices fraud regarding weights and measures, [the punishment is the same]. (Viṣṇu 5.122)
Viṣṇu 5.123: And [the same applies] to one who speaks falsely regarding what is not a fraud.
And for one who sells counterfeit goods, [the punishment is the same as for] Viṣṇu 5.124.
Viṣṇu 5.125: [The king shall punish] merchants who, having come together, withhold their merchandise at an unrighteous price.
And for those who sell [the articles] individually, [the fine is the same], according to Viṣṇu 5.126.
If one who has received the price does not deliver the merchandise to the buyer, he shall be compelled to pay it along with the profit (sa-udaya).
And the king shall fine him one hundred paṇas.
Whatever loss occurs to one who purchases what has been sold without [proper authorization] shall belong to the purchaser alone. (Viṣṇu 5.129)
Viṣṇu 5.130: For one who sells what is forbidden for a king, there shall be the forfeiture of that [property].
A ferryman who collects a land toll shall be fined ten paṇas. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 5.131)

Viṣṇu 5.132: A ferryman, a customs officer, and one who collects tolls [are liable for a fine] when they [cause harm to] a student, a forest-dweller, a mendicant, a pregnant woman, or one following a sacred ford.
And he should give that to them. (Viṣṇu 5.133)
Viṣṇu 5.134: In gambling, those who play with fraudulent dice shall have their hands cut off.
For those who gamble with fraudulent devices, the thumb and forefinger shall be cut off.
And for those who break open knots [of property], Viṣṇu 5.136.
And for those who commit acts of throwing down [another], there shall be the amputation of the hand. (Viṣṇu 5.137)
Viṣṇu 5.138: If cattle are harmed by wolves or other predators during the day while the herdsman is not present, the fault lies with the herdsman.
And he shall pay the value of the lost animal to its owner. (Viṣṇu 5.139)
One who milks a cow without permission shall pay twenty-five kārṣāpaṇas.
If a buffalo should cause the destruction of standing crops, its keeper shall be fined eight māṣas.
The owner of one who has no protector is Viṣṇu (the King).
But a horse, a camel, or a donkey [is the sacrificial animal]. Viṣṇu 5.143.
If it is a cow, half of that [penalty].
Half of that [is the fine for] goats and sheep. (Viṣṇu 5.145)
Viṣṇu 5.146: If they sit down after having eaten, the fine is double.
Viṣṇu 5.147: In all cases, the owner shall also pay the value of the destroyed crop.
There is no offense [if one urinates] on a path, in a village, or at the edge of a pasture (vivīta).
And [the same applies] when it is not enclosed, according to Viṣṇu 5.149.
Viṣṇu 5.150: For a short time.
And [the same applies] to the milk of cows that have calved after being set free as bulls. (Viṣṇu 5.151)
He who would employ men of the highest caste in servitude shall be punished with the highest amercement.
One who has abandoned the life of a renunciant shall perform service for the king. (Viṣṇu 5.153)
A hired servant who abandons his service before the agreed time has elapsed shall pay the full amount of the wages.
And according to Viṣṇu 5.155, he shall pay one hundred paṇas as a fine.
Viṣṇu 5.156: Whatever is destroyed through the fault of that [keeper] shall belong to the owner.
Except in the case of an act of God. (Viṣṇu 5.157)
Viṣṇu 5.158: If the master should dismiss the laborer before the term is completed, he must pay him the full value of his wages.
And one hundred paṇas to the king. (Viṣṇu 5.159)
Viṣṇu 5.160: Except in the case of the fault of a hired servant.
Viṣṇu 5.161: He who gives a girl, already betrothed to another, to someone else, shall be punished like a thief.
Viṣṇu 5.162: except in the case of a boon or a transgression.
Viṣṇu 5.163: By abandoning a woman who is free from fault.
And [he shall not touch] his wife, Viṣṇu 5.164.
If one who is unaware openly purchases another's property, he incurs no fault in that matter. (Viṣṇu 5.165)
The owner shall receive the property. (Viṣṇu 5.166)
Viṣṇu 5.167: If one should purchase [an item] that is unmanifested [in its true nature] and of low value, then both the buyer and the seller are to be punished like thieves.
One who misappropriates the property of a corporate body shall be banished.
And whoever should violate that agreement with him—Viṣṇu 5.169.
Viṣṇu 5.170: He shall be made to pay to the creditor the deposited wealth along with the interest on the money.
And by the king, he should be punished like a thief. (Viṣṇu 5.171)
And he who says that something was deposited when it was not deposited; Viṣṇu 5.172.
Having punished one who destroys a boundary with the highest amercement, the king should have the boundary re-established.
One who eats food that is unfit to be eaten because it causes loss of caste shall be banished. (Viṣṇu 5.174)
One who sells what is unfit for consumption or what is not to be sold, as well as one who destroys an image of a deity, shall be punished with the highest amercement.
A physician who practices deceitfully toward persons of the highest status [shall be punished].
Viṣṇu 5.177: For those of middling [strength], the middle [penance].
Among animals, [the first] is the first. (Viṣṇu 5.178)
One who fails to give what has been promised shall be compelled to give it and be fined the first amercement. (Viṣṇu 5.179)
Viṣṇu 5.180: For those who give false testimony, the confiscation of all their property shall be carried out.
Viṣṇu 5.181: [The same penalty applies] to members of the court who subsist on bribes.
He who, without having released from one person land measuring at least a *go-carman*, bestows it upon another as a pledge (*ādhi*), shall be put to death.
If it is less than sixteen suvarṇas, he shall be fined [the same amount]. Viṣṇu 5.183.
If a man were to eat for a year whatever fruit he could obtain alone,
that earth— whether it be small or vast— would be no more than the size of a cow-hide.
When two men dispute over a pledge that has been deposited with them,
he whose possession is accompanied by the enjoyment of its fruit prevails, provided it was done without force.
When property has been enjoyed for a long time with a valid title and accompanied by possession, the original acquirer obtains it;
that may never be taken away from him.

Whatever property has been enjoyed by the father in accordance with lawful custom through the act of possession, when he has died, he [the son] need not be questioned regarding it; for that was acquired by him through possession.
But land that has been enjoyed by three persons in due order,
even in the absence of a written document, may be acquired there by a fourth person.
In the case of killing clawed animals, horned animals, fanged animals, or assassins,
as well as elephants, horses, and other such creatures, the killer incurs no guilt.
Whether it be a teacher, a child, an elder, or a Brāhmaṇa deeply learned in the Vedas—
one should indeed slay an approaching *ātatāyin* (aggressor) without hesitation.
In the killing of an *ātatāyin* (one who seeks to kill), no fault whatsoever attaches to the slayer;
whether done openly or in secret, it is simply fury meeting fury.
One who raises a sword, poison, or fire; likewise one who raises his hand to utter a curse;
one who kills by means of the Atharvan [mantras]; and a slanderer among kings.

One should know that there are seven who are immediate assailants (*ātatāyin*): one who violates another's wife, and others who take away fame or wealth, as well as those who seize righteousness and property.
O Earth, I have described to you in brief the procedure for punishment regarding all offenses; it would be too extensive to detail at length.
In other offenses as well, having ascertained the caste, wealth, and age [of the offender],
the king shall determine the punishment after consulting with Brāhmaṇas.

One who releases an offender from punishment shall incur a fine double that of the offender. Furthermore, a man appointed [to oversee justice] who inflicts punishment upon those who do not deserve it is the lowest of men.
In whose city there is no thief, no one who covets another's wife, and no one of wicked speech—[that king is truly a ruler].
That king who does not inflict corporal punishment or fines upon those who commit acts of violence partakes in the world of Śakra.
Viṣṇu 6.01: Now, the creditor of superior rank shall receive from the debtor of inferior rank the amount of wealth as it was given.
Two, three, four, five, and a hundred [days] per month, according to the sequence of the castes.
Or all castes may pay the interest they themselves have agreed upon. (Viṣṇu 6.03)
Even for one who has not performed [the rite], it should be done as prescribed upon the lapse of a year.
Viṣṇu 6.05: When there is enjoyment [of the object] through use, there shall be no interest.
Except in the case of destruction caused by the king or fate, the debtor who possesses the highest security must pay back the lost pledge.
Viṣṇu 6.07: Even when the night has entered its final increase.
A pledge consisting of immovable property cannot be forfeited except by a specific agreement.
Whatever immovable property has been given solely for the purpose of recovering the money received, that shall be returned once the money received has been recovered.
When the interest on a debt has been paid or stipulated, it ceases to increase from that point onward for one who does not accept the principal amount.
The maximum interest on gold is double the principal.
For grain, the interest is threefold.
For a cloth, it is fourfold. *Viṣṇu Smṛti* 6.13.
The eight qualities of taste are as follows: Viṣṇu 6.14.
VIṢṆU 6.15: The offspring belongs to the woman and the cattle.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 6.16: [The gift of] fermenting yeast, cotton thread, leather, weapons, bricks, and minerals is inexhaustible.
For those not mentioned, the fine is double. (Viṣṇu 6.17)
One who accomplishes a matter entrusted to him by any means whatsoever should not be censured by the king. (Viṣṇu 6.18)
If one being interrogated approaches the king, he shall be fined an amount equal to that [of the offense].
If the debtor of the superior kind approaches the king, then the debtor of the inferior kind, having been proven by him, shall pay to the king a fine equal to one-tenth of the amount of the debt.
And one who has obtained wealth and is thus freed from his highest debt shall pay a twentieth part [as a fee].
Viṣṇu 6.22: Even if it is proven that [the debtor] denied the whole, he shall pay the whole, even if only one part has been demonstrated.
And regarding that [debt], there are three means of proof: a written document, witnesses, and a formal agreement.
What has been received in the presence of witnesses should be returned in the very same manner, in the presence of witnesses.
When the person for whom the document was written has entered [to claim his right], one should have the document read aloud. (Viṣṇu 6.25)
If the payment is not complete or if the document is not present, the debtor who owes the highest amount shall provide his own written acknowledgment.
Viṣṇu 6.27: If the deceased was a debtor, or has gone forth as a wandering ascetic, or has been abroad for twenty years, the debt must be paid by his sons or grandsons.
Viṣṇu 6.28: There is nothing higher than this for those who are free from desire.
Whether he has sons or is sonless, the inheritor of the estate shall pay the debt. (Viṣṇu 6.29)
Viṣṇu 6.30: One who seizes the wife of a man destitute of wealth [is liable for punishment].
Viṣṇu Smṛti 6.31: A woman does not [attain heaven] through what is performed by her husband or her sons.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 6.32: [The impurity] caused by a woman does not apply to her husband or her son.
Viṣṇu Smṛti 6.33: Nor [is one purified] by the act performed by a son for his father.
He who remains among those who have contracted a debt jointly shall pay it.
Viṣṇu 6.35: And the paternal debt belongs to brothers who have not divided their inheritance.
And they shall be divided into shares according to their respective inheritance. (Viṣṇu 6.36)
According to Viṣṇu 6.37, the husband of women belonging to the castes of cowherds, vintners, actors, washermen, hunters, or prostitutes shall pay the fine.
That which has been promised by word of mouth must not be withheld from anyone.
And that which is done for the sake of one's family (Viṣṇu 6.39).
He who, having received a loan with the agreement, "I shall repay it all tomorrow," subsequently fails to pay it out of greed,
shall likewise incur interest on that amount.
Suretyship is ordained for appearance, for confidence, and for payment;
however, in the case of the first two types failing, the debt must be paid by the sons of the other type as well.

If there are many sureties, they shall pay the debt according to their respective agreements; however, if no specific distinction has been made among them regarding the amount, the payment shall be made according to the will of the creditor.
Whatever amount the surety may pay when pressured by the creditor,
the debtor ought to give that same amount doubled to the surety.
Viṣṇu 7.01 Now, documentary evidence is of three kinds.
Viṣṇu 7.02: [Evidence] is of three kinds: witnessed by the king, witnessed by ordinary witnesses, and without witnesses.
Viṣṇu 7.03: In the royal court, a document executed by a scribe appointed by the king and marked with the hand-seal of its presiding officer is considered to have the king as its witness.
Viṣṇu 7.04: Wherever, by whomever, and in whatever manner it may have been written—whether attested by witnesses or marked with one's own hand—it is valid as a document with witnesses.
A document written by one's own hand is valid even without witnesses. (Viṣṇu 7.05)
That which is caused by force is invalid, according to Viṣṇu 7.06.
All those things brought about by fraud (upadhi) are likewise invalid. (Viṣṇu 7.07)
Even if it is accompanied by witnesses, a document is invalidated if it is marked by tainted actions or corrupted witnesses. (Viṣṇu 7.08)
And it was written by a scribe of such a kind as that. (Viṣṇu 7.09)
Viṣṇu 7.10: And [an act] committed by a woman, a child, one who is not independent, one who is intoxicated, one who is insane, one who is terrified, or one who has been beaten.

Viṣṇu Smṛti 7.11: A legal instrument is authoritative when it is not contrary to local custom, when its subject matter and the characteristics of the parties are clearly stated, and when its sequence and wording are not omitted.

One should establish a doubtful document by means of the castes [of the scribes], the marks made by them, the paper itself, and logical arguments, as well as by evidence corresponding to those circumstances.
Viṣṇu 7.13: Wherever a debtor, a creditor, a witness, or even a scribe dies, one should validate that document by means of their own handwriting.
Viṣṇu 8.01 Now, those who are not witnesses.

Viṣṇu 8.02: Nor [should one give evidence] for a king, a learned brahmin (*śrotriya*), a renunciant, a gambler, a thief, one dependent on another, a woman, a child, a violent person, one who is very old, one who is intoxicated, one who is insane, one accused of a crime, an outcast, one afflicted by hunger or thirst, one in distress, one addicted to vices, or one blinded by passion.
And those who have enemies, friends, or financial interests; those who have committed forbidden acts; those whose faults have been observed; and those who lack capable assistants. (Viṣṇu 8.03)
But one who, though not specifically designated as a witness, comes forward and speaks [in court], is also [considered a witness].
And a single person is not a witness. (Viṣṇu 8.05)
Viṣṇu 8.06: In cases of theft, violence, verbal or physical assault, and adultery, witnesses need not be examined.
Now, concerning witnesses. (Viṣṇu 8.07)

Those born of noble lineage, endowed with good conduct and wealth, performers of sacrifices, ascetics, possessed of sons, knowers of dharma, students of the Vedas, truthful, and advanced in the knowledge of the three Vedas—[these are the qualities of the bridegroom].* *Note: This verse describes the ideal groom according to the traditional criteria.*
One who is endowed with the aforementioned qualities and is approved by both parties, even if he is alone.
Viṣṇu 8.10: When two parties are disputing, the witnesses of that one who has the prior claim are to be questioned.
Viṣṇu 8.11: Where, due to the requirements of the case, the burden of proof falls upon the plaintiff, there it shall also fall upon the defendant.
Viṣṇu 8.12: When the designated witness has died or gone to another country, those who have heard what he stated are the authority.
A witness is one who has seen [the event] before his eyes or heard it. (Viṣṇu 8.13)
And witnesses are purified by truth. (Viṣṇu 8.14)
Viṣṇu 8.15: Where there is the killing of those belonging to the [four] orders of life, there it is [expiated] by a falsehood.
To purify that [sin], a twice-born man should offer oblations of clarified butter into the fire with the Kūṣmāṇḍī verses.
A Śūdra should give a single day's meal for ten cows.
Viṣṇu 8.18: One should recognize as a false witness one who undergoes a change of natural disposition, whose facial complexion fades, and who utters incoherent prattle.
And having summoned the witnesses at sunrise, he shall question them after they have taken their oaths.
He should ask the Brāhmaṇa, "Speak. (Viṣṇu 8.20)
"Speak the truth," [he says] to a Kshatriya. *Viṣṇu* 8.21.
A Vaiśya [is purified] by means of cows, seeds, and gold.
But for a Śūdra who has committed all the great mortal sins (mahāpātaka), [the penance is] that of a Śūdra.
And he should cause the witnesses to hear [the following]: Viṣṇu 8.24.
Viṣṇu 8.25: "Those worlds which are for the perpetrators of great sins and those which are for the perpetrators of minor sins, they belong also to false witnesses."
And between birth and death, there is the loss of whatever good deeds have been performed. (Viṣṇu 8.26)
By truth the sun gives heat. (Viṣṇu 8.27)
By truth the moon shines. (Viṣṇu 8.28)
By truth the wind blows. (Viṣṇu 8.29)
By truth the earth is supported. (Viṣṇu 8.30)
By truth the waters stand firm. (Viṣṇu 8.31)
By truth, Agni [is established]. (Viṣṇu 8.32)
And space [is established] by truth. (Viṣṇu 8.33)
By truth, the gods [are pleased]. Viṣṇu 8.34.
By truth, the sacrifices [are sustained]. (Viṣṇu 8.35)
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale;
indeed, truth alone outweighed a thousand horse-sacrifices.
For those who, though knowing the facts, remain silent and indifferent when called upon as witnesses,
are equal to false witnesses in their sin and also in their punishment.
Thus indeed the king shall question the witnesses according to the order of their castes. He whose claim the witnesses declare to be true shall be the victor;
for him who speaks otherwise, defeat is certain.

In a conflict between witnesses, O lord of men, the king should accept the majority; when they are equal in number, he should accept those distinguished by their qualities; and when there is a conflict between those possessing qualities, he should accept the best among the twice-born.
In whatever legal dispute a false witness should speak untruth, that very matter shall be reversed; even if it has been executed, it shall be as if undone.
Viṣṇu 9.01 Now, the performance of oaths.
In cases of treason against the king and acts of violence, [the punishment shall be] as desired.
In cases of deposits and theft, the value of the object shall be the standard of measure.
In all matters concerning property, one should determine the value in terms of gold.
In that case, if it is short by one *kṛṣṇala*, he should cause a Śūdra to swear an oath with *dūrvā* grass in his hand.
A handful of sesame seeds deficient by two kṛṣṇalas [is the measure].
If it is deficient by three kṛṣṇalas, he shall pay a fine of silver.
If it is less than four kṛṣṇalas, the fine shall be one suvarṇa.
Viṣṇu 9.09: [He who holds] the plow, with his hand raised from the earth, [is seen] at the five black nights.
In the case of a Śūdra, a fine of half a suvarṇa less than one gold coin (kośa) shall be imposed.
Thereafter, as appropriate, one of the ordeals by the balance, fire, water, or poison [should be administered].
When the object is of double value, the rules regarding transactions as previously stated apply to the Vaiśya.
Viṣṇu 9.13: For a Kṣatriya, [the penance is] threefold.
For a Brāhmaṇa, the fine shall be fourfold, excluding the confiscation of his property.
One should not administer an ordeal to a Brāhmaṇa. (Viṣṇu 9.15)
Viṣṇu 9.16: Except for an action bound to a future time and occasion.
In the case of a treasury, one should cause a Brāhmaṇa who has taken earth dug up from a furrow to swear an oath.
Viṣṇu 9.18: Even when the offense previously observed is slight and the matter is of minor importance, one should cause the defendant to undergo one of the divine ordeals.
The virtuous do not disclose the conduct of the virtuous, even when a great matter is at stake.
The accuser shall pay the fine for the head. Viṣṇu 9.20.
And one who is accused shall undergo an ordeal.
Viṣṇu 9.22: In cases of treason against the king or acts of violence, [punishment may be inflicted] even without cutting off the head.
Viṣṇu 9.23: A balance should be provided for women, Brāhmaṇas, the deformed, the infirm, and the sick.
And that [fragrance] does not waft when there is no wind.
Viṣṇu 9.25: Fire must not be given to lepers, the infirm, or blacksmiths.
And during the autumn and summer seasons, Viṣṇu 9.26.
Viṣṇu 9.27: Poison must not be administered to lepers, those suffering from bile disorders, or Brāhmaṇas.
And during the rainy season, [he should bathe] at Viṣṇu. 9.28.
Viṣṇu 9.29: Water [should not be offered] for those afflicted by phlegm or disease, for the cowardly, for those suffering from asthma or coughing, nor for those who live by water.
And during the two seasons of Hemanta and Śiśira, [the same applies]. Viṣṇu 9.30.
Viṣṇu 9.31: A treasury must not be given to atheists.
Nor in a region afflicted by disease or pestilence. (Viṣṇu 9.32)
Having summoned one who has fasted overnight and bathed with his clothes on at sunrise,
he shall cause all the ordeals to be performed in the presence of the gods and Brahmins.
Viṣṇu 10.01 Now follows the ordeal by balance (dhaṭa).
Viṣṇu is four cubits in height and two cubits in width.
There, a balance made from a strong tree, five cubits long and with scales on both ends, [should be used].
And she shall be maintained by one among the following: a goldsmith, a brazier, or a blacksmith.
And there, he should place a man capable of performing divine feats in one scale, and a counterweight such as a stone in the second.
Having made two persons of equal weight well-marked—one as Viṣṇu and the other as the man—he should cause the man to descend.
And one should take up the ordeal by balance according to the established rule.
And [he saw] Tulādhāra, Viṣṇu 10.08.
Those worlds that are ordained for the slayers of Brahmins, and those worlds for false witnesses— those same worlds belong to the one who handles the scales dishonestly when weighing falsely.
O Viṣṇu, you are designated as the "Dhaṭa" by means of words that are synonyms for Dharma; O Dhaṭa, you alone know those things which human beings do not perceive.
"O Viṣṇu, this man, accused in a legal dispute, is being weighed upon you;
therefore, you ought to save him from this doubt in accordance with Dharma."
Then he should place that man once again upon the scale in the pan;
if, when weighed, he increases [in weight], then he is pure according to the law.
If the carrying-sling breaks or the axle snaps, one should again mount the man [on the scale]. For in this way, knowledge free from doubt arises, which leads to a definitive conclusion.
Viṣṇu 11.01 Now, concerning the fire.
One should draw seven circles with an interval of sixteen finger-breadths each.
Then, one should place seven *aśvattha* leaves in the hands of [the person] who is facing east with both arms extended.
And one should wrap those two hands, together with the thread, with a cord.
Then, there, one should place an iron ball weighing fifty palas, which is even and glowing with the color of fire.
Having taken him up, he should proceed, neither too quickly nor too slowly, placing his feet in measured steps within the circles.
Then, having passed beyond the seventh circle, one should drop a ball of iron upon the ground.
Viṣṇu 11.08a: One whose hands are burnt anywhere [during the ordeal] should be declared impure. Viṣṇu 11.08c: But that man who is not burnt at all shall be considered pure.
But if one causes [the accused] to fall out of fear, or if he is burnt and cannot be clearly discerned,
one should make him carry the metal again because the ordeal has not been purified by the agreement.
One should first examine his hands for signs of having crushed grains;
then, having consecrated them with mantras, one should place a lump of iron upon his hands.
O Agni, you move within all beings like a witness;
O Agni, you alone know those things which human beings do not know.
"Viṣṇu 11.12a: This man, accused in a legal dispute, desires purification.
Viṣṇu 11.12c: Therefore, you ought to save him from this uncertainty in accordance with dharma."
Viṣṇu 12.01 Now, regarding water.
In water that is free from mud, moss, wicked crocodiles, fish, leeches, and the like—Viṣṇu 12.02.
There, having grasped the knees of another person who is immersed up to the navel and is free from disease and malice, one should enter the consecrated water.
At that same moment, another man should discharge an arrow with a bow that is neither too harsh nor too soft.
And another man would swiftly bring that arrow back.
Among those, he who is not seen is proclaimed pure;
otherwise, he would be impure even upon the sight of a single limb.
O Viṣṇu, you move within the waters of all beings like a witness;
you alone know those waters which mortals do not know.
"O Viṣṇu, this man, accused in a legal dispute, is sinking into you."
Therefore, you ought to save him from this doubt in accordance with dharma.
Viṣṇu 13.01 Now, concerning poison.
Viṣṇu 13.02: All kinds of poisons are not to be given [as gifts].
Except for the Śārṅga bow produced from the Himālaya mountains.
And one should give seven barley grains soaked in clarified butter to the person under accusation.
If the poison is digested easily, free from its initial impulse and fatigue,
then knowing him to be pure, one should release him at the end of the day.
O Poison, because of your nature as poison and your treacherous character, you are cruel toward all embodied beings;
you alone, O Poison, know those things which human beings do not know.
"This man, accused in a legal dispute, desires purification;
therefore, you ought to rescue him from this doubt in accordance with dharma."
Viṣṇu 14.01 Now, the treasury.
Having worshipped the fierce deities, one should drink three handfuls of water from their ritual bathing.
Saying, "This was not done by me," he stands facing the installed deity.
Within fourteen days, or even within twenty-one days,
he shall see disease, fire, the death of a kinsman, or perhaps a royal calamity.
One should recognize him as impure, and likewise as pure in the opposite case;
and the righteous king should honor a man who has been proven pure in an ordeal.
Viṣṇu 15.01 Now, there are twelve kinds of sons.
Viṣṇu 15.02: One begotten by oneself upon a wife of one's own caste who has been consecrated is the first [type of son], the legitimate (aurasa).
A son begotten by a man of the highest caste upon a woman who has been duly authorized by her sapinda relative is the second [type], the *kṣetraja*.
Viṣṇu 15.04: The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra) is the third.
"She who is given by her father with the stipulation, 'Whosoever is her son shall be my son,' is a *putrikā*. (Viṣṇu 15.05)

Even if she was bestowed according to the rite for an appointed daughter (*putrikā-vidhi*) without [the formal agreement], if she is without a brother, she is indeed an appointed daughter (*putrikā*).
The fourth is the paunarbhava (the son of a remarried woman).
A woman who has been consecrated again with the *akṣata* rite is called a *punarbhū*.
Furthermore, even one who has previously belonged to another man is not [considered] unrefined [if she has been married according to the rites].
The fifth is the son of an unmarried woman (kānīna), according to Viṣṇu 15.10.
Viṣṇu 15.11: He who is begotten by one who has not been consecrated while still in her father's house.
And he [is the master] of the one who takes her hand.
And the sixth is one born in secret within the house.
Viṣṇu 15.14: He belongs to the one from whose bed he was born.
The son born of a pregnant bride (sahoḍha) is the seventh.
Viṣṇu 15.16: The son of a woman who undergoes the sacramental rite while pregnant belongs to her [biological father].
And he [belongs] to the one who took his hand in marriage. Viṣṇu 15.17.
And Dattaka is the eighth. (Viṣṇu 15.18)
And he belongs to those by whom he was given to his mother and father. (Viṣṇu 15.19)
And the ninth is the purchased [son]. Viṣṇu 15.20.
And he belongs to the one by whom he was purchased. (Viṣṇu 15.21)
The tenth [type of gift] is that which comes to one of its own accord; this is [the nature of] Viṣṇu. 15.22.
And he belongs to whichever [deity] he has approached.
The eleventh, however, is the apaviddha.
Viṣṇu 15.25: One who has been abandoned by his father and mother.
And he [is the one] by whom that [sacrifice] was undertaken.
And wherever he was born, he became the twelfth [in that lineage]. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 15.27)
Among these, each preceding one is superior to the next.
He alone is the inheritor of the estate. (Viṣṇu 15.29)
And he should support others as well. (Viṣṇu 15.30)
For those who have not been married, he should perform the sacramental rite according to his own means.
Those who are outcastes, eunuchs, those with incurable diseases, or those who are physically deformed do not receive a share of the inheritance.
Viṣṇu 15.33: They are to be maintained by those who inherit their property.
And their legitimate sons (aurasa) are the heirs to their shares.
But not for one who has fallen [from his caste]. (Viṣṇu 15.35)
Viṣṇu 15.36: But when a patanīya act has been committed, those born subsequently [are also affected].
And those born of women in the inverse order of castes have no share in the inheritance. (Viṣṇu 15.37)
His sons [acted] even regarding the property of their grandfather, Viṣṇu 15.38.
Those who take portions [of the property] must be supported by them.
And he who takes the wealth shall also be the giver of the funeral cake (piṇḍa).
Viṣṇu 15.41: Even among women married to one man, the son of one is indeed the son of all.
And [the same applies] to brothers born of the same father. (Viṣṇu 15.42)
Viṣṇu 15.43: Even if a son does not obtain the paternal wealth, he should offer the funeral cake (piṇḍa).
Because a son saves his father from the hell named Put,
he was therefore called "putra" by the Self-existent One himself.
In this son, the father pays off his debt and attains immortality,
provided that he beholds the face of the son who has been born alive.
Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains infinity;
and through the grandson of a son, one reaches the realm of the Sun.
Viṣṇu 15.47a: In this world, no distinction is found between a grandson and a daughter’s son.
Viṣṇu 15.47c: For even a daughter’s son delivers a man who has no son, just like a grandson.
Viṣṇu 16.01: Sons born of women of the same caste as their father are of the same caste as themselves.
Viṣṇu 16.02: From women of the same caste as their mothers, born in the direct order of castes, [the sons] are of the same caste as their mothers.
Those born from women of inverse order are despised by the noble.
Among them, the son of a Vaiśya woman by a Śūdra father is an Āyogava.
Viṣṇu 16.05: The Pulkasa and the Māgadha are the sons of a Kṣatriya woman by Vaiśya and Śūdra fathers, respectively.
And the Caṇḍāla, the Vaidehaka, and the Sūta are the sons of a Brāhmaṇī woman by a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, and a Kṣatriya, respectively.
And the mixtures of mixtures are innumerable.
Viṣṇu 16.08: The descent of the stage for the Āyogavas.
The state of being a hunter belongs to the Pulkasas.
Viṣṇu 16.10: The act of praise belongs to the Māgadhas.
And for Caṇḍālas, the occupation is the execution of those condemned to death (Viṣṇu 16.11).
The protection of women and their livelihoods belong to the Vaidehakas.
Viṣṇu 16.13: For charioteers, the management of horses and chariots.
Viṣṇu 16.14: For Caṇḍālas, the specific rules are dwelling outside the village and wearing the clothes of the deceased.
And for all [these], marriage shall be with those of the same caste.
And the embezzlement of one's father's wealth. (Viṣṇu 16.16)
Viṣṇu 16.17a: These castes born of intermixture have been shown according to their fathers and mothers;
Viṣṇu 16.17c: whether they are concealed or manifest, they are to be known by their own respective occupations.
The self-sacrifice of the body for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or for the sake of cows, performed without seeking reward,
as well as [dying] in the protection of women, children, and others, is the cause of liberation for those outside [the fold].
Viṣṇu 17.01: If a father divides his property among his sons, he may do so according to his own will regarding wealth acquired by himself.
But regarding property inherited from a grandfather, the ownership of both father and son is equal.
Viṣṇu 17.03: Those who have divided the paternal estate shall give a share to one born after the partition.
The property of one who dies without a son goes to his wife.
In the absence of that, it goes to the daughter (Viṣṇu 17.05).
In the absence of that [heir], it goes to the paternal ancestors (Viṣṇu 17.06).
In the absence of those, it goes to the mother (Viṣṇu 17.07).
In the absence of that [heir], it goes to the brother (Viṣṇu 17.08).
In the absence of those, it goes to the brother's son (Viṣṇu 17.09).
In the absence of that [heir], it goes to the kinsman (Viṣṇu 17.10).
In the absence of those, it goes to a kinsman (sakulya).
In the absence of that [heir], it goes to one who studied together with him (Viṣṇu 17.12).
Viṣṇu 17.13: In the absence of those [heirs], the property goes to the king, with the exception of the wealth of a Brāhmaṇa.
The purpose of the Brahmins is for the sake of the Brahmins. (Viṣṇu 17.14)
The preceptor shall take the property of a forest hermit (vānaprastha). Viṣṇu 17.15.
Or a student [may do so]. Viṣṇu 17.16.
A reunited coparcener shall inherit the share of one who was reunited, and a uterine brother that of a uterine brother;
he shall both give and take the share of one who is born or one who has died.

Viṣṇu 17.18: What is given by the father, the mother, the son, or the brother; what is received at the nuptial fire; what is given upon supersession; what is given by a kinsman; the bride-price (śulka); and the subsequent gift (anvādheya)—these constitute the woman’s property (strīdhana).
In the case of the four marriages beginning with the Brāhma, if she dies childless, [the property] belongs to her husband.
And among the remaining [heirs], the father shall take [the share].
Viṣṇu 17.21: Whatever wealth exists among all [the brothers] when [the mother] has given birth [to a daughter], that goes to the daughter.
If ornaments have been worn by women while their husband was still living, the heirs shall not divide them; those who do divide them fall from their caste.
But for those who have multiple fathers, the allotment of shares is according to the father;
whatever paternal inheritance belongs to a man, he shall take that, and no other.
Viṣṇu 18.01: If a Brāhmaṇa should have sons from the four castes, they shall divide the paternal inheritance into ten parts.
In that case, the son of a Brāhmaṇa woman shall take four shares.
A son of a Kṣatriya woman [from a Brāhmaṇa father] inherits three shares. Viṣṇu 18.03.
The son of a Vaiśya woman has two shares. (Viṣṇu 18.04)
But the son of a Śūdra woman inherits one share, according to Viṣṇu 18.05.
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa should have three sons, excluding a Śūdra, then they shall divide that wealth into nine parts.
According to the sequence of castes, they shall take shares divided into four, three, and two parts respectively.
Excluding the Vaiśya, [the remaining castes] shall take four, three, and one [shares] respectively from the property divided into eight parts.
Viṣṇu 18.09: [The earth] was divided into seven parts, excluding the Kṣatriyas—four, two, and one.
Viṣṇu 18.10: With the exception of the Brāhmaṇas, [the other castes] are divided into six groups—three, two, and one.
Viṣṇu 18.11: Among the sons of a Kṣatriya by a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, and a Śūdra wife, this same division [of inheritance] applies.
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa should have two sons, a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya, then from the wealth divided into seven parts, the Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares.
A member of the royal caste [should recite] three [verses]. (Viṣṇu 18.13)
Now, if there is a Brāhmaṇa [father] with two sons, a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya, then, when the estate is divided into six parts, the Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares.
A Vaiśya has two shares. (Viṣṇu 18.15)
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa should have two sons, a Brāhmaṇa and a Śūdra, then they should divide that wealth into five parts.
A Brāhmaṇa, however, may take four shares. (Viṣṇu 18.17)
A Śūdra [should perform penance] for one year. (Viṣṇu 18.18)
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should have two sons who are a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, then they should divide that wealth into five parts.
A Kṣatriya, however, may take three shares. (Viṣṇu 18.20)
A Vaiśya has two shares. (Viṣṇu 18.21)
Now, if a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should have two sons, one a Kṣatriya and the other a Śūdra, then they should divide that wealth into four parts.
A Kṣatriya, however, may take three shares, according to Viṣṇu 18.23.
Viṣṇu 18.24: A Śūdra [shall pay] one [paṇa].
Viṣṇu 18.25: Now, if a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya should have two sons who are a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, then they should divide that wealth into three parts.
A Vaiśya may take two shares. (Viṣṇu 18.26)
Viṣṇu 18.27: A Śūdra [shall pay] one [paṇa].
Now, the sons of a Brāhmaṇa born of a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya wife, if he has only one son, shall take the entire inheritance.
Viṣṇu 18.29: For a Kṣatriya, [the sons] are a Rājanya and a Vaiśya.
Viṣṇu 18.30: For a Vaiśya, [the witness] must be a Vaiśya.
A Śūdra [is the heir] for a Śūdra. (Viṣṇu 18.31)
Among the twice-born, however, a Śūdra son alone shall take half the inheritance.
Whatever destiny awaits the inheritance of one who dies without a son, that same destiny belongs here to the second half [of the estate].
The mothers take away their shares according to the portion of the son. (Viṣṇu 18.34)
And unmarried daughters [shall receive a share]. Viṣṇu 18.35.
Sons of the same caste as their father shall take equal shares.
Viṣṇu 18.37: They should give the best extra portion to the eldest.

Viṣṇu 18.38: If there should be two sons of a Brāhmaṇī and one son of a Śūdrā, then, of the property divided into nine parts, the two sons of the Brāhmaṇī shall take eight shares and the son of the Śūdrā shall take one.

Now, if there should be two sons by a Śūdra woman and one son by a Brāhmaṇa woman, then of the property divided into six parts, the Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares, and the two Śūdra sons shall take two shares.
By this sequence, the allotment of portions occurs elsewhere as well.
If those who were previously divided, living together again, should divide once more, the division there shall be equal; in that case, the right of primogeniture does not exist.
That which one acquires through one's own labor without depleting the paternal estate— being obtained by one's own effort— that, if not desired, one is not obliged to give away.
But when one recovers ancestral property that had not been obtained, he shall not share it with his sons; likewise, what he has acquired by himself without desire [for gain] belongs to him alone.
Clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, women, security of possession, pasture grounds, and books are not to be divided.
Viṣṇu 19.01: One should not have a deceased twice-born man carried out by a Śūdra.
A twice-born man shall not [teach] a Śūdra.
Viṣṇu 19.03: Sons shall carry out the funeral rites for their father and mother.
Śūdras [should not eat] even a twice-born father.
Those Brahmins who carry out the funeral rites for a Brahmin who is without a protector partake in the heavenly world.
Having carried out the deceased relative and performed the funeral rites, they should approach the pyre from the left and perform an immersion in water while still wearing their clothes.
Having performed the offering of water for the deceased, they should offer a single funeral ball (*piṇḍa*) upon *kuśa* grass.
Having changed their garments and bitten neem leaves, they should place their foot upon a stone at the doorway and then enter the house.
And they should throw unbroken grains (*akṣata*) into the fire. (Viṣṇu 19.09)
On the fourth day, they should perform the collection of the bones.
Viṣṇu 19.11: Their [bones] are to be cast into the waters of the Gaṅgā.
As many thousands of years as the bones of a person remain in the waters of the Gaṅgā, for that long he dwells in the heavenly world.
Viṣṇu 19.13: For as long as the period of impurity lasts, they should offer water and one funeral cake (piṇḍa) for the deceased.
And they should subsist on food that has been purchased or obtained [as alms].
And they shall abstain from eating meat. (Viṣṇu 19.15)
Viṣṇu 19.16: [They are] those who sleep on the bare ground.
And those who sleep separately [from their wives]. Viṣṇu 19.17.

Having departed from the village at the end of the period of impurity, and having had their beards shaved, they should enter their homes after bathing with a paste of sesame or mustard seeds and changing their clothes.
Having performed the rite of pacification there, they should perform the worship of the Brahmins.
Viṣṇu 19.20: The gods are the invisible gods; the Brāhmaṇas are the visible gods.
The worlds are sustained by the Brahmins. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 19.21)
By the grace of the Brāhmaṇas, the deities abide in heaven;
a word spoken by a Brāhmaṇa never becomes false anywhere.

Whatever the Brāhmaṇas, being most highly satisfied, declare, that the deities welcome with approval. When those who have the gods manifest before them are satisfied, the gods who are beyond the senses are likewise constantly satisfied.
Those of undaunted spirit should offer consolation to those afflicted by grief who have lost their kinsmen;
O Earth, delightful to the mind, I shall now declare to you those words with which they should do so.
That which is the northern course of the sun is the day of the gods.
The southern solstice is night for Viṣṇu.
A year is a day and night for Viṣṇu.
Thirty of those [fortnights] constitute a month.
Twelve months constitute a year. Viṣṇu 20.05.
The Kali Yuga consists of twelve hundred divine years.
The Dvāpara age consists of twice that number [of years].
The three qualities [of the age] constitute the Tretā.
The Kṛta Yuga consists of four such units.
Twelve thousand divine years constitute a cycle of four ages (catur-yuga).
Seventy-one cycles of four yugas constitute a manvantara.
And a thousand cycles of the four yugas constitute a kalpa.
And that [period] is one day of the Grandfather (Pitāmaha).
And his night is of the same duration.
By means of such a day-and-night, according to the calculation of months and years, the lifespan of the entire Brahmā is one hundred years.
A day of Puruṣa is delimited by the lifespan of Brahmā.
At the end of that [day], there is a great kalpa (mahākalpa).
His night is of exactly the same duration.
Viṣṇu Purāṇa 20.19: There is simply no number for the days and nights of human beings that have already passed.
And not for those yet to come. (Viṣṇu 20.20)
Because time has neither beginning nor end. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 20.21)
Thus, in this supportless time that is constantly moving forward,
I do not perceive any being whose stability would be permanent.
The grains of sand in the Gaṅgā and the drops of rain when Indra pours it down can be counted in this world, but the deceased ancestors cannot.
In every kalpa, fourteen lords of the gods perish,
as do the fourteen Manus who are the foremost in all the worlds.
Many thousands of Indras and millions of lords of Daityas have perished here through time; what then can be said of human beings?
Many royal sages, endowed with all virtues,
as well as gods and celestial rishis, have met their end through the power of time.
Those who are capable of being the cause of creation and destruction in this world—
even they are led away by Time, for Time is indeed difficult to overcome.
Having been overtaken by time, every living being is led to the next world; since a creature is subject to the fetters of its own actions, what cause for lamentation is there in that?
For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain.
Since this matter is unavoidable, there is no companionship in this world.
Since people grieving here do not benefit the deceased, one should therefore not weep; rather, the funeral rites should be performed according to one's own ability.
For one who departs with both his good deeds and his evil deeds as his companions,
