what need has he for kinsmen, whether they grieve or not?
While his kinsmen are in a state of impurity, the deceased finds no rest;
therefore, he returns to those very people who offer the funeral cakes and water.
One who has died remains a *preta* until the performance of the *sapindīkaraṇa* rite;
to that *preta* who has gone to the world of the dead, one should offer food along with a water-pot.
And having gone to the world of the ancestors, one eats food at a śrāddha that is equal to the svadhā offering;
therefore, offer the śrāddha for him who has gone to the world of the ancestors.
Whether in the state of a god, in a place of torment, in the womb of an animal,
or likewise in the human state, one receives the śrāddha offered by one's own kinsmen.
When a śrāddha has been performed, nourishment for both the deceased and the performer of the śrāddha is certain.
Therefore, having abandoned useless grief, a śrāddha should always be performed.
Only this much should always be done for the deceased by his kinsmen;
a man should not seek to benefit the deceased by grieving, for he only harms himself.
"Seeing the world without refuge and kinsmen dying,
O men, always choose Dharma alone as your companion."
Even when dead, a kinsman is unable to follow a deceased man;
for, with the exception of a wife, the path to Yama is closed to everyone else.
"Virtue alone follows him wherever he goes;
indeed, in this worthless world of mortals, practice virtue without delay."
One should do tomorrow's work today, and the afternoon's work in the forenoon;
for death does not wait to see whether one's task is finished or unfinished.
Death seizes and departs with one who is attached to fields, shops, or houses, while his mind is elsewhere, just as a she-wolf seizes a lamb.
No one is dear to Time, nor is anyone its enemy;
when the lifespan resulting from one's karma is exhausted, it forcibly carries away the person.
One whose time has not yet arrived does not die, even if pierced by hundreds of arrows;
but one whose time has come does not live, even if merely touched by the tip of a blade of kusha grass.
Neither medicines, nor mantras, nor burnt offerings,
nor even recitations can save a human being who is overtaken by death or even by old age.
For even with hundreds of precautions, one is not able to ward off a future calamity;
what lamentation can there be in that regard?
Just as a calf finds its mother among a thousand cows,
so does the deed performed in the past certainly find its doer.
Beings are unmanifest in their origin and manifest in their middle state, and indeed unmanifest again in their end; what cause for lamentation is there in this?
Just as the embodied soul passes through childhood, youth, and old age within this body, so too does it attain another body; the wise man is not deluded by this.
Just as a person here takes up a garment after discarding one previously worn,
even so the embodied soul takes up a new body bound by its past actions.
Weapons do not cut him; fire does not burn him;
water does not moisten him; and the wind does not dry him up.
This [Self] is incapable of being cut, incapable of being burnt, incapable of being moistened, and indeed incapable of being dried;
it is eternal, ever-moving, fixed, immovable, and ancient.
"He is called unmanifest, inconceivable, and immutable;
therefore, knowing him thus, you ought not to grieve."

Viṣṇu 21.01 Now, upon the cessation of the period of impurity, having bathed well, having thoroughly washed his hands and feet, and having sipped water according to the rules, he should feed Brāhmaṇas of such a kind as he is able, facing northward, and honored with perfumes, garlands, garments, ornaments, and other such items.
Viṣṇu 21.02: One should modify the mantras in the singular when only one person is intended.
In the vicinity of the remnants, one should offer a single *piṇḍa* using his name and lineage (*nāma-gotra*).

When the Brahmins have finished eating and have been honored with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), he should offer inexhaustible water (akṣayyodaka) under the name and lineage of the deceased; then he should make three furrows, four finger-breadths wide, that much apart from each other, and that much deep, each one span (vitasti) long.
And having established three fires near the trench (karṣū) and strewn sacrificial grass around them, he should offer three oblations into each of them.
To Soma, who honors the ancestors, Svadhā! Homage!
To Agni Kavyavāhana, Svadhā! Homage! Viṣṇu 21.07.
To Yama, to Aṅgiras, svadhā, obeisance! Viṣṇu 21.08.
And at the three places, one should perform the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) as before.
Having filled three trenches with rice, curd, ghee, honey, and meat, one should mutter the mantra "etat te" (this is for you).
In this manner, one should perform [the rites] for the deceased every month until the anniversary of death.
At the end of the year, one should feed Brahmins, preceded by the gods, for the deceased, his father, his grandfather, and his great-grandfather.
Viṣṇu 21.13: Here, one should perform the offering into the fire (agnaukaraṇa), the invocation (āvāhana), and the water for the feet (pādya).
One should join [the water] from the vessel for the guest's feet with the three vessels for the ancestors' feet, reciting: "May the earth unite with you" (Viṣṇu 21.14).
Viṣṇu 21.15: One should place four rice-balls (piṇḍas) in the vicinity of the remnants of the meal.
And having followed the Brahmins who have finished their meal and been given sacrificial fees, he should dismiss them.
Then, one should place the *preta*-piṇḍa among the three piṇḍas, just like the water from the vessel for the *pādya* offering.
Viṣṇu 21.18: Even when in close proximity to the three trenches, the procedure is exactly the same.

Having performed the Śrāddha for twelve days according to the procedure for the monthly rites including the Piṇḍīkaraṇa, one should perform the Sapindikarana on either the thirteenth day or at the conclusion of the monthly rites.
For Śūdras, however, [the rite] on the twelfth day is performed excluding the recitation of mantras.
If an intercalary month (adhimāsa) should occur within the course of a year, then one should add one day for the purpose of the monthly rite.
The *piṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for women should be performed in the same manner;
likewise, one should perform the *śrāddha* every year for as long as one lives.
For one whose *sapindīkaraṇa* has been performed before the completion of a year,
one should also give food along with a water-pot to a twice-born man for the duration of a year.
Viṣṇu 22.01: For a Brāhmaṇa, there is ten days of impurity (*āśauca*) upon the birth or death of those who share the funeral rice-ball (*sapinda*).
For a Kṣatriya, the period is twelve days.
For a Vaiśya, it is fifteen days. (Viṣṇu 22.03)
For a Śūdra, it is one month. (Viṣṇu 22.04)
And the offering of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) ceases with the seventh person [in the lineage].

During a period of ritual impurity (āśauca), the performance of fire-oblations (homa), giving gifts (dāna), receiving gifts (pratigraha), and the private recitation of the Veda (svādhyāya) are suspended.
Viṣṇu 22.07: One should not eat the food of anyone during a period of impurity.
If one eats food even once from those who are in a state of impurity, such as Brāhmaṇas and others, his own period of impurity lasts for as long as theirs.
Viṣṇu 22.09: Upon the cessation of impurity, one should perform an expiation.

Viṣṇu 22.10: If a twice-born man eats while there is impurity due to a death or birth in his own caste, he should go to a flowing river, immerse himself therein, recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, and having emerged, recite the Gāyatrī eight thousand times.
Viṣṇu 22.11: But a Brāhmaṇa, having fasted during the period of impurity caused by the death of a Kṣatriya, becomes pure after performing this very same rite.
And a Kṣatriya [is subject to impurity] during the period of impurity of a Vaiśya. (Viṣṇu 22.12)
During the period of impurity for a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa shall fast for three nights.

Viṣṇu 22.14: During the period of impurity for a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, and during the period of impurity for a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya shall go to a flowing river and mutter the Gāyatrī five hundred times.
And a Vaiśya, during the period of impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, should mutter the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times.
If a twice-born man eats during the period of impurity of a Śūdra, he shall perform the Prājāpatya penance.
And a Śūdra shall perform a ritual bath during the period of impurity of the twice-born.
A Śūdra, having bathed during the period of impurity caused by a Śūdra's death, should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
ViṣṨu 22.19: For wives and slaves, the period of impurity is equal to that of their master, according to the order of their castes.
When the master has died, [the property] belongs to the self (the heirs).
Viṣṇu 22.21: For those of lower caste who have sapinda relations among those of higher caste, purification occurs at the end of that [higher caste’s] period of impurity.
For a Brāhmaṇa, among sapinda relations who are Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, the periods of impurity are six nights, three nights, and one night respectively.
For a Kṣatriya, [the penance for killing] a Vaiśya or a Śūdra is six nights or three nights respectively.
For a Vaiśya among Śūdras, purification occurs after six nights.
In the case of a miscarriage, the penance lasts for as many days and nights as there were months of pregnancy.
In the case of a child born dead or one who dies shortly after birth, there is immediate purification for the family.
In the case of a child who has not yet grown teeth, if it dies, purification occurs immediately.
For him there is no cremation with fire, nor the ritual offering of water.
But if [the child] has teethed but the tonsure ceremony (*cūḍā*) has not yet been performed, [the impurity lasts] for one day and night.
But for one whose tonsure ceremony has been performed yet who remains unsanctified by other rites, [the impurity lasts] three nights.
Thereafter, at the time as previously stated.
Viṣṇu 22.32: Marriage is the sacramental rite for women.
Viṣṇu 22.33: Among women who have been consecrated [in marriage], there is no impurity for the paternal kin.
Viṣṇu 22.34: If her birth or death should occur while she is in her father’s house, then there shall be impurity for one night and three nights, respectively.
Viṣṇu 22.35: If another birth-impurity should occur during the midst of an impurity caused by birth, then purification occurs upon the cessation of the first impurity.
Viṣṇu 22.36: At the end of the night, [the purification is] by two days.
Viṣṇu 22.37: [If performed] at dawn, [the result is obtained] in three days.
Viṣṇu 22.38: Likewise, if a relative dies during the period of impurity caused by a death, the same rule applies.
Having heard [of a birth or death] while staying in another country, one shall become pure by means of the remainder of the period of impurity for birth and death.
Viṣṇu 22.40: When the period of impurity has passed, [the purification] at the end of a year is by means of a single night.
After that, [it is purified] by bathing. (Viṣṇu 22.41)
When the preceptor and the maternal grandfather have passed away, [the impurity lasts] for three nights.
Viṣṇu 22.43a: When sons other than the legitimate son of the body have been born or have died;
Viṣṇu 22.43c: and when wives who had previously belonged to another have given birth or have died.

Viṣṇu 22.44: In the case of the death of the teacher’s wife, a son, a sub-teacher, a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, a brother-in-law, a fellow student, or a pupil, purification occurs after one night.
And [one should not eat] in the house of the king of one's own country (Viṣṇu 22.45).
And when one who is not a *sapiṇḍa* has died in one's own house. (Viṣṇu 22.46)
According to Viṣṇu 22.47, there is no period of impurity for those killed by Bhṛgu (a sage), fire, fasting, water, in battle, by lightning, or by a king.
Nor [is there any fault] for kings in their kingly duties.
Not [is there any fault] for those observing vows while they are in the state of a vow. (Viṣṇu 22.49)
Nor [should one study] during the sacrificial session of those performing a long-term sacrifice (sattra).
Viṣṇu 22.51: Not [impurity] for artisans in the performance of their craft.
For those who carry out the king's commands, there is no fault by his will.
Viṣṇu 22.53: [The impurity does not apply] during the installation of a deity or a marriage, provided the preparations for them have already been made.
Viṣṇu 22.54: Not during a disturbance of the country.
And even in times of dire distress, Viṣṇu 22.55.
Those who commit suicide and those who are outcasts do not participate in the impurity rites or the water libations.
On the day of death, the female slave of one who has fallen [from caste] should kick away a pot of water with her foot.
He who cuts the noose of one who has died by hanging is purified by the *tapta-kṛcchra* penance. (Viṣṇu 22.58)
Viṣṇu 22.59: And one who performs the funeral rites for those who have committed suicide [is also not purified].
And one who causes the shedding of tears for that [person] [is also liable]. Viṣṇu 22.60.
Viṣṇu 22.61: For every deceased person, [the purification] occurs through bathing after the relatives have shed tears together.
If the collection of bones has not yet been performed, purification occurs by bathing with one's clothes on.

Having followed the funeral procession of a Śūdra deceased, a twice-born man should go to a river, immerse himself therein, recite the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, and upon emerging, recite the Gāyatrī eight thousand times.
Viṣṇu 22.64: For the funeral rites of a deceased twice-born man, one hundred and eight [oblations] are prescribed.
A Śūdra, having followed a deceased person, should perform a ritual bath.
Upon inhaling the smoke from a funeral pyre, all social classes (varṇas) should perform a ritual bath.
Viṣṇu 22.67: [One should bathe] after sexual intercourse, a bad dream, when the throat is filled with blood, and after vomiting or purging.
And also when the act of shaving the beard has been performed. (Viṣṇu 22.68)
And having touched one who has touched a corpse, or a menstruating woman, a Caṇḍāla, or a sacrificial post (yūpa), [one must bathe].
Except for edible [meat], one should avoid the corpse of a five-clawed animal, as well as its bones and fat.
In all these baths, one should not wear a garment that has not been washed.
A woman in her menses becomes pure by bathing on the fourth day.
Viṣṇu 22.73: A menstruating woman, having touched another menstruating woman of lower caste, shall not eat until she has become purified.
Having touched a woman of the same caste or of a higher caste, one becomes pure immediately by bathing.

Having sneezed, slept, eaten, or being desirous of eating or studying; having drunk, bathed, spat, put on a garment, walked upon a road, voided urine or feces, or touched the bone of a five-clawed animal that is not fatty—one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
And [the same applies] to conversing with Caṇḍālas or Mlecchas (Viṣṇu 22.76).
Viṣṇu 22.77: One who is defiled below the navel or on the forearms by bodily impurities, or by spirituous liquors or wines, shall become pure by washing that limb with earth and water.
If one is struck elsewhere [by poison], one should wash that limb with water mixed with earth and then bathe.
But one who has been struck by [the breath from] the mouth [of a corpse] should fast and bathe with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
And one who has been struck by the lip [of another]. Viṣṇu 22.80.
Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, earwax,
sweat, nails, phlegm, tears, and rheum from the eyes— these twelve are the impurities of human beings.
Gauḍī, mādhvī, and paiṣṭī are to be known as the three kinds of *surā*.
Just as one is, so are all; they must not be drunk by the twice-born.
Mādhūka, ikṣu-ṭāṅka, kaula, dates and jackfruit juice,
grape juice, honey-wine (mādhvīka), maireya, and coconut liquor.
"These ten kinds of liquor are impure for a Brāhmaṇa;
however, a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya do not incur sin by touching them."
But a disciple, performing the ancestral rites for his deceased teacher,
becomes pure there after ten nights, together with those who consume the funeral food.
Having carried out the funeral rites for his own teacher, sub-teacher, father, mother, or guru who has died, one who is under a vow is not deprived of his vow.
One who has been assigned a penance shall not perform the water-libation until the completion of the vow;
but once it is completed, having performed the water-libation, he becomes pure after three nights alone.
Knowledge, austerity, fire, food, earth, mind, water,
smearing with cow-dung, wind, ritual action, the sun, and time— these are the purifiers of embodied beings.
Among all forms of purity, the purity of food is declared to be supreme. He who is pure regarding food is truly pure; one who is merely purified by earth and water is not pure.
The learned are purified by forbearance; those who have committed improper acts are purified by charity;
those whose sins are concealed are purified by the recitation of prayers; and those most proficient in the Vedas are purified by austerity.
That which is to be purified is cleansed by earth and water; a river is purified by its current;
a woman is purified by her menses; and the best of the twice-born are purified by renunciation.
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the inner self (bhūtātman) is purified by learning and austerity; and the intellect is purified by knowledge.
Viṣṇu 22.93a: This decision regarding bodily purification has been declared to you.
Viṣṇu 22.93c: Now hear the decision concerning the purification of various kinds of objects.
Viṣṇu 23.01: That which is defiled by bodily impurities, by fermented liquors, or by intoxicants is considered "extremely defiled."
Viṣṇu 23.02: All metal vessels that have been excessively defiled shall be purified by being cast into fire.
Viṣṇu 23.03: A vessel made of jewels or stone, as well as one made of lotus-fiber, [is purified] by burying it in the earth for seven nights.
Viṣṇu 23.04: [An image] made of horn, ivory, or bone, by means of carving.
One should discard [an image] made of wood or clay. Viṣṇu 23.05.
If a garment that has been excessively damaged becomes clean after being washed, one should cut it away.
Gold, silver, lotuses, and objects made of gems are purified by water, as they are not subject to defilement.
Viṣṇu 23.08: [The purification] of cups made of stone, as well as of the *graha* vessels.
Viṣṇu 23.09: [The purification] of the *caru* vessel, the *sruk*, and the *sruva* ladles is performed with hot water.
Viṣṇu 23.10: By wiping the sacrificial vessels with the hand during the performance of a sacrifice.
Viṣṇu 23.11: By sprinkling [water] upon the wooden sword, the winnowing basket, the cart, the pestle, and the mortar.
And [the same applies] to beds, vehicles, and seats. (Viṣṇu 23.12)
And [the same applies] to many [wives]. (Viṣṇu 23.13)
And [the same rules apply] to grains, skins, ropes, woven cloth, wickerwork, thread, and cotton garments.
And [the same applies] to vegetables, roots, fruits, and flowers. (Viṣṇu 23.15)
And [the same applies] to grass, wood, and dry leaves. (Viṣṇu 23.16)
Viṣṇu 23.17: By washing these [limbs].
And [the same applies] to small quantities. (Viṣṇu 23.18)
Viṣṇu 23.19: [The purification] of silk and woolen cloth is by means of alkaline substances.
Viṣṇu 23.20: With *ariṣṭaka* wood for the *kutapa* vessels.
Viṣṇu 23.21: [The purification] of silk cloths is by means of *śrī-phala* fruits.
For linen garments, [the purification is] with white mustard seeds; thus says Viṣṇu (23.22).
And [the same applies] to objects made of horn, bone, and ivory. (Viṣṇu 23.23)
Viṣṇu 23.24: [The price] of deer-skin garments is measured by lotus-eyes.
For those made of copper, brass, tin, and lead, [cleaning] is done with acidic water.
One should purify bell-metal and iron with ashes. (Viṣṇu 23.26)
Viṣṇu 23.27: [The purification] of wooden objects is by planing.
With cow-hair [brushes], [one should clean] vessels made of fruit.
According to Viṣṇu 23.29, [the purification] of things that are joined together is by means of sprinkling (prokṣaṇa).
For liquids, purification is by means of straining.
Viṣṇu 23.31: By means of extinguishing water and fire, [one may destroy] abundant products of sugarcane, such as molasses and the like, which have been stored in the house.
And [the same applies] to all types of salt, Viṣṇu 23.32.
Viṣṇu 23.33: [The purification] of earthen vessels is by means of firing them again.
Viṣṇu 23.34: By re-consecrating images of deities that have been purified like material objects.
Regarding food that has not been rendered impure by ritual means, one should discard only that portion which is defiled and then perform the threshing and washing of the remainder.
Viṣṇu 23.36: Food that has been prepared in an amount exceeding one *droṇa* is not defiled even if it has been touched by a corpse.
Having removed only that which has been defiled from it, one should pour gold-infused water consecrated with the Gāyatrī mantra into it, and one should show it to a goat and to fire.
Food that has been pecked by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon, or sneezed over,
as well as that defiled by hair or insects, becomes pure by the scattering of earth over it.
As long as the odor and the stain caused by contact with impure matter do not depart from an object smeared by it,
so long must earth and water be applied in all purifications of substances.
A goat and a horse are pure by their very mouths; neither a cow nor humans produce impurities from them.
Roads are purified by the rays of the moon and sun and by the wind.
Roads, mud, and water touched by outcastes, dogs,
or crows are purified by the wind alone, as are those constructed with baked bricks.
Now, for all living beings, one should effect purification with earth and water;
and for those who are excessively defiled, purification must be performed constantly and without negligence.
Water on the ground is meritorious where a cow would satisfy her thirst; likewise, water that has not been defiled by impurity is pure even when it has collected upon a stone.
From a well in which a five-toed animal has died, or from one that is otherwise utterly defiled,
one should draw out all the water and purify the remainder with a cloth.
One should perform the kindling of fire in a well that has been lined with baked bricks;
subsequently, one should pour the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) into a well newly filled with water.
O Earth, in small and stagnant reservoirs of water, purification is declared to be as in the case of a well; however, in large bodies of water, there is no defilement.
The gods ordained three purifiers for Brāhmaṇas:
that which is unseen [by the eye], that which is cleansed with water, and that which is commended by word.
The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise displayed for sale;
likewise, almsfood mediated by a Brāhmaṇa and all mines are pure.
The mouth of women is always pure; a bird is pure when causing fruit to fall;
a calf is pure while discharging milk; and a dog is pure when seizing a deer.
The meat of an animal killed by dogs is declared to be pure;
likewise, the meat of one killed by carnivorous beasts, or by others such as Caṇḍālas and robbers, is pure.
Viṣṇu 23.51a: One should declare those apertures which are above the navel to be pure; Viṣṇu 23.51c: those which are below are impure, as are the excretions that have fallen from the body.
Flies, droplets, shadows, a cow, an elephant, a horse,
rays of light, dust, the earth, wind, fire, and a cat are always pure.
The primary drops that fall upon the body do not make one impure;
nor do those which enter the mouth via the beard, nor those caught between the teeth. (Viṣṇu 23.53)
The drops that touch the feet of one who is providing water for others to sip are to be known as equal to those on the ground; one does not become impure because of them.
If one who holds an object in his hand is somehow touched by something defiled by food remnants,
he shall attain purity by sipping water (ācamana) without first setting that object down.
A house is purified by sweeping and smearing; a book, by sprinkling;
and [the ground] by sweeping, smearing, sprinkling, and scraping.
The purification of the ground is achieved by burning it or by the dwelling of cows upon it. Cows are purifying and auspicious; in cows, all the worlds are established.
Cows extend the sacrifice; cows are the destroyers of all sins.
Cow urine, cow dung, clarified butter, milk, curd, and gorocanā [are likewise sacred].
This supreme water from the horns of cows is a sixfold, most auspicious, and supreme blessing; it is meritorious and destroys all sins.
Scratching the bodies of cows indeed destroys all impurities;
by giving morsels of food to cows, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
For the Gaṅgā dwells here in the footprint of cows, and nourishment is increased by their dust;
Lakṣmī resides in their dried dung, and Dharma in bowing to them; therefore, one should always perform obeisance to them.
Viṣṇu 24.01 Now, a Brāhmaṇa may have four wives according to the order of the castes.
For a Kṣatriya, there are three [wives]. (Viṣṇu 24.02)
For a Vaiśya, there are two [fingers]. Viṣṇu 24.03.
Viṣṇu 24.04: One [wife] for a Śūdra.
Viṣṇu 24.05: Among these women, the hand should be taken in marriage according to their respective caste-status.
In the case of marrying a girl of a different caste, a Kṣatriya girl may shoot an arrow at him.
Viṣṇu 24.07: A goad [is the gift] for a daughter of a Vaiśya.
Viṣṇu 24.08: [The marriage] with the daughter of a Śūdra within the hem of one's garment.
One should not take as a wife a woman who belongs to the same *gotra* or who has the same *ṛṣi*-lineage (*pravara*).
Viṣṇu 24.10: [She should be taken] from the mother’s side up to the fifth generation and from the father’s side up to the seventh. Viṣṇu 24.11: Not one who is of no noble family.
Nor one who is diseased. (Viṣṇu 24.12)
Nor one with an extra limb. Viṣṇu 24.13.
Nor one who has a missing limb. (Viṣṇu 24.14)
Viṣṇu 24.15: Nor one who is excessively tawny.
Nor one who is talkative. Viṣṇu 24.16.
Now, there are eight forms of marriage.
According to Viṣṇu 24.18, [the forms of marriage] are the Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, Prājāpatya, Gāndharva, Āsura, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca.
According to Viṣṇu 24.19, the Brāhma marriage consists of inviting a virtuous man and giving a daughter to him.
A gift given to a priest officiating at a sacrifice is called *daiva*.
By the mention of "a pair of cattle," the [verse] is that of a seer (ārṣa).
The Prajāpatya [penance] consists in granting what has been requested. (Viṣṇu 24.22)
Viṣṇu 24.23: The union of two who are mutually desirous, in the absence of mother and father, is the Gāndharva [form of marriage].
Through purchase, one becomes an Asura. (Viṣṇu 24.24)
By seizing him in battle, he becomes a Rākṣasa. (Viṣṇu 24.25)
Viṣṇu 24.26: From approaching a woman while she is asleep or intoxicated is the Paiśāca rite.
Viṣṇu 24.27: Among these, the first four are lawful.
Even the Gāndharva marriage is permissible for Kṣatriyas, according to Viṣṇu 24.28.
The son of a Brāhmaṇa woman purifies twenty-one generations of men.
The son of Devī was Caturdaśa. Viṣṇu 24.30.
And there are seven sons of Ārṣī; thus [there are] twenty-four [in total]. Viṣṇu 24.31.
The Prājāpatya penance lasts for four days.
Viṣṇu 24.33: By giving a daughter in the Brāhma form of marriage, one causes her to go to the world of Brahmā.
By means of fate, one attains heaven. (Viṣṇu 24.34)
According to Viṣṇu 24.35, that which belongs to Viṣṇu is indeed [attained] through the Ṛṣi lineage.
By the Prājāpatya penance, one attains the world of the gods.
By the Gāndharva rite, one goes to the world of the Gandharvas. (Viṣṇu 24.37)
The father, the grandfather, the brother, a kinsman, the maternal grandfather, and the mother—these are the givers of a daughter in marriage.
In the absence of the former, the latter is situated in primordial nature; thus it is said, "the higher than the high."
A maiden, having waited for three menstrual periods, may choose a husband for herself;
but once three periods have passed, she is always free to dispose of herself as she wishes.
A maiden who, while still in her father’s house and remaining unconsecrated by marriage, sees her menses—that maiden is to be known as a *vṛṣalī*; he who carries her away does not incur guilt.
Viṣṇu 25.01 Now, the duties of women.
Viṣṇu 25.02: [The wife] shares in the observance of vows and conduct with her husband.
Viṣṇu 25.03: Worshiping one's mother-in-law, father-in-law, teachers, deities, and guests.
Viṣṇu 25.04: The state of having well-refined implements.
Viṣṇu 25.05: Not having an open hand [in giving].
Viṣṇu 25.06: The state of having well-secured vessels.
Viṣṇu 25.07: Lack of interest in fundamental ritual acts.
Viṣṇu 25.08: Devotion to auspicious conduct and practices.
When the husband has gone abroad, she should refrain from the practice of personal adornment.
Viṣṇu 25.10: Not entering the houses of others.
Viṣṇu 25.11: One should not remain standing at the doorway, nor at the windows, nor at the openings for light.
Viṣṇu 25.12: Lack of independence in all actions.
In childhood, youth, and old age alike, there is dependence upon the father, the husband, and the son.
When her husband has died, she shall remain celibate or ascend the funeral pyre after him. (Viṣṇu 25.14)
For women there is no separate sacrifice, no vow, and no fasting;
by serving her husband, however, she is exalted in heaven.
If a woman observes a fast or a vow while her husband is still living,
she takes away his life-span and goes to hell as well.
When her husband has died, a virtuous woman who remains steadfast in celibacy goes to heaven even if she is childless, just like those students devoted to the Veda.
Viṣṇu 26.01: When there are many wives of the same caste, he should perform religious duties together with the eldest.
Viṣṇu 26.02: And when they are of mixed castes, he may do so even with one of the same caste who is the youngest.
In the absence of a woman of the same caste, however, one may take a woman of the next lower caste, even in times of distress.
But a twice-born man must never [beget a son] by means of a Śūdra woman.
A Śūdra wife for a twice-born man may never serve the purpose of dharma;
she is declared to exist for the sake of pleasure alone for him who is blinded by passion.
Twice-born men who, out of delusion, marry a woman of inferior caste,
quickly lead their entire families, along with their offspring, to the status of Śūdras.
But for him whose rites for the gods, the ancestors, and Atharvans are dominated by that [impurity],
the ancestors and gods do not eat his offerings, and he does not go to heaven.
Viṣṇu 27.01: When the presence of the embryo is clearly known, the rite of impregnation (niṣeka) is performed.
Viṣṇu 27.02: Before the fetus moves, the *puṃsavana* rite [should be performed].
Viṣṇu 27.03: In the sixth or eighth month, the parting of the hair (sīmantonnayana) is performed.
Viṣṇu 27.04: And when a son is born, the birth-rite (jātakarman) is performed.
Viṣṇu 27.05: At the end of the period of impurity, the naming ceremony (nāmadheya) should take place.
For a Brāhmaṇa, the auspicious [mark] is on the right hand.
For a Kṣatriya, it is twenty-seven years.
For a Vaiśya, [the sacrificial fee] consists of wealth (Viṣṇu 27.08).
Viṣṇu 27.09: [The same applies to] the food of a Śūdra that is held in contempt.
In the fourth month, the ceremony of showing the sun takes place.
Viṣṇu 27.11: In the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) takes place.
Viṣṇu 27.12: In the third year, the tonsure ceremony (cūḍākaraṇa) is performed.
Viṣṇu 27.13: These same rites for women are performed without mantras.
Viṣṇu 27.14: Their marriage is performed with mantras.
Viṣṇu 27.15: For a Brāhmaṇa, the initiation ceremony (upanayana) takes place in the eighth year from conception.
Viṣṇu 27.16: [The initiation] of a king [should take place] in the eleventh month from conception.
Viṣṇu 27.17: For Vaiśyas, [initiation] occurs in the twelfth year from conception.
Viṣṇu 27.18: For them, the girdles made of muñja grass, bowstring, or balbaja grass are of the muñja type.
Viṣṇu 27.19: The sacred threads and garments may be made of cotton, hemp, or wool.
Viṣṇu 27.20: Deer, tiger, and goat skins [are prescribed as coverings].
The staffs are made of palāśa, khādira, or audumbara wood. (Viṣṇu 27.21)
Viṣṇu 27.22: The hairline, the forehead, and the region of the nose are equal [in measure].
Or indeed all [of them] together, according to Viṣṇu 27.23.
They are not crooked and possess their bark. Viṣṇu 27.24a.
Begging for alms from those beginning with you, from those in the midst of you, and from those ending with you.
The Sāvitrī does not lapse for a Brāhmaṇa until the sixteenth year;
for a Kṣatriya until the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya until the twenty-fourth.
From this point forward, if these three [classes] likewise remain uninitiated at the proper time,
they become fallen from the Sāvitrī, known as Vrātyas, and are censured by the Āryas.
Whatever skin, sacred thread, and girdle are prescribed for him, whatever staff and whatever garment [are prescribed], those same shall be used by him even during his religious observances.
Having cast his girdle, deerskin, staff, sacred thread,
and water-pot into the water when they are worn out, he should take others while reciting the appropriate mantras.
Viṣṇu 28.01 Now follows the residence in the teacher’s family for those practicing the vow of studentship (brahmacārins).
Viṣṇu 28.02: The performance of the two twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsana).
Viṣṇu 28.03: One should recite the morning twilight prayer while standing, and the evening twilight prayer while seated.
Viṣṇu 28.04: At two times of the day, one should perform the ritual ablution and the fire-rite.
Viṣṇu 28.05: Submerging in water like a staff.
28.06 Viṣṇu: Study when summoned.
Viṣṇu 28.07: Acting for the pleasure and welfare of the guru.
Viṣṇu 28.08: Wearing a girdle, a staff, a deerskin, and the sacred thread.
Viṣṇu 28.09: Except for the family of one's teacher, he should wander for alms among those who possess virtuous qualities.
Viṣṇu 28.10: Eating almsfood authorized by one's guru.
Viṣṇu 28.11: One should avoid salt, fermented liquids, stale food, dancing, singing, women, honey, meat, collyrium, the remnants of others' food, injury to living beings, and vulgar speech.
Viṣṇu 28.12: Sleeping on the ground.
Viṣṇu 28.13: One should rise before the teacher and go to sleep after him.
Having performed the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), he should perform the salutation to his guru.
And with his hands crossed, he should touch his feet.
Viṣṇu 28.16: [He should touch] the right [eye] with the right [hand], and the other [eye] with the other [hand].
And at the conclusion of his salutation, he should announce his own name, ending with the word "bhoḥ. (Viṣṇu 28.17)
Whether standing, sitting, lying down, eating, or with his face turned away, one should not address him.
Standing, one should attend to him who is seated; going toward him, to him who is walking; going out to meet him, to him who is coming; and running after him, to him who is running.
Facing one who has turned his face away. (Viṣṇu 28.20)
Having approached the presence of one who is far away.
Having bowed down to Viṣṇu as he lies asleep, [verse] 28.22.
And he should not sit at his ease within the range of that person's vision.
And one should not utter his name alone.
One should not imitate his gait, gestures, speech, or the like.
One should not remain in a place where there is either censure or slander directed against him.
Viṣṇu 28.27: He should not sit on the same seat as him.
Except for traveling by stone, wooden plank, or boat. (Viṣṇu 28.28)
Viṣṇu 28.29: When the teacher's teacher is present, one should behave toward him as toward the teacher.
And one who has not been instructed by his teacher should not salute his own elders.
Viṣṇu 28.31: Toward a young boy, one of equal age, a teacher, or the son of a teacher, one should behave as toward a teacher.
One should not wash his feet. (Viṣṇu 28.32)
One should not eat what is left over from another's meal.
In this manner, one should acquire a Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas.
Then, from Viṣṇu 28.35, the Vedāṅgas.
But he who, having not studied the Veda, exerts himself in another [field], he, along with his progeny, attains the state of a Śūdra. (Viṣṇu 28.36)
Viṣṇu 28.37: The first birth is from the mother; the second is the binding of the girdle of muñja grass.
In that regard, Sāvitrī becomes his mother and the teacher (ācārya) becomes his father. By this very means, they attain the status of the twice-born.
Viṣṇu 28.40: Prior to the tying of the girdle of muñja grass, a twice-born man is equal to a Śūdra.
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) should be either shaven-headed or wear matted hair.
After completing the acquisition of the Vedas, having been permitted by his teacher and having given him a gift, he should perform the ritual bath.
Therefore, one should spend the remainder of one's life in the family of the guru alone.
In that case, when the teacher has passed away, one should behave toward the teacher's son as one would toward the teacher himself.
Viṣṇu 28.45: [The same applies] toward the wives of one's teacher or toward women of the same caste.
In the absence of that [marriage], one should remain a lifelong celibate student (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārī*), devoted to the service of the sacred fire.
The Brahmin who thus practices celibacy without sloth goes to the highest station and is not born again in this world.
Viṣṇu 28.48a: [The penance for] the intentional emission of semen by a twice-born man who is observing a vow.
Those who know the Dharma say that for a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*), this constitutes a transgression of his vow.
When this sin has been incurred, having worn the skin of a donkey,
he shall go for alms at seven houses, proclaiming his own deed.
Subsisting on alms obtained from them and eating only once a day,
and performing ablutions three times a day, he becomes purified in one year.
If a twice-born student (*brahmacārī*) should involuntarily emit semen during sleep, he should bathe, worship the sun, and recite three times the verse beginning with "punar mām. (Viṣṇu 28.51)

If, while not being ill, he fails to go for alms and fails to kindle the sacred fire for seven nights, he shall perform the penance prescribed for one who has broken his vow of celibacy (avakīrṇi-vrata).
If the sun should rise while he is sleeping out of his own volition,
or if it should set while he is unaware of it, he shall fast for the day while reciting [prayers].
Viṣṇu 29.01: One should know him as an *ācārya* who, having performed the initiation (*upanayana*) and prescribed the observances (*vrata*), teaches the Veda.
But he who should teach this for a fee, that teacher [is liable] for one-fourth [of the penalty].
Viṣṇu 29.03: One should know that he who performs the sacrificial rites for another is the officiating priest (ṛtvij) for him.
One should not employ anyone who has not been tested. (Viṣṇu 29.04)
Viṣṇu 29.05: One should not teach [during these times].
Viṣṇu 29.06: He shall not initiate him [into the Vedic study].
He who speaks unrighteously and he who asks unrighteously—
one of these two perishes or incurs enmity.
Where neither virtue nor wealth exists, nor even a corresponding desire to serve, there knowledge must not be imparted, just as one would not sow good seed in barren soil.
"Knowledge indeed approached a Brahmin and said: 'Guard me; I am your treasure.'"
O Viṣṇu, do not speak of me to one who is envious, dishonest, or crooked; in that way, I shall remain possessed of power.

"O Brahmin, you should teach me to that person whom you know to be pure, vigilant, intelligent, and endowed with celibacy; to one who would never deceive you and who would never say anything unkind—teach me to such a guardian of the treasure."
Having performed the ritual commencement (*upākaraṇa*) of the Vedic meters on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, he should study for four and a half months.
Then, one should perform their dismissal outside.
Between the rites of Utsarjana and Upākarma, one should engage in the study of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (Vedāṅgas).
One should not study for a day and a night on the fourteenth and eighth days of the lunar fortnight.
Nor during the period of impurity caused by the birth of another officiating priest (Ṛtvij).
Viṣṇu 30.06: Not during the departure of Indra.
And one should not recite when a fierce wind is blowing.
Viṣṇu 30.08: [One should not study] during unseasonal rain, lightning, or thunder.
Viṣṇu 30.09: [One should not study] during earthquakes, the falling of meteors, or when the quarters of the sky appear to be ablaze.
Viṣṇu 30.10: Nor in a village where a corpse lies within.
Not when there is a conflict between scriptural authorities. (Viṣṇu 30.11)
Nor when there is the barking of dogs, the howling of jackals, or the braying of donkeys. (Viṣṇu 30.12)
Nor when there is the sound of musical instruments. (Viṣṇu 30.13)
Viṣṇu 30.14: [One should not study] in the presence of a Śūdra or an outcaste.
Nor [should one study] in a temple, a cremation ground, a crossroads, or on a main road. (Viṣṇu 30.15)
Viṣṇu 30.16: Nor [should one urinate] within the water.
One should not sit with the feet placed upon a seat.
Viṣṇu 30.18: Not while riding on an elephant, a horse, a camel, a boat, or a cow.
Viṣṇu 30.19: Nor one who has vomited.
Viṣṇu 30.20: Nor one who has been purged.
Viṣṇu 30.21: Not when one has indigestion.
Viṣṇu 30.22: [There is no penance] for walking between five-clawed animals.
Nor [should one eat] during the calamity of a king, a Vedic scholar, a cow, or a Brāhmaṇa. (Viṣṇu 30.23)
Viṣṇu 30.24: Not at the ceremony for the commencement of Vedic study (anupākarmaṇi).
Viṣṇu 30.25: Not during the discharge [of urine or excrement].
In the sound of the Sāman, the Ṛc and Yajus do not exist.
One should not go to sleep after studying during the final watch of the night.
Even when engaged in study, one should avoid reciting during the periods when study is forbidden.
Viṣṇu 30.29: Because that which is studied during a time unfit for study does not bestow fruit either in this world or in the next.
By the study of that [text], there is a depletion of the lifespan of both the teacher and the pupil. (Viṣṇu 30.30)
Therefore, with the exception of the days when study is forbidden, one who desires the world of Brahman should sow knowledge in the field of a worthy disciple by means of the teacher.
Viṣṇu 30.32: At the beginning and at the conclusion of the study of the Veda, the pupil must perform the clasping of the teacher's feet.
And the *praṇava* (the syllable Om) should be uttered.
And therein, whatever Ṛgvedic verses he recites, by that his ancestors obtain satisfaction through the clarified butter.
Whatever *yajus* formulas there are, by that honey [it is purified].
Viṣṇu 30.36: "The Sāman chants are milked by him with that milk."
That which belongs to the Atharvans, with that meat [one should worship].
Viṣṇu 30.38: By that [food] which one studies—the Purāṇas, Itihāsas, Vedas, Vedāṅgas, and Dharmaśāstras—his food [is purified].
And he who, having acquired knowledge in this world, should live by it [alone], that knowledge shall not yield fruit for him in the next world.
And he who destroys the fame of others by means of his own learning.
And one should not acquire knowledge from another who is studying without having been granted permission.
The theft of that [Veda] from him constitutes the stealing of Brahman, which leads to hell.
Whether it be worldly, Vedic,
or even spiritual knowledge, one should never cause harm to him from whom one has received it.
Between the progenitor and the giver of the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is more venerable;
for the birth from the Veda is eternal for a Brahmin, both in this world and after death.
Viṣṇu 30.45a: One should know that his birth is that which his mother and father produce for him through their union; Viṣṇu 30.45c: namely, that he is born here from a womb.
But that caste which his preceptor, who has mastered the Vedas, produces for him according to the rule by means of the Sāvitrī— that is real, undecaying, and immortal.

He who fills one's ears with that which is not false, causing no suffering and bestowing immortality—he should be regarded as both father and mother; knowing what he has done, one should never bear him malice.
Viṣṇu 31.01: There are three things that are exceedingly heavy for a man.
Viṣṇu 31.02: The mother, the father, and the teacher.
Viṣṇu 31.03: One must always be intent on serving them.
Whatever they may tell you, that you should do.
One should act for their pleasure and welfare. (Viṣṇu 31.05)
One should not do anything at all without being authorized by them.
These three are indeed the Vedas; these three are indeed the gods;
these three are indeed the worlds; and these three are indeed the sacred fires.
Viṣṇu 31.08: The father is the Gārhapatya fire, the mother is the Dakṣiṇa fire, and the teacher is the Āhavanīya fire.
All the duties of that man are honored who honors these three;
but for him who does not honor them, all his ritual acts are fruitless.
Through devotion to his mother he attains this world; through devotion to his father, the middle world;
and indeed, through service to his teacher, he reaches the world of Brahman.

Viṣṇu 32.01: A king, an officiating priest, a learned śrotriya, one who prevents unrighteousness, a teacher, a paternal uncle, a maternal grandfather, a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, an elder brother, and a relative are to be treated like an ācārya.
Viṣṇu 32.02: Their wives are of the same caste (savarṇā).
The mother's sister, the father's sister, and the elder sister [are also to be treated as such]. Viṣṇu 32.03.
Viṣṇu 32.04: For one's father-in-law, paternal uncle, maternal uncle, and officiating priest who are younger than oneself, rising to meet them is itself the salutation.
Viṣṇu 32.05: For women of lower castes who are the wives of one's gurus, one should perform a salutation from a distance, but not the touching of their feet.
Viṣṇu 32.06: One should not perform the uprooting of hair from the wives of one's gurus, nor the application of collyrium, nor the binding of their hair, nor the washing of their feet, and so forth.
Even if she is not a relative, another's wife should be addressed as "sister," "daughter," or "mother. (Viṣṇu 32.07)
And one should not address one's teachers by the word "thou."
If he transgresses that, he should remain without food and, having propitiated him at the end of the day, eat.
And one should not engage in contentious speech with one's teacher.
And he should certainly not engage in the censure of others.
And not that which is undesired. (Viṣṇu 32.12)
But a young wife of one's teacher must not be saluted by touching her feet here in this world by a man who has completed twenty years of age and is capable of discerning virtues and faults.
But on this earth, a young man may at his pleasure perform a salutation according to the rule before the wives of his elders who are young women, saying, "I am so-and-so."
Having returned from a journey, one should clasp the feet of the teacher’s wives and offer daily salutation,
remembering the dharma of the virtuous.
Wealth, kinship, age, action, and learning as the fifth—these are the grounds for respect; each subsequent one is weightier than the preceding.
A ten-year-old Brahmin and a hundred-year-old king—one should recognize these two as father and son; however, of the two, the Brahmin is the father.
The seniority of Brahmins is determined by knowledge; that of Kṣatriyas, by valor;
that of Vaiśyas, by grain and wealth; and that of Śūdras, solely by birth. (Viṣṇu 32.18) [End of Part 1] (Viṣṇu 33)
Now, for a person, there exist three most terrible enemies known as desire, anger, and greed.
Viṣṇu 33.02: Especially for one in the householder stage of life, [this applies] due to the attachment to possessions.
Therefore, being overcome by this, he engages in minor offenses, great sins, secondary sins, and minor transgressions.
In [the case of] acts that cause loss of caste, acts that cause mixture of castes, and acts that render one unworthy of receiving gifts; Viṣṇu 33.04.
Viṣṇu 33.05: And in the case of miscellaneous minor offenses that bring about impurity.
This threefold gate of hell, which leads to one's own destruction—
namely, lust, anger, and greed— one should therefore conquer these three.
Viṣṇu 34.01: Sexual intercourse with one’s mother, sexual intercourse with one’s daughter, and sexual intercourse with one’s daughter-in-law are crimes of extreme gravity (atipātaka).
But those who have committed these most heinous sins (atipātakin) should enter the fire;
for no other expiation for them exists in any way whatsoever.
Viṣṇu 35.01: Killing a Brāhmaṇa, drinking liquor, stealing the gold of a Brāhmaṇa, and violating the teacher’s wife—these are the great sins (mahāpātakas).
And union with that [Viṣṇu]. Viṣṇu 35.02.
One falls by associating with an outcast for a year.
Viṣṇu 35.04: By means of a single vehicle, food, meals, and beds.
But through relationships such as those by marriage, by the sacrificial ladle, or primarily by blood, [the impurity ceases] immediately.
"Those who have committed these great sins may be purified by the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha),
as well as by visiting all the sacred fords (tīrtha) on earth."

Viṣṇu 36.01: For a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice, for a woman in her menses, for a pregnant woman, for a woman of the Atri lineage, for an embryo of unknown sex, and for one who has come for refuge—killing any of these is equal to the murder of a Brāhmaṇa.
False testimony and the killing of a friend—these two are equal to the drinking of liquor.
For a Brahmin, the seizure of land or the theft of a deposit is equal to the theft of gold.
Viṣṇu 36.04: Sexual intercourse with the wives of a paternal uncle, a maternal grandfather, a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, or a king is equal to violating the wife of one's guru.
And approaching a paternal aunt, a maternal aunt, or a sister [is a secondary offense], according to Viṣṇu 36.05.
And sexual intercourse with the wives of a learned Vedic scholar, an officiating priest, a teacher, or a friend.

Viṣṇu 36.07: [One incurs guilt by having sex with] one’s own sister, a female friend, a girl of the same lineage (*sagotra*), a woman of a higher caste, a maiden, a woman born of the lowest caste, a menstruating woman, one who has sought refuge, a female ascetic (*pravrajitā*), or one who has been entrusted to one’s care.

Viṣṇu 36.08a–c: These are secondary sinners (*anupātakin*), just like the perpetrators of the great sins (*mahāpātakins*). They are purified by the Aśvamedha sacrifice or by visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*).
Viṣṇu 37.01: Speaking untruth for the purpose of self-exaltation.
Slander directed toward the king is [a secondary offense], according to Viṣṇu 37.02.
And [the sin of] persisting in falsehood toward one's teacher is equal to that of Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu 37.04: Censuring the Vedas.
And the abandonment of what has been studied [is a cause for loss of caste]. (Viṣṇu 37.05)
And [the same applies] to fire, one's father, mother, son, and wife.
Viṣṇu 37.07: Eating food that should not be eaten or consuming what is unfit for consumption.
Viṣṇu 37.08: Stealing the property of others.
Viṣṇu 37.09: Sexual intercourse with the wife of another.
Viṣṇu 37.10: Officiating at a sacrifice for one for whom it is forbidden to sacrifice.
Viṣṇu 37.11: Living by means of improper action.
And accepting gifts from the wicked (is a cause of loss).
The killing of a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or a cow.
Viṣṇu 37.14: Selling what ought not to be sold.
Viṣṇu 37.15: The state of being a *parivitti* (one whose younger brother marries before him) occurs when the elder brother [marries after his younger brother].
Viṣṇu 37.16: Crying out in lamentation.
And for him, there is the giving away of his daughter.
And officiating at sacrifices for others (Viṣṇu 37.18).
Viṣṇu 37.19: The state of being a Vrātya.
Teaching for a fee (Viṣṇu 37.20).
And the taking of study from a hired teacher [is a cause for loss of caste]. (Viṣṇu 37.21)
Viṣṇu 37.22: He has authority over all mines.
Viṣṇu 37.23: The setting in motion of the great machine.
Viṣṇu 37.24: The harming of trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and medicinal herbs.
Viṣṇu 37.25: [The livelihood] of a woman.
And there is engagement in acts of sorcery and rites for the sake of power.
Viṣṇu 37.27: Undertaking actions for one's own sake.
Not maintaining the sacred fires (an-āhitāgnitā). Viṣṇu 37.28.
Viṣṇu 37.29: The non-discharge of debts owed to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors.
Viṣṇu 37.30: Associating with false scriptures.
Viṣṇu 37.31: Atheism.
Viṣṇu 37.32: [The same applies to] one who is like a bard (kuśīlava).
Viṣṇu 37.33: Drinking intoxicants and consorting with women [who drink].
Thus end the minor offenses (upapātakas), according to Viṣṇu 37.34.
But these men who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
likewise, they should perform the Parāka penance or sacrifice with the Go-sava rite.
Viṣṇu 38.01: Causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa.
Viṣṇu 38.02: Smelling that which should not be smelled and intoxicating liquor.
Viṣṇu 38.03: Crookedness.
Viṣṇu 38.04: Engaging in sexual intercourse with animals.
And [the suffix *viṣṇu*] is used after a masculine [noun]. Viṣṇu 38.05 puṃsi ca.
Thus end the acts that cause loss of caste, according to Viṣṇu 38.06.
Having intentionally committed any one of the acts that cause loss of caste, one should perform the Sāṃtapana Kṛcchra; if done unintentionally, one should perform the Prājāpatya.
Viṣṇu 39.01: The killing of domestic or wild animals is an act that causes the mixture of castes (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*).
Having committed an act that causes the mixing of castes (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*), one should eat barley-gruel for a month,
or else perform the *kṛcchra* or *atikṛcchra* penance as an expiation.
Viṣṇu 40.01: Accepting gifts from those who are censured, engaging in trade, living by usury, speaking untruths, and serving Śūdras—these acts constitute "degrading" (apātrīkaraṇa).
Having rendered someone unworthy of receiving gifts (apātrīkaraṇa), one becomes pure by performing the taptakṛcchra penance,
or alternatively, the śītakṛcchra, or again, the mahāsāṃtapana.
Viṣṇu 41.01: The killing of birds, of aquatic animals, and of those born in water.
And [the same applies] to worms and insects. (Viṣṇu 41.02)
Viṣṇu 41.03: Eating after having followed [the rules] for the middle [period].
Thus, according to Viṣṇu (41.04), these [acts] bring about impurity.
For acts that cause defilement, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is the means of purification;
or else, the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* penance is the purifying expiation.
Viṣṇu 42.01: That which has not been mentioned is the miscellaneous (prakīrṇaka).
Having ascertained the gravity or lightness of a miscellaneous offense,
a wise man shall perform the penance with the approval of Brāhmaṇas, according to the rule.
Viṣṇu 43.01 Now, the hells.
Viṣṇu 43.02 Tāmisra.
Viṣṇu 43.03: Andhatāmisra.
Viṣṇu 43.04: Raurava.
Viṣṇu 43.05: [The hell called] Mahāraurava.
Viṣṇu 43.06: Kālasūtra.
Viṣṇu 43.07: Mahānaraka.
Viṣṇu 43.08: The restoration of life.
Viṣṇu 43.09: Avīci.
Viṣṇu 43.10 Tapanam.
Viṣṇu 43.11: Saṃpratāpana (the "Scorching" hell).
Viṣṇu 43.12: Saṃghātakam.
Viṣṇu 43.13: [The hymn] beginning with "kākolam."
Viṣṇu 43.14: A bud.
Viṣṇu 43.15: [The water] containing foul-smelling mud.
Viṣṇu 43.16: An iron spike.
Viṣṇu 43.17: Ṛbīsa.
Viṣṇu 43.18: A path that is uneven.
Viṣṇu 43.19: The thorny silk-cotton tree (*śālmali*).
Viṣṇu 43.20: Dīpanadī.
Viṣṇu Purāṇa 43.21: The Forest of Sword-Leaves.
Viṣṇu 43.22: "The iron prison."
Viṣṇu 43.23: Those who have committed heinous sins (atipātakin) and have not performed expiation for them are cooked in these [hells] in succession for an entire kalpa.
Viṣṇu 43.24: Those who have committed great sins [remain so] for the duration of a Manvantara.
And those who have committed secondary sins (anupātakin). Viṣṇu 43.25.
Those who have committed minor offenses [must remain outside] for the duration of four yugas.
And those who have performed acts that cause the mixture of castes must remain so for a thousand years.
And those who have committed acts that cause the loss of caste. (Viṣṇu 43.28)
And those who have been rendered unworthy by the *apātrīkaraṇa* acts [are also excluded]. (Viṣṇu 43.29)
And those who have committed acts that cause defilement. (Viṣṇu 43.30)
And those who have committed miscellaneous sins [remain there] for many series of years.
Viṣṇu 43.32a-c: Sinful men who have committed crimes, immediately after giving up their lives, reach the path of Yama and experience terrible suffering.
Just as they are dragged here and there by the terrible messengers of Yama,
being led along with great difficulty and distress.
Being devoured by dogs, jackals, and flesh-eaters, as well as by crows, herons, cranes, and the like; and likewise by fire-mouthed serpents and scorpions.
Being burned by fire, pierced by thorns, split apart by saws, and tormented by thirst; Viṣṇu 43.35.
Tormented by hunger and likewise by packs of fierce tigers,
they faint at every step from the stench of pus and blood.
Desiring the food and drink of others,
they are beaten by the servants with faces resembling those of terrifying crows, herons, cranes, and other such birds.
In some places they are boiled in oil; in some places they are beaten with pestles;
and in some places they are crushed upon iron hammers and likewise upon stone slabs.
In some places they eat vomit; in some, pus and blood;
in some, excrement; and in others, flesh that is foul-smelling like pus and most dreadful.
In some places they remain in dreadful darkness,
being devoured by worms with most terrible fire-like beaks.
In some places they are afflicted by cold, and in others they dwell amidst impurities;
moreover, in some places those most dreadful ghosts devour one another.
In some places they are struck by living beings while hanging there;
in some places they are hurled about by showers of arrows, and in others they are cut to pieces.
With their feet placed upon their necks and entwined by the coils of serpents,
they are likewise tormented by machines and dragged along by their knees.
With their backs, heads, and necks broken, with needle-like throats, and most dreadful,
they possess bodies as large as hollowed-out houses, yet incapable of enduring torment.
Thus, having experienced their sin as suffering sinners,
they become deeply distressed and enter into animal wombs and various other miseries.
Viṣṇu 44.01: Now, for those of sinful nature who have experienced suffering in the hells, there arise births in the animal realm.
Viṣṇu 44.02: For those who have committed extreme sins, there is a succession through all the stationary wombs.
And for those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin), there are births as worms.
For those who have committed minor offenses, the wombs of birds [are the result]. —Viṣṇu 44.04
Viṣṇu 44.05: Those who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) are born from aquatic wombs.
For those who have committed acts that cause the loss of their caste, there are births among the species of aquatic creatures.
Those who have performed the act of causing the mixture of castes (saṃkarī-karaṇa) are born into the wombs of animals. (Viṣṇu 44.07)
For those who have committed acts that cause loss of caste, there are births among the animal kingdom. (Viṣṇu 44.08)
Among humans, those who have performed acts that cause impurity are born into untouchable wombs.
Viṣṇu 44.10: Among those scattered [in various states], the violent ones indeed become eaters of raw flesh.
One who eats food that should not be eaten or consumes what should not be consumed becomes a worm.
Viṣṇu 44.12: A thief becomes a hawk.
Viṣṇu 44.13: A hole-dweller (snake) that carries away the excellent path.
Viṣṇu 44.14: A mouse that steals grain [is the expiation].
Viṣṇu 44.15: A swan is one who steals bell-metal.
Viṣṇu 44.16: One who carries water [in a vessel] on the heart, and one who bathes in water.
Viṣṇu 44.17: A honey-gatherer is a stinger.
Viṣṇu 44.18: Milk is like a crow.
A dog [steals] the essence (rasa). Viṣṇu 44.19.
Ghee is the nakula. Viṣṇu 44.20.
Viṣṇu 44.21: A vulture [is born] from meat.
The water-fowl [eats] fat. Viṣṇu 44.22.
Viṣṇu 44.23: One who drinks oil [becomes] oil-drinking.
Viṣṇu 44.24: *lavaṇa* is the speech of a woman.
In the case of curd, the crane is the indicator.
Having stolen silk, one becomes a partridge.
Dardura [became] a linen garment. Viṣṇu 44.27.
A crane [kills] one who wears clothing made of cotton thread. (Viṣṇu 44.28)
A lizard [kills] a cow. Viṣṇu 44.29.
Viṣṇu 44.30: A Vālguda is one who eats molasses.
The muskrat [is the presiding deity] over odors. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 44.31)
Viṣṇu 44.32: A peacock [is the deity] of leafy vegetables.
Viṣṇu 44.33: Sedhā is one who has prepared food.
Viṣṇu 44.34: A Śalyaka bird eats uncooked grain.
Viṣṇu 44.35: Agni [was born] from Baka.
Viṣṇu 44.36: Household utensils for domestic work.
Red garments belong to Jīvajīvaka; Viṣṇu 44.37.
The tortoise [carries] the elephant. Viṣṇu 44.38.
A tiger [kills] a horse. (Viṣṇu 44.39)
A monkey [eats] the fruit or the flower. (Viṣṇu 44.40)
A bear [kills] a woman. Viṣṇu 44.41.
For a Vaiśya, the vehicle is a camel. (Viṣṇu 44.42)
A vulture [devours] animals; [Viṣṇu 44.43].
Having forcibly seized any property whatsoever belonging to another, or having consumed an offering that has not been consecrated by sacrifice, a man inevitably goes to the state of an animal.
Women also, by stealing according to this same rule, incur the same guilt;
they become wives of those very creatures [from whom the theft was committed].
Viṣṇu 45.01: For those who have been overcome by the sufferings of hell and have emerged from the state of animals, these marks appear among human beings.
One who suffers from leprosy is a perpetrator of a most heinous sin.
A killer of a Brahmin becomes afflicted with consumption.
A drinker of liquor becomes one with blackened teeth.
A stealer of gold becomes one with deformed nails.
One who fails to repay a debt to a teacher, or one who steals a cow, becomes afflicted with skin disease.
Viṣṇu 45.07: A slanderer has a putrid nose.
One who has a foul-smelling mouth is a slanderer. (Viṣṇu 45.08)
A thief of grain becomes deficient in limbs. (Viṣṇu 45.09)
Viṣṇu 45.10: A thief caught with stolen goods has an extra limb.
But one who steals food becomes afflicted with chronic illness.
One who steals speech becomes mute. (Viṣṇu 45.12)
One who steals clothing becomes afflicted with vitiligo.
One who steals a horse becomes lame.
One who reviles gods or Brahmins becomes mute.
One with a flickering tongue is a poisoner. (Viṣṇu 45.16)
One who sets fire [to another's property] becomes insane, according to Viṣṇu 45.17.
One who acts in opposition to the guru becomes afflicted with epilepsy. (Viṣṇu 45.18)
But one who kills a cow becomes blind.
And one who steals a lamp [is reborn as a moth]. Viṣṇu 45.20.
And one who extinguishes a lamp becomes one-eyed. (Viṣṇu 45.21)
A washerman is one who sells tin, chowries, and lead. *Viṣṇu* 45.22.
A seller of one-hoofed animals and a hunter of wild beasts [are born as such]. (Viṣṇu 45.23)
One who eats from a sacrificial pit has a vulva for a mouth. (Viṣṇu 45.24)
A bell-ringer and a thief [are both excluded from the Śrāddha]. Viṣṇu 45.25.
A usurer becomes a bee. (Viṣṇu 45.26)
One who eats refined food alone becomes afflicted with a wind-tumor (vātagulma).
One who breaks an agreement becomes a bald-headed man. Viṣṇu 45.28.
Viṣṇu 45.29: A man with elephantiasis is one who has violated his vow of celibacy.
One who destroys the livelihood of others becomes poor. (Viṣṇu 45.30)
One who causes suffering to others becomes afflicted with a chronic disease.
Thus, by virtue of specific past actions, they are born endowed with particular marks;
likewise, they may be afflicted by diseases, or be blind, humpbacked, lame, or one-eyed.
Dwarfs, the deaf, the mute, and others who are weak—
therefore, one should perform expiation with every possible effort.
Viṣṇu 46.01 Now follow the kṛcchra penances.
Viṣṇu 46.02: He should not eat for three days.
And one should perform the ritual bath three times every day—at dawn, noon, and sunset.
Viṣṇu 46.04: Three times during each bath, he should immerse himself in the waters.
Immersed in water for forty-six and a fifth of a moment, one should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times.
During the day, while standing, he should remain standing.
Viṣṇu 46.07: At night, he should remain seated.
At the conclusion of the rite, one should give a milch cow.
"Viṣṇu 46.09"—thus [ends] the Aghamarṣaṇa.
One should eat in the evening for three days, in the morning for three days, and eat food obtained unasked for three days; this is the Prājāpatya penance.
For three days one should drink hot water, for three days hot ghee, for three days hot milk, and for three days one should not eat at all; this is the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
By these very same [substances] when cold, it is the Śītakṛcchra.
The *Kṛcchrātikṛcchra* consists of subsisting on milk for twenty-one days.
The *udaka-kṛcchra* consists of consuming barley-meal with water for one month.
By subsisting on lotus stalks, one performs the mūla-kṛcchra penance.
The Śrīphalakṛcchra consists of subsisting on bilva fruits. (Viṣṇu 46.16)
Or with lotus-seeds, [as stated in] Viṣṇu 46.17.
For one who abstains from food, the *parāka* penance is completed in twelve days.
Viṣṇu 46.19: One should eat cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass for one day; on the second day, one should fast. This is the *sāṃtapana* penance.
The Mahāsāṃtapana penance consists of the daily practice of consuming cow urine and other substances.
And the Atisāntapana consists of [the same] practiced for three days.
The consumption of oil-cake, rice-scum, buttermilk, water, and barley-meal, with an interval of fasting between them, constitutes the Tulāpuruṣa penance.
The *parṇakṛcchra* consists of drinking water boiled with the leaves of each of the following: *kuśa*, *palāśa*, *udumbara*, *padma*, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *vaṭa*, *brāhmī*, and *suvarcalā*.
Having undergone a shave, one should perform all these *kṛcchra* penances,
bathing daily at the three sessions of the day, sleeping on the ground, and keeping the senses subdued.
One should avoid excessive conversation with women, Śūdras, and outcasts; one should constantly recite purificatory prayers and offer oblations according to one's ability.
Viṣṇu 47.01 Now follows the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One should eat forty-seven mouthfuls of food that does not cause transformation.

Viṣṇu 47.03: One should increase those morsels during the waxing phase of the moon and decrease them during the waning phase; on the new moon day, one should not eat at all. This is the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance known as "barley-shaped" (*yava-madhya*).
Or it may be like a termite's waist, in the middle of Viṣṇu.
That [lunar month] in which the new moon occurs at the middle [of the lunar fortnight] is called *pipīlikā-madhya* (ant-middle).
Viṣṇu 47.06: That [lunar month] whose full moon day falls on the middle of the month is called *yavamadhyama*.
If one eats eight morsels every day for a month, that is the *yaticāndrāyaṇa*.
Eating four mouthfuls in the evening and four in the morning constitutes the *śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa*.
If one should eat in any manner whatsoever three hundred meals minus sixty within a month, that is the ordinary *cāndrāyaṇa*.
O Earth, in ancient times, the stainless Seven Sages,
as well as Brahmā and Rudra, performed this vow and attained the supreme abode.
Viṣṇu 48.01 Now, if one should consider oneself heavy with sins committed by one's own actions, one should cook a *prasṛti* measure of barley-gruel for the sake of purification.
Viṣṇu 48.02: One should not offer oblations into the fire after that.
And there is no offering of oblations (bali) here.
Viṣṇu 48.04: One should consecrate with mantras the uncooked, the being cooked, and the cooked [food].
While it is being cooked, one should perform the protection ritual.

Viṣṇu is the path of the gods, the leader of the poets, the seer among the wise, the buffalo among wild beasts, the hawk among vultures, the axe of the forests; as Soma, he goes forth chanting across the filter.
With the verse "Viṣṇu" (48.06), he ties the darbha grass together.
And having poured that boiled [milk-rice] into a vessel, he should eat it.

"O gods who are born of the mind, who delight in the mind, who are highly skillful, and whose father is Dakṣa—may they protect us! May they aid us! To them be homage! To them be *svāhā*!"—with these words, one should offer the oblation into oneself.
Then, having finished eating, he should touch his navel.

"O Waters, having been bathed in you, may you become drinkable; O Yavas, dwell within our bellies! May they be for us free from disease, free from consumption, and free from sin—divine, immortal, and increasers of Truth. Thus [he says].
One who desires intelligence [should observe this] for three nights.
One who commits a sin [becomes purified] after six nights.
Having drunk it for seven nights, one purifies oneself from any one of the great sins.
By means of twelve nights [of fasting], one burns away even the sin committed by one's ancestors.
Having drunk [it] for a month, all sins [are destroyed].
And for twenty-one nights, [the penance consists of subsisting on] barley from which the husks have been removed by means of a cow's tail.
"You are barley; you are the king of grains; you belong to Varuṇa and are mixed with honey.
You are the cleanser of all sins, a purifier upheld by the seers."
Ghee is barley, honey is barley, and water is barley—the nectar of immortality.
May all of them purify whatever sin or any evil deed whatsoever I have committed.
O barley grains, destroy the misfortune and the ill-omened Kālakarṇī that have been committed by speech, performed through action, or conceived as evil thoughts in the mind.
O Yavas, purify for me that which has been licked by a dog or a pig, that which is defiled by food-leavings,
and the failure to serve my mother and father.

The food of a *gaṇa*, the food of a courtesan, the food of a *śūdra*, food from a funeral rite (*śrāddha*), food from a birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), the food of a thief, and food from a recent funeral rite (*nava-śrāddha*): purify these for me with barley.

"O barley grains, purify for me the child-thief, the unrighteous man, and whatever [sin] is committed at the king's gate; the theft of gold, the state of being a *avrātya*, the officiating at a sacrifice for one unfit to sacrifice, and the reviling of Brahmins."
Viṣṇu 49.01: Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship the Blessed Lord Śrī Vāsudeva on the twelfth day.
Viṣṇu 49.02: By means of flowers, incense, ointments, lamps, and food offerings, as well as by the gratification of the fire and the Brahmins.
Having performed this vow for one year, O Viṣṇu, one becomes purified from sins.
Having performed this for as long as one lives, one attains Śvetadvīpa.
By performing this on the twelfth days of both fortnights for one year, one attains the heavenly world.
Having performed this for as long as one lives, [one attains] the world of Viṣṇu.
In this very same way, it is also [to be understood] regarding the fifteenth days.
By attending upon Keśava, who has become Brahman on the new moon day and likewise on the full moon day, and who has become Yoga, one shall attain the Great.
In that year in which the moon and Jupiter are seen together in the sky on the full-moon day,
that full-moon day is declared to be the "Great" (Mahatī) Paurṇamāsī.
On that day, acts such as giving gifts and observing fasts are proclaimed to be inexhaustible;
likewise, so too is the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) which falls on a Monday and is conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism.
Having constructed a leaf-hut in the forest, he should dwell there.
Viṣṇu 50.02: He should bathe three times a day.
And proclaiming his own deed, he should practice begging for alms from village to village.
And he should sleep on a bed of grass.
This is the great vow (mahāvrata) of Viṣṇu.
Having killed a Brāhmaṇa, one should perform [expiation] for twelve years.
A Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who is present at a sacrifice [is one whom he may initiate]. (Viṣṇu 50.07)
Viṣṇu 50.08: [One should not approach] a woman who is pregnant or one who is menstruating.
Or a woman of the Atri lineage, O Viṣṇu.
Or a friend, according to Viṣṇu 50.10.
In the case of killing a king, one should perform the Great Vow (mahāvrata) itself twice over.
In the case of killing a Kṣatriya, [the penance is] one-quarter less than that for a Vaiśya.
For killing a Vaiśya, the penance is half [of that for a Kṣatriya].
Half of that [penance] is for the killing of a Śūdra.
In all [these cases], according to Viṣṇu 50.15, he should have a corpse's head as his banner.
For one month, having shaved his head, he should follow after cows.
While they are seated, he should sit.
And he should remain standing when they are standing. (Viṣṇu 50.18)
And he should rescue those who are sinking.
And Viṣṇu shall protect [them] from fears.
Viṣṇu 50.21: Without providing protection for them against cold and other such hardships, one should not provide it for oneself.
One should bathe with cow urine.
And he should subsist on cow-products.
Viṣṇu 50.24: One should perform this cow-vow in the event of killing a cow.
Having killed an elephant, one should give five blue bulls as a gift.
Viṣṇu 50.26: A horse or a garment.
For killing a donkey, one should give a one-year-old ox to a Vaiṣṇava.
And for the killing of rams and goats, [the penance is] as prescribed by Viṣṇu (Viṣṇu 50.28).
For killing a camel, the fine is one *suvarṇa-kṛṣṇala*.
Having killed a dog, one should fast for three nights.

Having killed any one of a mouse, a cat, a mongoose, a frog, a water-snake, or a python, one who has fasted should feed a *brāhmaṇa* with *kṛsara* (rice and pulse) and give an iron staff as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
For killing a monitor lizard, an owl, a crow, or a fish, one should fast for three nights.
Having killed any one of a swan, a crane, a balākā crane, a water-fowl, a monkey, a hawk, a vulture, or a ruddy goose, one should give a cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having killed a snake, one should give a hoe made of black iron.
Having killed a eunuch, one [is purified] by [carrying] a load of straw.
Having killed a boar, [one obtains] a jar of ghee; [Viṣṇu 50.36].
Viṣṇu 50.37: A partridge for a droṇa of sesame seeds.
A parrot two years old, like a calf. Viṣṇu 50.38. śukaṃ dvi-hāyana-vatsam //
A three-year-old Krauñca bird [is the sacrificial fee]. Viṣṇu 50.39.
For killing a flesh-eating beast, one should give a milch cow.
For killing a carnivorous wild animal, [one should give] a heifer.
For the killing of an animal not specifically mentioned, one should subsist on milk for three nights.
Upon killing a bird, one should eat only at night.
Or he should give a silver māṣa.
Having killed an aquatic creature, one should fast.
But for the killing of a thousand creatures possessing bones,
or for a full cartload of boneless creatures, one should perform the penance prescribed for the murder of a Śūdra.
For killing vertebrate animals, one should give even a small gift to a Brahmin;
for injuring boneless creatures, however, one is purified by the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma).
For the cutting of fruit-bearing trees, one hundred Ṛg-verses are to be recited;
likewise for shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and flowering herbs.
For all beings born from food and drink,
as well as those born from fluids, and those arising from fruits and flowers, the consumption of clarified butter (ghṛta) is the complete purification.
For the unauthorized taking of cultivated plants or those grown spontaneously in the forest,
one should follow a cow for one day while subsisting on milk alone.
A drinker of spirituous liquor, excluded from all ritual acts, shall subsist on grains for a year.
Upon consuming any one of the impure intoxicants, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
And [the same penance applies] for eating garlic, onion, leek, anything having a similar odor, village-pig, village-cock, monkey, or beef. (Viṣṇu 51.03)
Viṣṇu 51.04: After the penance for all these [offenses] among the twice-born, one should perform the sacramental rite (saṃskāra) once again.
Shaving the head, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows are to be avoided during the rite of re-consecration.
If one eats the flesh of five-toed animals, excluding the hare, the porcupine, the monitor lizard, the rhinoceros, and the tortoise, one should fast for seven nights.
Having eaten the food of a member of a religious guild, a prostitute, a thief, or a singer, one should subsist on milk for seven nights.
Viṣṇu 51.08: [The food] of Takṣaka and of a leather-worker.
And [the food] of usurers, misers, initiated sacrificers, those bound in fetters, the accused, and eunuchs [is forbidden]. Viṣṇu 51.09.
And [the food] of a wanton woman, a hypocrite, a physician, a hunter, a cruel person, a fierce person, and those who eat the remnants of others [is forbidden].
Viṣṇu 51.11: And [the food] of a woman whose husband is not a hero, of a goldsmith, of one whose husband has been defeated by another, and of those who have fallen from their caste.
And for those who speak slander and falsehoods, those who have violated dharma, and those who sell their own vital essence (semen).
And [the food] of actors, weavers, murderers, and washermen. (Viṣṇu 51.13)
And [the same applies] to those who work with leather, Niṣādas, actors, wrestlers, lute-players, and sellers of weapons. (Viṣṇu 51.14)
And [the food] of dog-cookers, vintners, oil-pressers, weavers, and washermen [is forbidden]. Viṣṇu 51.15.
And [the same applies to] those who dwell in the house of a menstruating woman together with her paramour.
That which has been looked upon by a killer of an embryo, touched by a woman in her courses, licked by a bird, touched by a dog, or smelled by a cow [is unfit for consumption].
If [the food] has been intentionally touched with the foot or sneezed upon (Viṣṇu 51.18).
Viṣṇu 51.19: And [the testimony] of those who are intoxicated, angry, or afflicted by disease [is not admissible].
Viṣṇu 51.20: [One should not eat] meat that has not been honored [with offerings], nor meat obtained in vain.
In the case of eating the flesh of any fish except for the *pāṭhīna*, *rohita*, *rājīva*, *siṃhatuṇḍa*, and *śakula* species, one should fast for three nights. (Viṣṇu 51.21)
And [the same applies] to eating the flesh of any water-born creature, Viṣṇu 51.22.
Having drunk water contained in a vessel that held liquor, one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for seven nights.
And those who have stayed in a vessel that held liquor [become pure] after five nights.
