One who drinks soma, having smelled the breath of one who drinks liquor, should immerse himself in water, mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times, and then consume clarified butter.
For eating the flesh of a donkey, a camel, or a crow, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Having eaten unknown meat from a slaughterhouse and dried meat, [one must perform penance]. (Viṣṇu 51.27)
For eating the flesh of carnivorous beasts or birds, one must perform the Taptakṛcchra penance.
Regarding the eating of the flesh of the kalaviṅka, plava, cakravāka, haṃsa, rajjudāla, sārasa, dātyūha, śuka, sārikā, baka, balākā, kokila, and khañjarīṭa birds, one should fast for three nights.
And [the same applies] to eating animals with uncloven hooves or those with two rows of teeth.
Viṣṇu 51.31: And for eating the meat of any bird, with the exception of the partridge, the grey partridge, the quail, the francolin, and the peacock, there is a fast for one day and night.
Having eaten the flesh of insects for one day, one should drink *brahmasuvarcalā*.
And for eating the flesh of dogs, [one must perform penance] according to Viṣṇu 51.33.
For eating mushrooms or *kavaka* fungi, one must perform the *sāṃtapana* penance.

Having avoided preparations of barley, wheat, and milk, as well as those treated with fats, fermented liquids (śukta), and *khāṇḍava*, one should fast after consuming whatever has become stale (*paryuṣita*).
And tree exudations that are red, or those produced from incisions or impure substances.
Viṣṇu 51.37: Lotus roots, food prepared without ritual purpose, kṛsara, saṃyāva, milk-rice, cakes, fried pastries, food belonging to the gods, and sacrificial offerings [are forbidden].
And all types of milk, with the exception of that from cows, goats, and buffaloes. (Viṣṇu 51.38)
Even those [days] that are less than ten days [are included]. (Viṣṇu 51.39)
And the milk of a cow that is flowing, one in heat, or one whose calf is absent. (Viṣṇu 51.40)
And those who eat impure food [are also excluded]. Viṣṇu 51.41.
And those things that have turned sour, with the exception of curd.
A student in the stage of celibacy (brahmacaryāśramin) who eats at a funeral feast (śrāddha) shall fast for three nights.
And he shall dwell in water for one day.
For eating honey or meat, one must perform the Prājāpatya penance. (Viṣṇu 51.45)
If one eats the leavings of a cat, a crow, a mongoose, or a rat, one should drink *brahmasuvarcalā*.
Having eaten the leavings of a dog, one should fast for one day and drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
For eating food containing five-clawed animals, or excrement and urine, [one must fast] for seven nights. (Viṣṇu 51.48)
If one eats at an *āma-śrāddha*, one should subsist on milk for three nights.
A Brāhmaṇa who eats the leavings of a Śūdra shall undergo this for seven nights.
For eating the remnants of a Vaiśya's meal, one must observe the five-night penance.
For eating the leavings of a Kṣatriya, one must observe a fast for three nights.
But for eating the leavings of a Brāhmaṇa, the penance is one day.
A Kṣatriya who eats the leavings of a Śūdra shall fast for five nights.
One who eats the leavings of a Vaiśya shall fast for three nights.
A Vaiśya who eats the remnants of a Śūdra's meal [is likewise excluded].
Having eaten the food of a Caṇḍāla, one should fast for three nights.
Having eaten prepared food [from such a person], one must perform the Parāka penance.
A Brahmin, adhering to the eternal rule, should never eat animals that have not been consecrated with mantras;
however, he may eat those consecrated with mantras, established in the perpetual ordinance.
For as many hairs as there are on the animal,
so many times does the one who slaughters an animal in vain undergo death here and suffer atonement after passing away.
"Beasts were created by the Self-existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice;
for sacrifice is for the prosperity of all. Therefore, killing in a sacrifice is not killing."
The sin of a hunter seeking wealth does not become as great as the sin that accrues after death to one who eats meat in vain.
Herbs, domestic animals, trees, beasts, and likewise birds,
having met their death for the sake of sacrifice, attain exalted states once again.
In the honey-mixture offering (madhuparka), in a sacrifice, and in rites for the ancestors or the gods—
only in these instances may animals be slain, and by no means otherwise.
A twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Vedas, by killing animals for the sake of sacrifice,
leads both himself and the animals to the highest state.
Whether living at home, with his teacher, or in the forest, a self-possessed twice-born man should never practice violence not ordained by the Veda, even in times of distress.
Whatever injury to the moving and unmoving beings in this world is ordained by the Veda,
one should know that indeed to be non-injury (ahiṃsā), for dharma has shone forth from the Veda.
He who harms harmless beings out of a desire for his own pleasure finds no happiness anywhere, neither while living nor after death.
He who does not desire to inflict the sufferings of bondage or death upon living beings,
and who seeks the welfare of all, attains ultimate happiness.
Whatever one meditates upon, whatever one performs, and toward whatever one forms an attachment—
that very thing one obtains without effort, provided that one does not harm anything whatsoever.
Meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings, and the slaughter of living beings does not lead to heaven; therefore, one should abstain from meat.
Having thoroughly considered the origin of meat and the slaughter and binding of embodied beings, one should desist from eating all kinds of meat.
He who does not eat meat, even while disregarding the [prescribed] rule, like a Piśāca—
he becomes beloved in this world and is not afflicted by diseases.

The one who consents, the one who dismembers, the one who kills, the buyer and the seller, the one who prepares the meat, the one who serves it, and the eater— all these are slayers, according to Viṣṇu 51.74.
He who desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another,
without having first worshipped the ancestors and the gods— there is no doer of more demerit than he.
He who might perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice every year for a hundred years,
and he who does not eat meat— the merit and fruit of these two are equal.
One does not obtain that fruit by means of divine foods consisting of fruits and roots, nor by the consumption of the grains of sages, which one obtains from the total avoidance of meat.
"He shall devour me in the hereafter, whose flesh I eat here"—
the wise declare this to be the true nature of "meat" (*māṃsa*).
One who has stolen gold, confessing his deed to the king, shall hand over a wooden pestle.
Through killing or through renunciation, one becomes purified, O Viṣṇu.
One should perform the Mahāvrata for twelve years, or for Viṣṇu [specifically].
And one who misappropriates a deposit is [guilty of the same offense]. Viṣṇu 52.04.
And one who steals grain or wealth shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance for one year.
For the theft of a human being, a woman, a well, a field, or a pond, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed.
Viṣṇu 52.07: For substances of little value, the Sāntapana penance [is prescribed].
Viṣṇu 52.08: For those who consume food, drink, vehicles, beds, seats, flowers, roots, and fruits, the penance is the drinking of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
For stealing grass, wood, trees, dried food, molasses, clothing, leather, or meat, one shall fast for three nights.
For stealing gems, pearls, coral, copper, silver, iron, or bell-metal, one should eat small morsels for twelve days.
Viṣṇu 52.11: For stealing cotton, silk from insects, wool, and so forth, one should subsist on milk for three nights.
Viṣṇu 52.12: For stealing cloven-hoofed or single-hoofed animals, one should fast for two nights.
In the case of stealing birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, ropes, or articles made of split bamboo, one shall fast for a day.
Having recovered by any means the stolen property from the creditor,
one should then perform an expiation for the removal of that taint.
Whatever a man who is unrestrained may seize from others,
by that very thing he shall be deprived when he is born again in whatever state he enters.
Since life, virtue, and desire are all established upon wealth,
one should therefore avoid the destruction of wealth through every possible effort.
He who is intent on harming living beings as well as intent on harming wealth— of these two,
the one intent on harming wealth attains great suffering.

Viṣṇu 53.01 Now, regarding sexual intercourse with a woman who should not be approached, one shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year in the forest, wearing rags and observing the rules of the Mahāvrata.
And for approaching the wife of another, [the penance is] that of Viṣṇu (53.02).
Viṣṇu 53.03: And the cow-vow (go-vrata) [is prescribed] for approaching a cow.

Viṣṇu 53.04: In the case of a man [emitting semen] into a non-vaginal opening, into space, into water, during the day, or while riding in a vehicle drawn by oxen, he shall perform a bath along with his clothes.
And by having sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍālī woman, one shall attain equality with her.
If done unintentionally, one should perform two Cāndrāyaṇa penances. (Viṣṇu 53.06)
And for approaching a woman who is a prostitute or an animal, one must perform the Prājāpatya penance.
And a woman who has once been unfaithful to her husband shall perform that same vow which is prescribed for a man regarding another's wife.
Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by serving a *vṛṣalī* for a single night,
he removes that by subsisting on alms and constantly reciting [sacred texts] for three years.
Viṣṇu 54.01: Whatever sinner associates with another, he shall perform the same expiation as that person.
Having drunk water from a well containing a dead five-clawed animal or from one that is extremely defiled, a Brāhmaṇa shall fast for three nights.
A Kṣatriya [shall fast] for two days. (Viṣṇu 54.03)
Viṣṇu 54.04: For one day, he becomes a Vaiśya.
A Śūdra [should eat] at night. (Viṣṇu 54.05)
And at the conclusion of the vow, all should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
A Śūdra should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), whereas a Brāhmaṇa should drink liquor;
both of them go to the hell known as Mahāraurava.
If a man approaches his wife during her fertile period except on the forbidden days, he shall fast for three nights.
A false witness shall perform the penance prescribed for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa.
Viṣṇu 54.10: For voiding urine or excrement without water, one must bathe with one's clothes on and perform an oblation with the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
One who has been released after the sun has risen should bathe with his clothes on and repeat the Sāvitrī mantra one hundred and eight times.
One who has been bitten by a dog, jackal, village pig, donkey, monkey, crow, or an unchaste woman should go to a river and perform sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*).
One who has extinguished the Vedic fires shall bathe three times a day, sleep on the ground, and subsist for one year on alms-food received only once a day.
For falsehood regarding one's own excellence, for persistent lying to a teacher, and for reviling him, one should subsist on milk alone for one month.
An atheist, one who lives as an atheist, an ungrateful person, a fraudulent dealer, and one who destroys the livelihood of a Brāhmaṇa—these shall subsist on alms for one year.
The one who is superseded in marriage, the one who supersedes, she by whom he is superseded, the giver, and the officiating priest—all these should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One who sells living beings, land, merit, or Soma shall perform the Taptakṛcchra penance.

One who sells fresh herbs, fragrances, flowers, fruits, roots, skins, cane, bamboo, husks, potsherds, hair, ashes, bones, cow's milk, oil-cakes, sesame seeds, or sesame oil shall perform the Prājāpatya penance. (Viṣṇu 54.18)
One who sells substances produced from phlegm, lac, honey, wax, conch-shells, oyster-shells, tin, lead, black iron, copper, bronze, or swords shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (Viṣṇu 54.19)
One who sells dyed cloth, colored pigments, gems, perfumes, molasses, honey, liquids, or wool shall fast for three nights.
One who sells meat, salt, lac, or milk shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
And he should bring him back again.
Having traveled by camel or donkey, or having bathed naked, slept, or eaten, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). Viṣṇu 54.23.
Having recited the Sāvitrī mantra three thousand times with a concentrated mind,
and having drunk only milk for a month while staying in a cow-pen, one is liberated from the sin of accepting improper gifts.

Having performed sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice, having performed the funeral rites for others, and having practiced malevolent magic or the *ahīna* sacrifice, one removes that sin by means of three *kṛcchra* penances.
Those twice-born men for whom the Sāvitrī has not been recited according to the rule,
one should cause them to perform three Kṛcchra penances and then initiate them according to the rule.
But for those twice-born men who, having engaged in improper acts, desire to perform penance and have been cast out from the status of Brahmanhood,
one should prescribe this same [penance] for them as well.
Whatever wealth Brāhmaṇas acquire through a censurable occupation,
they are purified by its renunciation, as well as by the recitation of sacred texts and austerity.
Upon the omission of the obligatory rites prescribed by the Vedas,
and upon the violation of the vows of a *snātaka*, the penance is fasting.
Having threatened [to strike], one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance;

for actually striking, the *atikṛcchra*. One should perform the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* for causing blood to flow from a Brahmin. One should not have any dealings with those who have been purified of their sins.
A knower of dharma should not feel contempt for these [outcastes] once they have performed the prescribed purification rites.

One should not dwell with those who kill children, those who are ungrateful— even if they are pure according to dharma— nor with those who kill those who have sought refuge, nor with those who kill women.
One who is eighty years of age, or a child under sixteen,
as well as women and the sick, deserve only half of the prescribed penance.
But for the removal of those sins for which no expiation has been mentioned,
one should prescribe an expiation after considering both the capacity [of the offender] and the nature of the sin.
Viṣṇu 55.01 Now follow the secret penances.

Having reached the river Viṣṇu, one who has bathed and performed sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) according to the prescribed rules every day, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) once a day, becomes purified from the murder of a Brahmin within a month.
At the conclusion of the rite, one should give a milch cow.
Viṣṇu 55.04: By means of the vow and the Aghamarṣaṇa rite, a drinker of spirituous liquor becomes purified.
By reciting the Gāyatrī ten thousand times, one who has committed the theft of gold [is purified].
One who has violated the Guru’s bed is purified by fasting for three nights and performing the recitation and fire-offerings of the Puruṣasūkta.
Just as the Aśvamedha, the king of sacrifices, is the remover of all sins,
so too is the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn the remover of all sins.
A twice-born man should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) for the removal of all sins;
indeed, all the sins of a twice-born man are consumed by breath controls.
One should recite the Gāyatrī, together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras, three times while restraining the breath;
that is called Prāṇāyāma.
Prajāpati milked forth from the three Vedas the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m*, as well as the words *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*.
From the three Vedas alone, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out foot by foot that which is the "Tat" of this Sāvitrī verse.
A Brahmin who knows the Veda, reciting this syllable and this [Gāyatrī] preceded by the Vyāhṛtis at the two twilights, becomes endowed with the merit of the Veda.
But by practicing this triad externally a thousand times,
a twice-born man is released from even great sin within a month, just as a snake is freed from its skin.
Deprived of these three, and failing in his own duty at the proper time,
one born of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya caste incurs reproach among the virtuous.
The three imperishable Great Utterances (mahāvyāhṛtis) preceded by the syllable *oṃ*,
as well as the three-footed Gāyatrī, should be known as the mouth of the Brāhmaṇa.
He who studies this day after day for three years without weariness attains the supreme Brahman, becoming like the wind and possessing a form of space.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath-control is the highest austerity;
there is nothing higher than the Sāvitrī; and truth excels silence.
All Vedic acts of offering oblations and performing sacrifices flow away;
however, the Imperishable (akṣara) should be known as the Imperishable, as well as Brahmā and Prajāpati.
The sacrifice of recitation (japa-yajña) is ten times superior to the sacrifice of ritual (vidhi-yajña);
that which is whispered (upāṃśu) is a hundredfold more effective, and the mental (mānasa) is said to be a thousandfold.
Those four types of *pākayajñas* which are accompanied by the *vidhiyajñas*—
all of them do not equal even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*).
A Brāhmaṇa shall attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whether he performs other rites or not, one who is friendly toward all is called a Brāhmaṇa.
Now, next, there are the purifiers of all the Vedas.
Viṣṇu 56.02: By means of the recitations and burnt offerings of these, the twice-born are purified from their sins.
Viṣṇu 56.03: The Aghamarṣaṇa hymn.
Viṣṇu 56.04: [This is] composed by Deva.
Viṣṇu 56.05: The Śuddhavatī verses.
Viṣṇu 56.06: The hymn beginning with "taratsamandīya."
Viṣṇu 56.07: The Kūśmāṇḍī verses.
Viṣṇu 56.08: The Pāvamānī verses.
Viṣṇu 56.09 Durgā-Sāvitrī.
Viṣṇu 56.10: [The verses] beginning with "atīṣaṅgāḥ."
Viṣṇu 56.11: Verses in the *padastoma* meter.
The Vyāhṛtis are equal to Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu 56.13: The Bhāruṇḍa birds.
Viṣṇu 56.14: Candra-sāman.
The two *sāmans* are the *puruṣavrata*.
Viṣṇu 56.16: [The verse begins with] "ab-liṅgam".
Viṣṇu 56.17 [is] composed by Bṛhaspati.
Viṣṇu 56.18: The Gō-sūkta (Hymn to the Cow).
Viṣṇu 56.19: The Hymn to the Horse (Aśvasūkta)
And the two *sāmans* [named] *candrasūkta*.
Viṣṇu 56.21: The Śatarudriya.
Viṣṇu 56.22: The Atharvaśiras.
Viṣṇu 56.23: The Tri-suparṇa.
Viṣṇu 56.24: The Great Vow (mahā-vrata).
Viṣṇu 56.25: The Nārāyaṇīya.
And the Puruṣasūkta (Viṣṇu 56.26).
The three Ājyadohas, the Rathantara, the Agnivratam, the Vāmadevya, and the Bṛhat—these, when sung, purify living beings; and if one so desires, one obtains the memory of past births.
Viṣṇu 57.01 Now, those who are to be avoided:
Viṣṇu 57.02: The Vrātyas.
Viṣṇu 57.03: They have fallen.
Viṣṇu 57.04: Those who are impure for three generations on both the mother’s and the father’s side [are ineligible].
Viṣṇu 57.05: All such persons are indeed unfit to be fed and unfit to receive gifts from.
And one should avoid the habit of accepting gifts from those whose gifts should not be accepted.
Through accepting gifts, the Vedic splendor of Brahmins perishes. (Viṣṇu 57.07)
He who accepts gifts without understanding the rules for receiving various objects sinks into the depths together with the giver.
And he who, though capable of receiving gifts, avoids receiving them, attains the world of the givers.
One should not reject fuel, water, roots, fruits, protection from fear, meat, honey, a bed, a seat, a house, flowers, curd, or vegetables when they are offered.
Prajāpati has declared that alms offered spontaneously upon being invited, and not previously solicited, may be accepted even from one who has performed evil deeds.
The ancestors do not eat for fifteen years of him who treats with contempt that [cow],
nor does the fire carry his oblations.
Desiring to support his teachers and dependents, or wishing to honor the ancestors and the gods, he may accept gifts from anyone; however, he himself should not find satisfaction therein.
Even in these matters, though he may be capable of accepting gifts from them,
he shall not take [gifts] from an unchaste woman, a eunuch, an outcast, nor likewise from an enemy.
But when his teachers have passed away, or even while living at home without them,
he who seeks his own livelihood should always accept [gifts] from virtuous persons.
A partner in a business venture, a family friend, a slave, a cowherd,
and a barber— among Śūdras, these are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant].
Now, for one in the householder stage of life, there are three kinds of wealth.
Viṣṇu is white, brindled, and black.
When one performs funeral rites for the deceased with wealth acquired through honest means, by that he attains divinity.
That which was [performed] by Śabala, that was his human state.
Whatever was done by Kṛṣṇa resulted in his state as an animal.
According to Viṣṇu 58.06, that which is acquired by one's own labor is "white" for all.
Viṣṇu 58.07: That which is acquired through subsequent activity is variegated (śabala).
And Viṣṇu (58.08) [mentions] Kṛṣṇa, who is obtained through a function separated by one [intermediate stage].
That which has come down by succession, that which is given as a gift out of affection, and that which is acquired together with the wife—
all such wealth is declared to be "white" (śukla) for all heirs without distinction.
That which is obtained through bribery or as a fee for a sale of what should not be sold, and that which is received from one who has performed a service, is declared to be "spotted" (śabala) wealth.
That which is acquired through backbiting, gambling, theft, receiving gifts from improper persons,
violence, or by deceit, is declared to be "black" (kṛṣṇa) wealth.
Whatever a man performs with whatever kind of material substance, he obtains a corresponding fruit both here and after death.
A householder in the stage of the domestic life (gṛhāśramin) shall perform the pākayajñas in the nuptial fire.
Viṣṇu 59.02: And the Agnihotra sacrifice [is performed] in the evening and in the morning.
One should offer oblations to the deities.
During the conjunction and separation of the moon and the sun, one should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon offerings (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
Viṣṇu 59.05: [The expiation] for a false oath is a sacrifice with an animal.
And in the autumn and summer, [one should sacrifice] with the Āgrayaṇa.
Or, according to Viṣṇu (59.07), it is when rice and barley have been cooked.
Viṣṇu 59.08: [We shall provide] more than enough for three years.
Every year, [he should sacrifice] with the Soma sacrifice.
In the absence of wealth, one should indeed perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice.
One should bestow in its entirety all the wealth obtained by begging for the sake of a sacrifice.
One should offer the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice every evening and morning.
And one should give alms to the mendicant.
By giving alms that have been honored [with respect], one obtains the fruit of the gift of a cow.
In the absence of a mendicant, one should give at least a morsel of food to cows.
Or one may throw it into the fire. Viṣṇu 59.16.
Even when food is already being eaten, one should not refuse a beggar.
The mortar and pestle, the grinding stone, the hearth, the water-jar, and the broom—these are the five slaughter-houses of the householder.
And for the sake of expiating that [sin], one should perform sacrifices to Brahman, the gods, the spirits, the ancestors, and human beings.
The study of one's own Vedic texts is the sacrifice to Brahman.
Viṣṇu 59.21: An oblation offered to the gods is the *daiva* [rite].
The libation for the ancestors (pitṛ-tarpaṇa) belongs to the Pitṛs. (Viṣṇu 59.22)
Viṣṇu 59.23: Bali is a Bhūta.
And the sacrifice to men consists of honoring guests. (Viṣṇu 59.24)
He who does not offer sustenance to these five— the deities, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself— does not truly live, even though he breathes.
The student, the ascetic, and the mendicant live by means of the householder's stage of life;
therefore, a householder should not treat these guests with contempt.
Only the householder performs sacrifice; the householder practices austerity;
and the householder gives gifts. Therefore, the one in the stage of the householder is the most excellent.
The sages, the ancestors, the gods, all beings, and likewise guests, place their hopes upon householders; therefore, the householder stage of life is the most excellent.
Having constantly practiced the pursuit of the three aims of life, the giving of food, the worship of the gods, the honoring of Brahmins, the study of one’s own Veda,
and the libations to the ancestors, a householder goes to the station of Śakra.
Viṣṇu 60.01: Having risen during the *muhūrta* of Brahmā, he should perform the voiding of urine and feces.
Viṣṇu 60.02: At night he should face south, during the day he should face north, and at the two twilights he should face both ways.
Viṣṇu 60.03: Not on ground that has not been covered.
Nor on ground ploughed by a plow. (Viṣṇu 60.04)
Nor in the shade. (Viṣṇu 60.05)
And not on saline soil.
Not on grassy ground. (Viṣṇu 60.07)
Viṣṇu 60.08: Not [in a place] containing living beings.
Not in a pit—Viṣṇu 60.09.
Nor on an anthill. (Viṣṇu 60.10)
Viṣṇu 60.11: Not on a path.
Viṣṇu 60.12: Not on a carriage road.
Viṣṇu 60.13: Nor [should one study] when another person is impure.
Not in a garden. (Viṣṇu 60.14)
Nor near a garden or water, Viṣṇu 60.15.
Not on ashes. (Viṣṇu 60.16)
Viṣṇu 60.17: Not on glowing coals.
Not on cow dung. (Viṣṇu 60.18)
Not in a cow-pen (Viṣṇu 60.19).
Not in the sky. (Viṣṇu 60.20)
Not in water. (Viṣṇu 60.21)
One should not look directly at the wind, fire, the moon, the sun, a woman, a teacher, or a Brahmin.
One should not have one's head uncovered. (Viṣṇu 60.23)

Having wiped his anus with clods of earth or bricks and holding his penis, he should rise and perform purification with water and earth drawn from a clean place until the odor and the coating of filth are removed.
One application of clay should be made on the penis, three on the anus, ten on one hand,
seven on both hands, and three on the two feet.
This is the purification for householders; it is twofold for students, threefold for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics.
Viṣṇu 61.01 Now, one should not use a tooth-stick made of *pālāśa* wood.
Nor [should one drink water] produced from the Śleṣmātaka, Ariṣṭa, Vibhītaka, Dhava, or Dhanvana trees.
Nor [should one use] that which is produced from the bandhūka, nirguṇḍī, śigru, tilva, or tinduka trees.
Nor [should one use] that which comes from the kovidāra, śamī, pīlu, pippala, iṅguda, or guggulu trees.
Viṣṇu 61.05: [One should not wear] that which is produced from the *pāribhadraka*, the *amlikā*, the *mocaka*, the *śālmalī*, or the *śaṇa*.
Viṣṇu 61.06: Not sweet.
Viṣṇu 61.07: Nor should it be sour.
Nor that which is dried above.
Viṣṇu 61.09: Nor should it have a hole.
Viṣṇu 61.10: Nor [should one eat] that which has a putrid odor.
Viṣṇu 61.11: Nor [should one eat] what is slimy.
One should not face south or west [while eating]. Viṣṇu 61.12.
And he should eat facing either northward or eastward. (Viṣṇu 61.13)
Of the *vaṭa*, *asana*, *arka*, *khadira*, *karañja*, *badara*, *sarja*, *nimba*, *arimeda*, *apāmārga*, *mālatī*, *kakubha*, and *bilva*, [one should take] any one of these.
Astringent, bitter, and pungent. (Viṣṇu 61.15)

Having become pure in the morning and restrained in speech, one should consume the tooth-cleansing twig, which is twelve finger-breadths long, as thick as the tip of the little finger, and provided with a brush-like end.
Having washed and broken it, one should carefully discard it in a clean place. One should never eat a tooth-stick on the new moon day (amāvāsyā).
Viṣṇu 62.01 Now, at the base of the pupils of the twice-born, there is a sacred site (tīrtha) named Prājāpatya.
At the base of the thumb is the region of Brahmā.
The divine [sacrifice] is performed at the tips of the fingers. (Viṣṇu 62.03)
At the base of the index finger is that of the ancestors (pitrya).

Viṣṇu 62.05: Seated in a clean place, with his knees apart, facing either east or north, with his mind fixed on that [act] and being well-disposed, he should sip water that is not heated by fire, not frothy, not poured by a Śūdra or with only one hand, and not alkaline.
One should sip water three times with the Brāhma-tīrtha.
One should wipe [the mouth] twice.
One should touch the cavities, the head, and the heart with water.
The twice-born are purified by water reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate respectively; a woman and a Śūdra are purified by water that merely touches the lips once.
Viṣṇu 63.01 Now, for the sake of acquisition and preservation (*yoga-kṣema*), one should approach the Lord.
One should not set out upon a journey alone.
Not with those who are unrighteous. (Viṣṇu 63.03)
Nor with Śūdras. (Viṣṇu 63.04)
Not by enemies, O Viṣṇu.
Not too early at dawn.
Not too late in the evening. (Viṣṇu 63.07)
Not during the two twilights.
Viṣṇu 63.09: Not at midday.
Viṣṇu 63.10: [A place] where water is not readily available.
Not too quickly. (Viṣṇu 63.11)
Nor with vehicles that are constantly ridden by children, the sick, or those who are afflicted. (Viṣṇu 63.12)
Nor with those who have missing limbs. (Viṣṇu 63.13)
Not with those who are dejected. (Viṣṇu 63.14)
Viṣṇu 63.15: Not with cows.
Not with those who are unsubdued. (Viṣṇu 63.16)
Viṣṇu 63.17: Without first providing fodder and water to his draft animals, one should not satisfy one's own hunger and thirst.
One should not stand upon a crossroads.
One should not [study] at night or at the foot of a tree.
One should not stay in an empty dwelling. (Viṣṇu 63.20)
Viṣṇu 63.21: Not even a blade of grass.
One should not [enter] a pen for tethering cattle. (Viṣṇu 63.22)
One should not [step on] hair, husks, skull-bones, bones, ashes, or charcoal. (Viṣṇu 63.23)
Viṣṇu 63.24: Not the core of cotton.
One should circumambulate the crossroads.
And [he should perform] the worship of the deity Viṣṇu (Viṣṇu 63.26).
And the well-known trees [are also to be honored]. Viṣṇu 63.27.
And [he sees] fire, a Brāhmaṇa, a courtesan, a full water-jar, a mirror, an umbrella, a banner, a flag, a śrīvṛkṣa tree, a vardhamāna vessel, and a nandyāvarta.
And [he should offer] palm-leaf fans, chowries, horses, elephants, goats, cows, curd, milk, honey, and white mustard seeds.
And [he should avoid] a lute, sandalwood, weapons, wet cow dung, fruits, flowers, fresh vegetables, gorocanā, and sprouts of dūrvā grass.
And [he gives] turbans, ornaments, jewels, gold, silver, garments, seats, vehicles, and material gifts.
Having seen a golden pitcher, a field of rich soil, a bound animal, a young maiden, and fish, one should set out on a journey—so says Viṣṇu (63.32).
Now, having seen those who are intoxicated, insane, or deformed, one should turn back.
And those who have vomited, those who have purged, those with shaven heads, those with matted hair, and dwarfs.
And those wearing saffron robes, those who have gone forth, and those who are soiled.
And oil, molasses, dried cow-dung, fuel, grass, palāśa leaves, ashes, and charcoal—Viṣṇu 63.36.
And those who are salt-dealers, eunuchs, liquor-sellers, hermaphrodites, cotton-growers, rope-makers, those bound in fetters, and those with disheveled hair.
At the time of departure, one should cause a lute, sandalwood, fresh vegetables, a turban, ornaments, and young maidens to be greeted with joy.
One should not step on the shadow of a deity, a Brahmin, a teacher, a tawny cow, or one who has been initiated for a sacrifice.
And the water used for bathing after spitting, vomiting, or voiding blood, feces, or urine. (Viṣṇu 63.40)
One should not step over a calf-rope.
One should not run while it is raining heavily.
One should not cross a river in vain.
One should not [eat] without having offered water to the deities and the ancestors.
Not with the two arms. (Viṣṇu 63.45)
Nor with a leaking boat. Viṣṇu 63.46.
One should not stand upon a riverbank.
One should not look down into a well. (Viṣṇu 63.48)
One should not transgress [this]. (Viṣṇu 63.49)
Viṣṇu 63.50a: The way must be yielded to the elderly, those carrying burdens, kings, those who have performed ritual ablutions, women, the sick, bridegrooms, and those in chariots.
Viṣṇu 63.50c: Among these, O Lord of the Earth, the king is to be honored, and the one who has performed the ablution is to be honored by the king.
Viṣṇu 64.01: One should not perform a ritual bath at watering places belonging to others.
Viṣṇu 64.02: In such an emergency, one should perform the rite after extracting five lumps of earth and [using] water.
Viṣṇu 64.03: Not when there is indigestion.
And one who is afflicted by illness [should not do so]. Viṣṇu 64.04.
Viṣṇu 64.05: Nor while naked.
Not at night. (Viṣṇu 64.06)
Viṣṇu 64.07: Except for the time of the appearance of Rāhu (eclipses).
Not during the two twilights. (Viṣṇu 64.08)
Viṣṇu 64.09: One who is habituated to the morning bath should bathe upon seeing the eastern quarter, ruddy with the dawn.
Having bathed, one should not shake one's head. (Viṣṇu 64.10)
One should not draw up water from one's limbs.
One should not touch [it] as one would oil, O Viṣṇu.
One should not wear a garment that was previously worn and has not been washed.
Having bathed, he should wear washed garments together with a turban.
One should not engage in conversation with Mlecchas, outcastes, or those who have fallen from their caste.
One should bathe in springs, divine pools, and excellent lakes. (Viṣṇu 64.16)

Water on the ground is more meritorious than water drawn up; flowing water is more meritorious than that which is stagnant; water accepted from a virtuous person is more meritorious than that; and water from the Gaṅgā is the most meritorious of all.

Having removed impurities with clay and water, and having immersed himself in the waters and sat down, he should consecrate the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, the four verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, and the verse *idam āpaḥ pravahata*. Viṣṇu 64.18.18. Having removed impurities with clay and water, and having immersed himself in the waters and sat down, he should consecrate the sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*) with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, the four verses beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, and the verse *idam āpaḥ pravahata*.
Then, submerged in water, he should mutter the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn three times.
Or [he may recite]: "That supreme abode of Viṣṇu" (Viṣṇu 64.20).
And the Drupadā and the Sāvitrī [verses]. (Viṣṇu 64.21)
Or [he may recite] the anuvāka beginning with "yuñjate manaḥ" (Viṣṇu 64.22).
Or the Puruṣasūkta, [which begins with] "Viṣṇo rarāṭam asi. (Viṣṇu 64.23)
Having bathed and while still wearing wet clothes, one should perform the libation to the gods and ancestors while remaining in the water.
If one has changed one's clothes, one should do so after having crossed over to the sacred bathing place (tīrtha).
Without having performed the libations to the gods and ancestors, one should not wring out the bathing cloth.
Having bathed and sipped water according to the rule, one should perform the ritual touching (upaspṛśet).
With the Puruṣasūkta, one should offer flowers to the Puruṣa verse by verse.
And [he should offer] handfuls of water, Viṣṇu 64.29.
At the very beginning, one should perform the libation for the gods with the *daiva* (divine) *tīrtha*.
Immediately after that, [he should offer] to the ancestors with the ancestral rite (pitrya).
There, first of all, one should perform the libation for those belonging to one's own lineage.
Then [he should perform it] for his relatives and kinsmen. (Viṣṇu 64.33)
Then, from his well-wishers... [Viṣṇu 64.34]
In this manner, one should be one who bathes daily.
And having bathed, one should recite the purificatory mantras according to one's ability.
Especially [the recitation of] the Sāvitrī. (Viṣṇu 64.37)
And the Puruṣasūkta, [as stated in] Viṣṇu 64.38.
There is nothing superior to these two.
One who has bathed becomes qualified for rites dedicated to the gods and the ancestors,
as well as for the recitation of purificatory texts and for giving gifts as prescribed by rule.
Misfortune, ill-fortune, bad dreams, and evil thoughts—these perish for one consecrated with even a mere amount of water; such is the established doctrine.
One who bathes daily does not behold the suffering of the torments of Yama;
indeed, even those men who have committed sins are purified by the daily bath.

Viṣṇu 65.01 Now, therefore, having bathed well, having thoroughly washed his hands and feet, and having sipped water according to the rules (ācamana), he should worship the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, who is without beginning or end, either in an image of the deity or on a consecrated spot.

Having given the "taking of the life-force" with the mantra "Of the Aśvins [is] the breath; those two are yours," and having performed the invocation with the hymn "They yoke the mind," he should perform a prostration with his knees, hands, and head.
One should offer the *arghya* with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
Viṣṇu 65.04: Water for the feet is offered with the four verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇā."
"May the waters of the desert be auspicious to us"—with these words, the water for sipping is offered.
"O Waters, carry away this [impurity]"—with these words, the bathing water is used.
On the chariot, on the axles, and on the horse, [one should apply] the ointment and ornaments with the mantra "vṛṣabhasya vāje" (Viṣṇu 65.07).
"Viṣṇu 65.08: 'yuvā suvāsāḥ'—with this [verse], the garment."
Regarding "puṣpāvatīḥ" (Viṣṇu 65.09), it means flowers.
"Thou art the yoke; drive away [evil]"—with these words, he offers incense.
"Thou art splendor, thou art semen"—with these words, [he offers] the lamp.
With the mantra "dadhi-krāvṇo akāriṣam," [he offers] the honey-mixture (madhuparka).
One should offer the food oblation (naivedya) with the eight verses beginning with "hiraṇyagarbha."
The fly-whisk, the fan, the measure, the umbrella, as well as the vehicle and the seat—
all that he should offer to the God with the Sāvitra mantra alone.
Having thus worshipped him, one should then recite the Puruṣa-sūkta;
and with that very [mantra], one should offer oblations of clarified butter, if one desires the eternal state.
Viṣṇu 66.01: One should not perform rites for the gods or the ancestors with water taken at night.
One should not offer an ointment that is devoid of sandalwood, musk, wood, camphor, saffron, and nutmeg.
Nor [should one wear] clothing dyed with indigo.
Viṣṇu 66.04: An ornament that is not a counterfeit of gems and gold [is not permitted].
Viṣṇu 66.05: Nor one who has a foul odor.
Viṣṇu 66.06: It is not even fragrant.
Nor that which is produced from thorns. Viṣṇu 66.07.
One should offer even that which grows on thorns, provided it is white and fragrant.
One should also offer red saffron and lotuses born in water.
One should not use any living creature for the purpose of incense.
For the purpose of a lamp, nothing at all [should be used] except ghee or oil. (Viṣṇu 66.11)
Viṣṇu 66.12: Nothing that is unfit to be eaten [should be offered] for the purpose of a food offering.
Viṣṇu 66.13: Nor even in the milk of goats or buffaloes, though it be fit for consumption.
And the flesh of five-clawed animals, fish, and boars [is forbidden].
Being self-restrained and having become pure, one should offer everything;
being focused on that [deity] and of good cheer, one should be free from haste and anger.

Viṣṇu 67.01: Then, having swept around the fire, sprinkled water around it, strewn grass around it, and poured water all around it, one should take the first portion from the cooked food and offer it as a libation.
To Viṣṇu, to Vāsudeva, to Saṃkarṣaṇa, to Pradyumna, to Aniruddha, to Puruṣa, to Satya, to Acyuta, to Vāsudeva.
Then [offerings] to Agni, Soma, Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra, Indra and Agni, the Viśvedevas, Prajāpati, Anumati, Dhanvantari, Vāstoṣpati, and to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
Then, with the remainder of the food, one should present the bali offering.
Viṣṇu 67.05: [The guilt is incurred] by means of both eating and consuming.
Viṣṇu 67.06: On all sides, to the east of the fire.
"Thou art named Ambā," "Thou art named Dulā," "Thou art named Nitantī," "Thou art named Cupuṇīkā"—thus for all of them.
"O Nandinī, O Subhagā, O Sumaṅgalī, O Bhadraṅkarī!"—thus he circumambulated his own cows, keeping them to his right.
To Viṣṇu at the pillar, to Dhruvā, to Śrī Hiraṇyakeśī, and to the lords of the forest.
Viṣṇu 67.10: At the gateway between dharma and adharma, and unto death.
To Varuṇa, at the water-vessel (uda-dhāna).
"O Viṣṇus," [he says] over the mortar.
"To the Maruts," [he offers] on the lower grinding stone.
Above, in the shelter, [one should offer] to King Vaiśravaṇa and to the spirits (bhūtas).
"To Indra and to Indra's men"—thus [one offers] in the eastern half.
"To Yama and to the messengers of Yama," [he offers] in the southern half.
"To Viṣṇu" and "to the attendants of Varuṇa"—thus [he offers] in the western half.
"To Soma, to the men of Soma"—thus [he offers] in the northern half.
"To Brahmā and to the attendants of Brahmā," [he says] in the middle.
To Ākāśa, [one should offer] upwards; (Viṣṇu 67.20)
On the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), one should offer [oblations] during the day with the words, "To the beings who roam by day."
"From those who roam at night"—thus [it is said] regarding the night.

Viṣṇu 67.23: Then, upon Darbha grass with its tips pointing south, one should perform the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) for the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, as well as for the mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother, by means of their names and lineages (*gotra*).
[With the tips pointing south] Viṣṇu 67.24: And one should present to the rice-balls unguents, flowers, incense, food offerings (*naivedya*), and so forth.
Having placed a water-pitcher nearby, one should cause a benediction to be recited.
One should offer [the food] upon the ground for dogs, crows, and outcaste dog-cookers.
And one should give alms. (Viṣṇu 67.27)
And one should exert the greatest effort in the honoring of guests.
One should diligently honor a guest who arrives in the evening. (Viṣṇu 67.29)
One should not allow an uninvited guest to stay in one's house without having been fed.
Just as the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of the social classes and as the husband is the lord of women, so is the guest the lord of the householder. (Viṣṇu 67.31)
By worshipping him, one attains heaven. (Viṣṇu 67.32)
If a guest turns away from someone's house with his hopes frustrated,
he takes away that person's merit and bestows his own demerit upon him.
A Brāhmaṇa staying for even a single night is considered a guest (atithi);
because he stays for an indefinite period, he is therefore called a guest.

One should not consider a Brahmin who is a resident of the same village, nor a mere acquaintance, to be a guest when he has arrived at one's house, whether it be where the wife resides or where the sacred fires are maintained.
But if a Kṣatriya has come to the house in the capacity of a guest, he may,
if desired, be fed even after the Brahmins have finished eating.
Even a Vaiśya or a Śūdra who have arrived at his household as guests should be fed along with his dependents, while he practices compassion toward them.
He should also, together with his wife, feed according to his ability ordinary food to others who have come to the house out of friendship and so forth.
One should feed these— those living in one's own house, a maiden, a sick woman, and likewise a pregnant woman— before the guests, without hesitation.
But that foolish man who, having failed to give to these [deities], eats first,
does not realize while eating that he is being devoured by dogs and vultures.
When the Brahmins, his own dependents, and the servants have indeed finished eating,
the husband and wife should afterwards eat what remains.
Having worshipped the gods, the ancestors, human beings, his dependents, and the household deities, the householder should thereafter eat the remains.
He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin;
for it is ordained that the food of the virtuous consists of what remains from sacrifice.
A householder does not attain such worlds through his own Vedic study, the Agnihotra sacrifice, the performance of other sacrifices, or even through asceticism as he does from honoring a guest.
Every evening and morning, one should offer a seat and water to a guest,
as well as food according to one's ability, having honored him in accordance with the prescribed rules.
By giving shelter, as well as a bed, an oil massage for the feet, and a lamp— each gift individually— one obtains a fruit equal to that of the gift of a cow.
Viṣṇu 68.01: During an eclipse of the moon or the sun, one should not eat.
Having bathed, one should eat from two vessels that have been purified.
When the two [suns] have set without being released, one should bathe and, on the following day, behold [the deity].
One should not eat during an eclipse of the moon or during an eclipse of the sun, nor when a cow or a Brāhmaṇa is eclipsed by the sun.
Nor during a calamity of the king—Viṣṇu 68.05.
When one whose *agnihotra* has been suspended considers the *agnihotra* to have been performed, then he may eat. (Viṣṇu 68.06)
When one considers the Vaiśvadeva offering also to have been performed, [then one may eat]. (Viṣṇu 68.07)
And when one considers that a festival day has been observed on the eighth day of the lunar fortnight dedicated to Viṣṇu.
And one should not eat while the previous meal is undigested.
Viṣṇu 68.10: Not at midnight.
Viṣṇu 68.11: Not during the day.
Viṣṇu 68.12: Not during the two twilights.
Nor [should one recite] while wearing wet clothes. (Viṣṇu 68.13)
Viṣṇu 68.14: One should not wear only a single garment.
Viṣṇu 68.15: Not naked.
Not in water. (Viṣṇu 68.16)
One should not sit with the knees raised.
One should not [recite] while seated on a broken seat. (Viṣṇu 68.18)
And one should not [recite] while lying on a bed.
Viṣṇu 68.20: Nor at a meal where the food is divided [into separate portions].
Viṣṇu 68.21: Not on one's lap.
Not on earth, O Viṣṇu, 68.22.
Not on the hand. (Viṣṇu 68.23)
And where one might offer salt, that one should not eat.
One should not revile children.
Viṣṇu 68.26: One person alone should not eat choice food.
Viṣṇu 68.27: [One should not eat] oil that has not been extracted.
One should not eat roasted grains during the day. (Viṣṇu 68.28)
Viṣṇu 68.29: One should not [perform] any connection with sesame seeds at night.
Viṣṇu 68.30: Nor [should one eat] barley-meal mixed with curd.
Viṣṇu 68.31: [One should not eat] the kovidāra, the vaṭa, the pippala, the śāṇa, or the śāka.
Viṣṇu 68.32: Not having given.
Viṣṇu 68.33: Not without having offered oblations.
One should not [enter] with unwashed feet. (Viṣṇu 68.34)
And neither his hands nor his face shall be moist. Viṣṇu 68.35.
And one who has not yet cleansed his mouth after eating should not take clarified butter.
One should not look at the moon, the sun, or the stars.
One should not touch the head. (Viṣṇu 68.38)
One should not recite the Veda.
One should eat facing the east. (Viṣṇu 68.40)
Or he may face the south. Viṣṇu 68.41.
Having honored the food, [one should eat]. Viṣṇu 68.42.
Viṣ�cheṣṇu 68.43: He should be cheerful in mind, wearing a garland, and anointed with unguents.
One should not consume it entirely. (Viṣṇu 68.44)
Except for curd, honey, ghee, milk, parched grain flour, and sweetmeat balls.

One should not eat together with one's wife, nor in the open air, nor likewise while standing; nor should many eat together while being watched by many others, nor should many eat together in a single place.
One should never drink water from one's cupped hands in an empty house, a fire-sanctuary, or a temple; nor should one practice overeating.
One should not eat a third meal, nor anything unwholesome under any circumstances; one should not eat too early, nor too late, nor having already eaten in the evening, should one eat in the morning.
One should not eat food that is corrupted in its nature, nor from a vessel defiled by its nature; nor while lying down, nor with feet raised, nor having placed a cloth between the knees.
Viṣṇu 69.01: On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the lunar fortnight, one should not approach a woman.
Viṣṇu 69.02: Nor after having eaten at a śrāddha.
Viṣṇu 69.03: Not having given [the gift].
Viṣṇu 69.04: One should not be invited to a śrāddha ceremony unless specifically requested.
Viṣṇu 69.05: One who observes a vow shall not [partake of it].
Viṣṇu 69.06: One who has been initiated [for a sacrifice] shall not [be so].
One should not [practice] in temples of the gods, cremation grounds, or deserted dwellings.
Nor at the roots of trees. (Viṣṇu 69.08)
Viṣṇu 69.09: Not during the day.
Viṣṇu 69.10: Not during the two twilights.
Viṣṇu 69.11: Not one who is impure.
Viṣṇu 69.12: He is not defiled.
Nor one who has anointed herself with oil (Viṣṇu 69.13).
Viṣṇu 69.14: Nor one who has anointed himself [with oil].
One should not [look at] one afflicted by disease. (Viṣṇu 69.15)
One who is afflicted by disease [is not qualified]. Viṣṇu 69.16.
One who desires to live a long life should not approach a woman who is deficient in a limb, nor one with an extra limb, nor likewise one who is older in age,
nor a woman who is pregnant.
Viṣṇu 70.01: One should not sleep with wet feet.
Viṣṇu 70.02: Nor with the head toward the north or the west.
One should not [bathe] naked. (Viṣṇu 70.03)
Viṣṇu 70.04: Not according to the lineage.
Not in the sky. (Viṣṇu 70.05)
Viṣṇu 70.06: Nor on a bed made of Palāśa wood.
Not [an image] made of the five kinds of wood. (Viṣṇu 70.07)
Viṣṇu 70.08: Not for the purpose of breaking an elephant.
Viṣṇu 70.09: Not for one killed by lightning.
Viṣṇu 70.10: Not when it is broken.
Nor on the back of a fire, O Viṣṇu.
Not [on wood] grown from a tree watered by a jar (Viṣṇu 70.12).
One should not [recite] in cremation grounds, deserted dwellings, or temples dedicated to deities.
Nor [should one sit] in the midst of the fickle.
Not in the midst of women. (Viṣṇu 70.15)
Nor [should one step] over grain, cattle, a guru, fire, or the gods.
One should not sleep while impure from food remnants, nor during the day, nor during the two twilights, nor on ashes;
nor in an unclean place, nor on damp ground, nor on the peak of a mountain.
Viṣṇu 71.01: Now, one should not despise anyone whatsoever.
And one should not mock those with missing or extra limbs, the foolish, or those destitute of wealth.
One should not serve those who are inferior. (Viṣṇu 71.03)
One should not perform any action that is contrary to one's own study of the Vedas.
Viṣṇu 71.05: One should adopt an attire appropriate to one's age.
Of learning, noble lineage, wealth, and country—Viṣṇu 71.06.
Viṣṇu 71.07: He should not be arrogant.
Viṣṇu 71.08: He should constantly consult the scriptures and other such sources.
When one possesses wealth, one should not wear worn-out or dirty clothes.
One should not speak thus: "It does not exist. (Viṣṇu 71.10)
One should not wear a garland that is scentless, foul-smelling, or red. (Viṣṇu 71.11)
One should carry even a red lotus.
And a staff made of bamboo. (Viṣṇu 71.13)
And a water-pot containing water. Viṣṇu 71.14.
Viṣṇu 71.15: The sacred thread shall be made of cotton.
And two earrings made of gold. (Viṣṇu 71.16)
One should not look at the rising sun. (Viṣṇu 71.17)
One should not look at the sun as it is setting. (Viṣṇu 71.18)
Nor [should one eat] that which is covered by a garment. (Viṣṇu 71.19)
Nor [should one look at his reflection] situated in a mirror or in the middle of water.
Viṣṇu 71.21: Not at midday.
One should not look at the face of an angry teacher. (Viṣṇu 71.22)
Viṣṇu 71.23: Nor one's own reflection in oil or water.
Not in a mirror that is dirty. (Viṣṇu 71.24)
One should not address one's wife by name at the time of eating. (Viṣṇu 71.25)
One should not look at a naked woman. (Viṣṇu 71.26)
Viṣṇu 71.27: Nor [should one look at] anyone who is urinating.
And one should not look at an elephant that has broken loose from its tethering post.
And one who is situated in an unfavorable position should not engage in a fight with a bull or similar animals.
Nor one who is insane. Viṣṇu 71.30.
Viṣṇu 71.31: Not from one who is intoxicated.
One should not throw impure substances into the fire.
Viṣṇu 71.33: Not blood.
Viṣṇu 71.34: Not poison.
Viṣṇu 71.35: Also [the same applies] to water.
One should not step over fire.
One should not warm one's feet [over a fire]. Viṣṇu 71.37.
One should not wipe oneself on *kuśa* grass.
One should not wash [the teeth] in a vessel made of bell-metal.
One should not place one foot upon the other.
One should not draw the earth.
One should not crush clods of earth. (Viṣṇu 71.42)
One should not be a cutter of grass. (Viṣṇu 71.43)
One should not cut one's nails or hair with the teeth.
And one should avoid gambling. (Viṣṇu 71.45)
Like the exposure to the morning sun. Viṣṇu 71.46.
Viṣṇu 71.47: One should not wear garments, sandals, garlands, or sacred threads that have been worn by another.
One should not impart sacred knowledge to a Śūdra. (Viṣṇu 71.48)
Viṣṇu 71.49: Neither leavings nor sacrificial offerings [should be eaten].
Viṣṇu 71.50: Nor sesame seeds.
And one should not teach him the Dharma.
Viṣṇu 71.52: It is not a vow.
One should not scratch one's head or belly with both hands joined together.
One should not refuse curd or flowers.
One should not pull at one's own garland. (Viṣṇu 71.55)
One should not awaken one who is asleep. (Viṣṇu 71.56)
One should not cause one who is attached to become dispassionate.
One should not speak to a woman in her courses.
Viṣṇu 71.59: [One should not look at] Mlecchas or those born of the lowest castes.
In the presence of the god Agni and a Brāhmaṇa, one should raise the right hand.
One should not point out a cow grazing in another's field. (Viṣṇu 71.61)
One should not drink while the calf is drinking. (Viṣṇu 71.62)
One should not cause those who are not haughty to exult.
One should not dwell in a kingdom ruled by a Śūdra.
Not in a place crowded with unrighteous people. (Viṣṇu 71.65)
One should not dwell with one who is devoid of a physician. *Viṣṇu* 71.66.
Viṣṇu 71.67: Not when it has been defiled.
Nor for long on a mountain—Viṣṇu 71.68.
One should not engage in futile exertion. (Viṣṇu 71.69)
Viṣṇu 71.70: [One should not eat] while dancing or singing.
Viṣṇu 71.71: One should not crack one's fingers.
One should not utter anything indecorous. (Viṣṇu 71.72)
Viṣṇu 71.73: Not untruth.
Viṣṇu 71.74: Not what is unpleasant.
One should not touch anyone on a vital spot.
One who desires to live a long life should not despise oneself.
One should perform the twilight worship for a long time. (Viṣṇu 71.77)
One should not play with snakes or weapons. (Viṣṇu 71.78)
One should not touch the bodily apertures without a specific cause. (Viṣṇu 71.79)
One should not raise a staff against another. (Viṣṇu 71.80)
One should strike one who is to be punished for the purpose of correction.
One should strike him on the back with a bamboo leaf or with a rope. (Viṣṇu 71.82)
One should avoid reviling gods, Brahmins, the scriptures, and those of great soul.
And wealth and pleasure that are contrary to righteousness [are not to be pursued]. Viṣṇu 71.84.
And even dharma that is loathed by the world [should not be practiced]. Viṣṇu 71.85.
And on the festival days (parvan), one should perform propitiatory fire-offerings (śānti-homa).
One should not cut even a blade of grass.
And he should remain adorned.
Thus one should be a practitioner of right conduct.
One who desires righteousness and has conquered his senses should practice that conduct which is declared in the Śruti and Smṛti, is consistent with dharma, and is practiced by the virtuous.
Through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct, the desired goal;
through right conduct, imperishable wealth; and through right conduct, one destroys inauspicious marks.
Even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks, the man who possesses good conduct,
is endowed with faith, and is free from malice, lives for a hundred years.
Viṣṇu 72.01: One should abide with self-restraint and self-control.
And the restraint of the senses is proclaimed as *dama*. Viṣṇu 72.02.
O Viṣṇu, this world and the next belong to the self-controlled.
Viṣṇu 72.04: No ritual action whatsoever succeeds for one who is not self-controlled.
Self-restraint is the supreme purifier; self-restraint is the supreme auspiciousness. Through self-restraint, one obtains everything that one desires in the mind.
If the horses do not carry away that chariot which travels with five [horses] yoked to it, moving at the speed of thought along the noble path,
then enemies shall likewise not overcome him who has gone thus.
Just as the waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet remains established in stillness, even so all desires enter him; he attains peace, but not the one who hankers after desires.
Viṣṇu 73.01 Now, one who desires to perform a Śrāddha should invite the Brāhmaṇas on the day before.

On the second day, during the forenoon of the bright fortnight or the afternoon of the dark fortnight, he should cause the Brahmins—who have bathed well and performed the ritual sipping of water—to sit upon seats covered with Kuśa grass, arranged from the north, according to their seniority in age.
Two for the gods facing east, and three for the ancestors facing north.
Viṣṇu 73.04: "One [offering] for each, or one for both."
In the case of *āma-śrāddhas* and those performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), one should offer oblations into the fire using the first pentad of verses dedicated to Viṣṇu.
In the animal *śrāddhas*, [one should perform it] with the middle five [fingers].
Viṣṇu 73.07: On new moon days, by means of the excellent group of five.
After the full moon of Āgrahāyaṇī, during the Kṛṣṇa-aṣṭakās, one should perform [the rites] respectively with the first, middle, and highest groups of five [days].
And also on each successive Aṣṭakā day, Viṣṇu 73.09.
Then, having been authorized by the Brahmins, he should invoke the ancestors.
Having performed the dismissal of the Yātudhānas with sesame seeds while reciting the two verses beginning with "apayantu asurāḥ" (Viṣṇu 73.11), [he should proceed].

"Viṣṇu 73.12: Having performed the invocation with the mantra, 'Come hither, O all you ancestors; may they come first to me; this is for you, O ancestors,' and having offered water for the feet mixed with *kuśa* grass and sesame seeds, reciting the mantras 'Yās tiṣṭhanti amṛtā vāk' and 'Yan me mātā'; and having prepared and offered the *arghya*, applied the unguent, and honored the Brahmins according to his ability with *kuśa* grass, sesame seeds, garments, flowers, ornaments, incense, and lamps; then, taking food soaked in ghee, [he says]: 'O Ādityas, Rudras, Vasus...'"
Having observed this and said, "I shall perform [the rite] in the fire," and having been told by the Brahmins, "Do so," he should offer three oblations.

Having performed the consecration of the oblation with the mantras, "O my ancestors, this is for you, O ancestors, this is the sacrifice," he should first present the food to those facing east with the words, "Salutation to all the gods (viśvebhyo devebhyaḥ)," placing it especially in vessels made of silver or whatever else is available.
To the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, by name and lineage, [he offers] to those facing north.
While the Brahmins are eating that [food], he should mutter: "Whatever [sin] I have committed through excess day and night, O you who devour raw flesh. (Viṣṇu 73.15)
And the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and Dharmaśāstras—thus [it is said]. (Viṣṇu 73.16)
Viṣṇu 73.17: Near the remnants of the food, upon *kuśa* grass with the tips pointing southward, he should place one *piṇḍa* for the father, reciting: "The earth is an inexhaustible ladle."
"Antarikṣaṃ darvir akṣitā" (The atmosphere is the imperishable ladle)—with these words, he offers the second pinda to the grandfather.
"dyaur darvir akṣitā" (the sky is the inexhaustible ladle)—with this third [verse], [he offers] to the great-grandfather.
Viṣṇu 73.20: "To those ancestors who have passed away here," thus [saying], a garment should be given.
"O Fathers, provide food for the hero"—with these words, he offers the food.
"O ancestors, rejoice here according to your respective portions"—with these words, one rubs the hands at the base of the *darbha* grass.

Having performed the scattering of water around the *piṇḍas* clockwise while reciting the verse beginning with "ūrjaṃ vahantīḥ," he should present the *argha*, flowers, incense, ointments, food, and other kinds of eatables and edibles.
And a water-vessel joined with honey, clarified butter, and sesame seeds. (Viṣṇu 73.24)

When the Brahmins have eaten and reached satiety, he should sprinkle food along with grass, saying, "May it not be exhausted for me," and place the scattered remnants of food before the leftovers. Having asked, "Are you satisfied? and "Is it well-prepared?", he should first give water for sipping (ācamana) to those facing north, then to those facing east. Then, having sprinkled the site of the Śrāddha with the words, "It is well-sprinkled," he should perform everything while holding Darbha grass in his hand.

Then, having circumambulated [the deity] from the front while facing east, saying "O Rāma, that which is mine," and having returned, he should honor [the guests] with sacrificial fees according to his capacity; then, having said, "May you be pleased," and when they have replied, "We are pleased," he should mutter the mantra: "The gods and the ancestors."

Having offered the water for the inexhaustible [libation] (akṣayyodaka) by means of the names and lineages [of the ancestors], he should then, with palms joined and mind focused on that, request with a well-disposed heart from those facing east: "May the Viśvedevas be pleased."
"May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give."
"Let it be so," they should say. (Viṣṇu 73.29)
May our food be abundant, and may we receive guests;
may there be those who ask of us, and may we never have to ask anything of anyone.
Having received these blessings with the two verses beginning with "Viṣṇu" (73.31).
Then, with the mantra "vāje vāje," he should dismiss the Brāhmaṇas,
having honored them according to the rule, followed them, and saluted them.

Viṣṇu 74.01: Having performed the Śrāddha on the Aṣṭakās preceded by offerings to the gods with vegetables, meat, and cakes, and having offered oblations into the fire on the Anvaṣṭakās as on the Aṣṭakās, one should likewise feed the Brāhmaṇas for the mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother, preceded by offerings to the gods; then, having honored them with sacrificial fees and followed them [as they depart], one should dismiss them.
Then, one should construct trenches.
At its base, having performed the kindling of the fires in the east, north, and southeast, the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) is made.
At the base of the three furrows for the males; at the base of the three furrows for the females.
Viṣṇu 74.05: One should fill the three pits for the person with water mixed with food.
Viṣṇu 74.06: [He should offer] three furrows for women, with food and milk.
With curd, meat, and milk, one should [fill] three pits respectively.
Having filled [the vessel], one should recite this: "May this be inexhaustible for you, O sirs, and for you, O ladies."
Viṣṇu 75.01: If one should perform a śrāddha while his father is still living, he should perform it for those for whom his father would have performed it.
O Viṣṇu, those whose grandfather is living while both their father and paternal grandfather are still alive [should perform the Śrāddha].
Viṣṇu 75.03: While one's father, grandfather, and great-grandfather are living, one must not perform [the śrāddha].
Viṣṇu 75.04: He whose father is deceased should, having placed a rice-ball (piṇḍa) for his father, offer [rice-balls] to the two ancestors beyond the grandfather.
Viṣṇu 75.05: He whose father and grandfather are deceased should, having offered two rice-balls (piṇḍas) to them, offer [one] to his great-grandfather.
If one's grandfather has become a *preta*, he should offer a *piṇḍa* to him and then give two *piṇḍas* beyond the great-grandfather.

In the same manner, a wise man should perform the Śrāddha for his maternal grandfathers as well; according to the rule, he should do so with modifications of the mantras, while for the remaining ancestors it is performed without mantras.

Viṣṇu 76.01: The three new-moon days, the three Aṣṭakās, the three Anvaṣṭakās, the full moon of Māgha, the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada, the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight following that, and the times of the ripening of rice and barley.
Prajāpati has declared these times for the Śrāddha to be obligatory;
one who does not perform the Śrāddha on these occasions falls into hell.
Viṣṇu 77: The Transit of the Sun.
Viṣṇu 77.02: The two equinoxes.
Viṣṇu specifically [ordains this] for the two solstices.
Viṣṇu 77.04: Vyatīpāta.
The birth constellation of Viṣṇu is Śravaṇā.
And there is prosperity, O Viṣṇu.
Prajāpati has declared these to be the optional times for the Śrāddha;
whatever Śrāddha is offered during these occasions leads to infinite results.
A wise person should certainly not perform a Śrāddha during the two twilights or at night; however, it may be performed even during those times if there is an eclipse of the moon.
For a Śrāddha offered at the time of the appearance of Rāhu remains as long as the moon and stars;
endowed with all virtues, it reaches the ancestors and fulfills every desire.
Viṣṇu 78.01: One who constantly performs a śrāddha on a Sunday attains good health.
Good fortune is attained under Viṣṇu and the Moon.
On a Tuesday, there is victory in battle through Viṣṇu.
Viṣṇu 78.04: All desires [are fulfilled] on a Wednesday.
Viṣṇu 78.05: [One obtains] the desired knowledge in the Jaiva [mantra].
In the asterism of Śukra (Anurādhā), there is wealth. Viṣṇu 78.06.
Life is [long] under Śanaiścara (Saturn). Viṣṇu 78.07.
Viṣṇu 78.08: [One attains] heaven under the Kṛttikās.
Viṣṇu 78.09: Offspring [is obtained] through the Rohiṇīs.
The *brahmavarcasya* [oblation] is in the north. (Viṣṇu 78.10)
Viṣṇu 78.11: Success in ritual action is attained through the Raudra [mudrā].
Viṣṇu 78.12: [One should give] land under the asterism Punarvasu.
One should perform the rite for nourishment under the Puṣya asterism.
Viṣṇu 78.14: [One attains] prosperity in the presence of serpents.
Viṣṇu 78.15: All desires [are fulfilled] at the rite for the ancestors.
In the case of *bhāgya*, [the word] *saubhāgya* [is substituted]. (Viṣṇu 78.16)
Viṣṇu 78.17: [The word] "dhanam" is used in the sense of "bringing forth."
Viṣṇu 78.18: The preeminence among kinsmen is in the hand.
From Viṣṇu, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, [were born] handsome sons.
Success in trade is attained under Svāti.
Gold [should be given] under the asterism Viśākhā.
Viṣṇu 78.22: Friends [should be honored] with friendliness.
Viṣṇu 78.23: Sovereignty [is attained] in the realm of Śakra.
Viṣṇu 78.24: [The penance for] agriculture is at the root [of the offense].
Success in sea-voyage is attained in the sign of Aquarius (Āpya).
Viṣṇu 78.26: Indeed, all desires [are fulfilled] through the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
Viṣṇu 78.27: Preeminence is attained through the Abhijit [nakṣatra].
Viṣṇu 78.28: All desires [are fulfilled] by hearing [this].
Or salt for Vāsava (Viṣṇu 78.29).
In the western quarter, there is health. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 78.30)
Viṣṇu 78.31: In a sacrifice, base metal is [the fee].
Viṣṇu 78.32: A house-rat [is inauspicious] when it enters from below.
One should give cows under the asterism of Puṣya.
In the month of Āśvina, [one should offer] horses to Viṣṇu. (Viṣṇu 78.34)
Life [is gained] in the southern quarter of Viṣṇu.
On the first lunar day (pratipad), beautiful women come to one's house. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 78.36)
On the second [tithi], one should worship Kanyā, the giver of boons, according to the Viṣṇudharmottara 78.37.
Viṣṇu 78.38: On the third lunar day, one obtains all desires.
On the fourth day, one should offer animals to Viṣṇu.
On the fifth [lunar day], one obtains handsome sons. (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 78.40)
On the sixth day, there is victory in gambling. (Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa 78.41)
Agriculture [should be undertaken] on the seventh lunar day. (Viṣṇu 78.42)
Trade on the eighth day [is forbidden], according to Viṣṇu 78.43.
On the ninth day, one should offer animals to Viṣṇu.
On the tenth day, [the offering is] for the Vājins.
On the eleventh lunar day, one obtains sons endowed with spiritual luster. (Viṣṇu 78.46)
Viṣṇu 78.47: [The gift of] gold and silver on the twelfth day.
Viṣṇu 78.48: On the thirteenth lunar day, there is good fortune.
Viṣṇu 78.49: On the fifteenth day [of the lunar fortnight], one obtains all desires.
For those killed by weapons, the fourteenth day is prescribed for the performance of the śrāddha rite.
Furthermore, there are two verses sung by the ancestors: Viṣṇu 78.51: "There are also two verses sung by the ancestors."
"May there arise in our lineage some preeminent man who,
with a concentrated mind, [worships] during the rainy season, in the dark fortnight, on the thirteenth day."
He who performs a *śrāddha* with honey-sweetened milk-rice (*pāyasa*) throughout the entire month of Kārttika, or during the time when the shadow of an elephant falls toward the east; Viṣṇu 78.53.
Viṣṇu 79.01 Now, one should not perform a śrāddha with water taken at night.
Viṣṇu 79.02: In the absence of *kuśa* grass, one should offer *kāśa* or *dūrvā* grass in place of *kuśa*.
For the purpose of clothing, thread made from cotton is used.
One should discard the [worn] state even if it arises from unwashed cloth. (Viṣṇu 79.04)
Viṣṇu 79.05: Flowers that have a pungent odor, those that are odorless, and those produced from thorny plants [are not to be used].
One should offer white, fragrant flowers—even those grown on thorny plants—as well as red flowers that grow in water.
One should not offer fat or marrow for the purpose of a lamp.
Viṣṇu 79.08: He should offer clarified butter or oil.
One should not offer anything produced from living beings for the purpose of incense.
One should offer guggulu mixed with honey and clarified butter.
Viṣṇu 79.11: Sandalwood, saffron, camphor, agallochum, and padmaka are for the purpose of unguents.
One should not give salt that is visible [to the recipient]. Viṣṇu 79.12.
And with his hand, [he offers] ghee, side-dishes, and so forth. (Viṣṇu 79.13)
One should give vessels made of metal.
Especially those made of silver, O Viṣṇu. (Viṣṇu 79.15)
One should place a sword, a kutapa blanket, a black antelope skin, sesame seeds, white mustard seeds, and unbroken grains—these being purifying and destructive of demons.

Viṣṇu 79.17: One should avoid long pepper (pippalī), mukundaka, bhūstṛṇa, drumstick tree (śigru), mustard (sarṣapa), surasā, sarjaka, suvarcala, pumpkin (kūśmāṇḍa), bottle gourd (alābu), eggplant (vārtāka), pālakyā, upodakī, taṇḍulīyaka, safflower (kusumbha), piṇḍāluka, and the milk of a buffalo (mahiṣī-kṣīra).
Viṣṇu 79.18: And black gram, lentils, food that has stood overnight, and prepared salt.
One should avoid anger. (Viṣṇu 79.19)
One should not shed tears.
One should not act with haste. (Viṣṇu 79.21)
Viṣṇu 79.22: For the gift of ghee and other substances, vessels made of precious metals, swords as vessels, and vessels of inferior metal are recommended.
And on this point, there is a verse: Viṣṇu 79.23.
A gift given with vessels made of gold or silver, or with a sword, or with one made of udumbara wood, or even with a vessel of common metal, attains imperishability.

Viṣṇu 80.01: With sesame seeds, rice, barley, mung beans, water, roots, fruits, vegetables, śyāmāka grain, priyaṅgu, nīvāra, and mung beans, as well as wheat, [the ancestors] are gratified for one month.
For two months, [one should subsist] on fish meat.
Viṣṇu 80.03: [One should offer] three [oblations] with the meat of a deer.
And one who is cunning [is overcome] by means of a ram. Viṣṇu 80.04.
Viṣṇu 80.05: [The rite] with the five [offerings] is performed with the Śākuna [sāman].
Viṣṇu 80.06: Six [cows] for a goat.
Viṣṇu 80.07: [One remains] seven times in the Raurava hell.
Viṣṇu 80.08: Eight [elephants] with spotted sides.
Viṣṇu 80.09: [One becomes pure] by means of nine cow-products.
Viṣṇu 80.10: Ten [cows] for a buffalo sacrifice.
Viṣṇu 80.11: But with a hornless goat, [the sacrifice is] elevenfold.
For one year, he should subsist on cow's milk or its derivatives.
Regarding this, there is a verse sung by the ancestors:
Kālaśāka, mahāśalka, and the meat of the vārdhrīṇasa,
as well as rhinoceroses that are devoid of horns— we shall eat these until the sun's end.
One should not place food upon a seat.
One should not touch Viṣṇu with one's foot.
One should not cause a sneeze to occur [upon the image of] Viṣṇu.
One should drive away the malevolent spirits (yātudhānas) with sesame seeds or mustard seeds.
And when it has been covered, one should perform the śrāddha.
One should not look at a woman in her menses.
Nor a dog, O Viṣṇu.
Not a village pig (Viṣṇu 81.08).
Nor [should one eat] a village cock.
One should diligently cause the Śrāddha for the Unborn One to be presented.
And the Brāhmaṇas should eat while restraining their speech.
Nor [should one eat] with the head wrapped [in a cloth]. (Viṣṇu 81.12)
Viṣṇu 81.13: Nor [should they enter] wearing sandals.
Viṣṇu 81.14: [The feet of the image] shall not rest upon a pedestal.
Neither those with missing limbs nor those with extra limbs should look upon the śrāddha.
Śūdras [are not entitled to this]. Viṣṇu 81.16.
Viṣṇu 81.17: They are not outcasts.
Not for those who are chronically ill. (Viṣṇu 81.18)
At that time, he should honor a Brahmin or a mendicant with the permission of the Brahmins.
O Viṣṇu, when asked by the donor, the Brāhmaṇas should not speak of the qualities of the sacrificial offering.
As long as there is steam from the food, as long as those who eat remain silent,
and as long as the qualities of the sacrificial offering have not been described, so long do the ancestors eat.
Having collected food of all kinds and sprinkled it with water,
one should cast it upon the ground before those who have finished eating, scattering it about.
For those who have died without the sacraments, for those who have abandoned their families, and for women of the household,
the portion of the leavings and whatever scattering of food is upon the *darbha* grass shall be their share.

The remnants of food that have fallen upon the ground at a funeral rite for the ancestors are declared to be the allotted share for the group of slaves belonging to one who is neither crooked nor deceitful.
Viṣṇu 82.01: In a rite for the gods, one should not examine a Brāhmaṇa.
One should examine [the recipient] with great care at a rite for the ancestors.
One should avoid those who have missing or extra limbs. (Viṣṇu 82.03)
And those who persist in improper actions, [he should punish].
Viṣṇu 82.05: [One should avoid] those who observe the "cat-vow" (baiḍāla-vratika).
Viṣṇu 82.06: Those who wear the marks of asceticism in vain.
Those who subsist by means of the lunar mansions (nakṣatra). Viṣṇu 82.07.
And [he should avoid] those who serve the gods for a livelihood.
Viṣṇu 82.09: [He should avoid] physicians.
The sons of unmarried women. (Viṣṇu 82.10)
Viṣṇu 82.11: His sons.
Viṣṇu 82.12: Those who perform many sacrifices.
82.13 Those who officiate as priests for an entire village.
Viṣṇu 82.14: Those who perform sacrifices for Śūdras.
Viṣṇu 82.15: [The sin of] one who performs sacrifices for those for whom it is forbidden to sacrifice.
The Vrātyas, Viṣṇu 82.16.
Viṣṇu 82.17: [The same applies] to those who sacrifice for him.
Viṣṇu 82.18: [He should punish] those who cause harm at the beginning of a festival.
Viṣṇu 82.19: [He should punish] informers.
And those who teach for a wage (Viṣṇu 82.20).
Those taught by hired teachers (Viṣṇu 82.21).
Those nourished by the food of a Śūdra. (Viṣṇu 82.22)
From association with those who have fallen [from their caste], Viṣṇu 82.23.
Viṣṇu 82.24: [Those] who do not study.
Those who have fallen away from the worship of the twilights (Viṣṇu 82.25).
Viṣṇu 82.26: [The duties toward] royal servants.
Viṣṇu 82.27: [One should not look at] those who are naked.
Viṣṇu 82.28: [Those who are] disputing with their father.
And those who abandon their father, mother, teacher, the sacred fire, or their own Vedic study.
For these have been declared to be outcasts among Brāhmaṇas, defilers of the assembly;
a wise man should carefully avoid them at the performance of a Śrāddha rite.
Viṣṇu 83.01 Now, those who purify the company (paṅktipāvanas).
Viṣṇu 83.02: One who has thrice performed the Nāciketa fire-sacrifice.
Viṣṇu 83.03: [He who maintains] the five fires.
Viṣṇu 83.04: One who chants the Jyeṣṭhasāman.
Viṣṇu 83.05: One who has reached the further shore of the Vedas.
Viṣṇu 83.06: He has also mastered one entire limb of the Veda.
Viṣṇu was one who had reached the further shore of the Purāṇas, the Itihāsas, and Grammar.
Viṣṇu 83.08: He is also one who has reached the further shore of the entire Dharmaśāstra.
Viṣṇu 83.09: Purified by the holy ford (tīrtha).
Viṣṇu 83.10: Purified by sacrifice.
Viṣṇu 83.11: Purified by austerity.
Viṣṇu 83.12: Purified by truth.
Viṣṇu 83.13: Purified by mantras.
Viṣṇu 83.14: Devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī.
Viṣṇu 83.15: The lineage of that which has been given as a brahmadeya.
Viṣṇu 83.16: The Trisuparṇa.
Viṣṇu 83.17: A son-in-law.
And a daughter’s son is also a worthy recipient.
And especially so for the yogins. (Viṣṇu 83.19)
In this regard, there is a verse sung by the ancestors (*pitṛ-gītā*): [Viṣṇu 83.20]
May he also be born in our lineage who,
with great effort, would feed a yogi— a brahmin— at a *śrāddha*, by which we ourselves are satisfied.
Viṣṇu 84.01: One should not perform a Śrāddha rite in a region inhabited by Mlecchas.
Viṣṇu 84.02: One should not go to the territory of the Mlecchas.
"Having drunk water at the drinking-troughs of others, one attains equality with them," so says Viṣṇu (84.03).
That country in which the establishment of the fourfold social order (cāturvarṇya) does not exist is to be known as a Mleccha country; beyond that is Āryāvarta.
Viṣṇu 85.01 Now, at Puṣkara, the Śrāddha is inexhaustible.
Viṣṇu 85.02: Recitation, burnt offerings, and austerities.
Viṣṇu 85.03: By merely bathing at Puṣkara, one becomes purified from all sins.
In this very same way, it is at Gayāśīrṣa.
Viṣṇu 85.05: At a banyan tree.
Viṣṇu [resides] on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka.
Viṣṇu [is worshipped] at Varāha-parvata.
Viṣṇu 85.08: anywhere whatsoever on the bank of the Narmadā.
Viṣṇu, on the bank of the Yamunā.
Especially at the Gaṅgā, [as stated in] Viṣṇu 85.10.
Viṣṇu 85.11 at Kuśāvarta.
Viṣṇu 85.12: [This applies] to the *bindu*.
